atom:entry.atom:title: Restart-Safe Stream Jobs: Checkpoints and Idempotent Writes
atom:entry.atom:summary: How to make a containerised stream-processing job survive restarts without duplicates or lost work, with a runnable Java sketch.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Stream jobs are different from stateless APIs. They carry progress, they read from an offset, and they have to pick up cleanly after a restart. In a container platform, restarts are routine, not exceptional. If a restart changes your output, the job does not really own its state. Two ideas fix most of this: store progress outside the process, and make every write safe to repeat.

Options and trade-offs

  • Keep progress in memory: fast, and all progress is lost on restart.
  • Checkpoint after every record: safest, but the overhead can dominate.
  • Checkpoint on a bounded interval and make writes idempotent: a crash replays a little work, and the replay changes nothing.

My recommendation

Write idempotent upserts keyed by a stable record ID, store the checkpoint atomically, and on startup resume from the last checkpoint. Treat exactly-once as a goal you approach by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent effects.

Worked example

The sketch below has no dependencies. It simulates a crash in the middle of a run, then restarts from the checkpoint. The replayed records are written again, but the output does not change.

import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.*;

public class IdempotentJob {

    record Event(String id, long offset, String value) { }

    static final Path CHECKPOINT = Path.of("checkpoint.txt");
    static final Map<String, String> sink = new TreeMap<>();   // upsert by id

    static long readCheckpoint() throws IOException {
        return Files.exists(CHECKPOINT) ? Long.parseLong(Files.readString(CHECKPOINT).strip()) : 0L;
    }

    static void writeCheckpoint(long offset) throws IOException {
        Path tmp = Path.of("checkpoint.tmp");
        Files.writeString(tmp, Long.toString(offset));
        Files.move(tmp, CHECKPOINT, StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE, StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);
    }

    static void run(List<Event> source, long crashAfterOffset) throws IOException {
        long start = readCheckpoint();
        int sinceCheckpoint = 0;
        for (Event e : source) {
            if (e.offset() < start) continue;
            sink.put(e.id(), e.value());                 // idempotent: same key, same value
            if (++sinceCheckpoint == 5) {
                writeCheckpoint(e.offset() + 1);
                sinceCheckpoint = 0;
            }
            if (e.offset() == crashAfterOffset) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("simulated crash at offset " + e.offset());
            }
        }
        writeCheckpoint(source.size());
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Files.deleteIfExists(CHECKPOINT);
        List<Event> source = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) source.add(new Event("evt-" + i, i, "value-" + i));

        try {
            run(source, 7);                              // crashes mid-run
        } catch (IllegalStateException crash) {
            System.out.println(crash.getMessage() + ", resuming from " + readCheckpoint());
        }
        run(source, -1);                                 // restart: replays 5..7, then finishes
        System.out.println("records in sink = " + sink.size());   // 20, not 23
    }
}

In a container, the checkpoint file would live on a volume or, better, in an external store, so it survives the container being replaced. The same idea applies when the source is a message broker with committed offsets and the sink supports upserts or transactions.

Checklist

  1. Persist progress outside the container.
  2. Write the checkpoint atomically, so a crash never leaves it half-written.
  3. Key writes by a stable ID, and make repeating them harmless.
  4. On startup, read the checkpoint and resume, and log what you recovered without logging payloads.
  5. Pace catch-up after an outage with bounded batches and concurrency.
  6. Test by killing the process mid-run and comparing the output with an uninterrupted run.

Where this doesn't apply

This sketch is single-threaded with an in-memory sink, to show the mechanics. Real jobs also need partitioning, ordering guarantees per key, and a sink that is itself durable.

One honest limitation

Idempotency limits what a write can be. Operations like incrementing a counter are not safe to repeat, so they need a composite key, a version, or a transactional sink to be handled correctly.

Sources

  • Apache Kafka Documentation: Message delivery semantics
  • Oracle Java Documentation: java.nio.file.Files.move (atomic move)
  • Docker Docs: Volumes

atom:entry.atom:title: API Evolution: Keep Wire Contracts Stable for Java Clients
atom:entry.atom:summary: Tolerant readers, batch error handling, and golden-file tests
atom:entry.atom:content:
What counts as the contract

  • Field names, types, and optionality.
  • HTTP status codes and which situations produce them.
  • The error envelope: its fields and their meaning.
  • Batch semantics: partial failures, ordering, and duplicates.
  • Behavior when a request omits optional parameters, such as projections.

Be a tolerant reader

import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonIgnoreProperties;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.JsonNode;

@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)
public record ErrorEnvelope(int status, String message, String code, JsonNode errorDetails) {

    public ErrorEnvelope {
        message = message == null ? "" : message;
    }
}
  • ignoreUnknown = true protects you from new server fields.
  • errorDetails stays a raw JsonNode. If the server's details are free-form, do not force them into a fixed class. Keep them untyped, and let the caller interpret them.
  • Missing message becomes an empty string, so downstream code does not need null checks.

Classify errors in one place

public enum ErrorKind { CLIENT_ERROR, NOT_FOUND, UNPROCESSABLE, SERVER_ERROR, UNKNOWN }

public static ErrorKind classify(int status) {
    if (status == 404) return ErrorKind.NOT_FOUND;
    if (status == 422) return ErrorKind.UNPROCESSABLE;
    if (status >= 400 && status < 500) return ErrorKind.CLIENT_ERROR;
    if (status >= 500 && status < 600) return ErrorKind.SERVER_ERROR;
    return ErrorKind.UNKNOWN;
}

Handle batch responses carefully

public static <V> BatchOutcome<V> split(Map<String, V> results, Map<String, ErrorEnvelope> errors) {
    Map<String, V> ok = new LinkedHashMap<>(results);
    Map<String, ErrorKind> failed = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    errors.forEach((id, env) -> {
        ok.remove(id);
        failed.put(id, classify(env.status()));
    });
    return new BatchOutcome<>(ok, failed);
}

public record BatchOutcome<V>(Map<String, V> succeeded, Map<String, ErrorKind> failed) { }

Server-side rules for safe evolution

  • Add fields as optional. Never remove or repurpose a field without a deprecation period.
  • Do not change status codes for existing situations.
  • Do not change the shape of the error envelope. Add to it instead.
  • Be careful with requests that send no projection or field selection. Defaults are part of the contract.
  • Version deliberately when you must break something, and announce it.

Golden-file tests

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

class ErrorEnvelopeTest {

    private final ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper();

    @Test
    void parsesCurrentShape() throws Exception {
        String json = """
            {"status":422,"message":"invalid","code":"VALIDATION","errorDetails":{"field":"email"}}
            """;
        ErrorEnvelope env = mapper.readValue(json, ErrorEnvelope.class);
        assertEquals(422, env.status());
        assertEquals("email", env.errorDetails().get("field").asText());
    }

    @Test
    void ignoresFieldsAddedLater() throws Exception {
        String json = """
            {"status":404,"message":"gone","futureField":{"x":1}}
            """;
        assertEquals(404, mapper.readValue(json, ErrorEnvelope.class).status());
    }

    @Test
    void missingOptionalFieldsDoNotFail() throws Exception {
        ErrorEnvelope env = mapper.readValue("{\"status\":500}", ErrorEnvelope.class);
        assertEquals("", env.message());
        assertNull(env.code());
    }
}

Failure modes

  • A status change (for example 400 to 422) with no announcement.
  • A strict client parser that rejects new fields.
  • Error details forced into a typed structure that drops data.
  • Batch handlers that fail the whole batch or hide partial failures.
  • Requests without projections returning a different shape than before.

Demo to build

Takeaways

  • The contract includes errors, status codes, and batch behavior.
  • Clients should be tolerant readers and keep free-form details untyped.
  • Golden-file tests turn accidental contract changes into visible diffs.

atom:entry.atom:title: Compartment design and movement: policy implications
atom:entry.atom:summary: How I structure compartments so access stays predictable when one has to move.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Compartments split resources and policy scope, and the layout you choose on day one is hard to change quietly. When a compartment moves, the set of policies that apply to it can change with it, and people can gain or lose access without anyone editing a statement.

I wanted a hierarchy that makes moves boring and lets me check the result afterwards.

Options and trade-offs

  • A flat design: simple, with few movement cases and limited delegation.
  • A hierarchical design: flexible, with inherited access, and it needs careful names and ownership.
  • Policies attached at a shared ancestor: they adjust automatically when a descendant moves under the same ancestor, and lower-level policies may need manual edits.

My recommendation

Use a clear hierarchy with named owners, and attach policies at an ancestor that will survive the moves you expect. After any move, verify access from the point of view of the people involved and fix anything that attached lower down.

Worked example

Take a move from A:B:C to A:D. Policies written at A, the common ancestor, keep working and update their path references. A policy attached inside B that named C by path no longer matches its target, and the access it granted disappears until someone rewrites it.

# Attached at A (the shared ancestor): survives the move
Allow group TeamA-Admins to manage all-resources in compartment A:Prod
Allow group TeamA-Users  to use instance-family in compartment A:Dev
 
# Attached inside A:B and naming C by path: must be reviewed after the move
Allow group TeamC to use instance-family in compartment A:B:C

Before a move, list the policies that mention the compartment and note which ancestor each is attached to. After the move, check access with a test user for each group. Quotas and budgets are set per compartment, so confirm them too.

Checklist

  1. Define the hierarchy, names and owners before creating compartments.
  2. Attach policies at ancestors that will not move.
  3. Before a move, list the policies that reference the compartment.
  4. After a move, test access for every affected group.
  5. Use quotas and budgets at the compartment level as guardrails.
  6. Avoid duplicate compartment names under the same parent.

Where this doesn't apply

Security zones have their own rules, and a move that crosses a zone boundary is restricted. Manage those through the Security Zones service.

One honest limitation

Changes in implicit access are easy to miss. Treat a move as a planned change with a validation step afterwards, and do not call it finished until you have checked.

Sources

  • OCI Documentation: Managing Compartments (moving a compartment)
  • OCI Documentation: Policy Syntax (compartment paths)
  • OCI Documentation: Compartment Quotas and Budgets

atom:entry.atom:title: Discussions as Your Community Front Door
atom:entry.atom:summary: How to enable Discussions, set up categories, pin canonical threads, and convert between issues and discussions as conversations change shape.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Issues should track work. Discussions suit open-ended questions, ideas, and announcements. Discussions supports categories with different formats, pinned threads, accepted answers, upvotes, and conversion between issues and discussions. Defining these early keeps the work queue clean and reduces duplicate issues.

Options and trade-offs

  • Categories: group conversations by purpose. Each category can have a format such as announcement, Q&A, or open-ended. Check the current category limit in the docs.
  • Pinning: highlight canonical threads such as the FAQ or onboarding guide.
  • Accepted answers and upvotes: surface solutions and priorities. They need moderator attention to stay useful.
  • Conversion: move a thread from issue to discussion, or back, when its nature changes.

My take

Keep a small set of categories, pin the threads newcomers need first, and use a category form for Q&A so questions arrive with the details needed to answer them.

Decision lens: new-contributor friction and review latency.

Example setup: categories for Announcements, Q&A, and Ideas. The FAQ and a first-thirty-minutes guide are pinned. The Q&A category uses a form that asks for version, steps to reproduce, and expected versus actual behavior.

Template

.github/DISCUSSION_TEMPLATE/qna.yml: a category form with prompts for version, steps, expected behavior, and actual behavior.

Welcome post: the purpose of the space, the code of conduct, and the rules for converting between issues and discussions.

Category setup: Announcements restricted to maintainers, and Q&A with accepted answers enabled.

Checklist

  1. Enable Discussions and create categories.
  2. Pin the FAQ and onboarding threads.
  3. Add a Q&A category form.
  4. Write down the conversion rules between issues and discussions.
  5. Review the category setup each quarter.

Common mistakes

  • Running without categories, which makes threads hard to find.
  • Not pinning canonical answers, so the same questions keep coming back.
  • Never converting issues, so the work queue fills with general chat.

Where this doesn't apply

  • Organizations required to use an external forum or ticketing system.

How to get involved

  • Good first issue: propose a new pinned FAQ entry.
  • Discussion: what should the Q&A form ask first?

Sources

  • Managing categories for discussions: https://docs.github.com/en/discussions/managing-discussions-for-your-community/managing-categories-for-discussions. Formats and limits.
  • Managing discussions: https://docs.github.com/en/discussions/managing-discussions-for-your-community/managing-discussions. Pinning, permissions, and transfers.
  • Collaborating with maintainers using discussions: https://docs.github.com/en/discussions/collaborating-with-your-community-using-discussions/collaborating-with-maintainers-using-discussions. Accepted answers, upvotes, and conversion.
  • Category forms: https://docs.github.com/en/discussions/managing-discussions-for-your-community/creating-discussion-category-forms.

atom:entry.atom:title: AI Language and Vision: secure triage pipelines (illustrative)
atom:entry.atom:summary: Wiring OCI Language and Vision into a document triage flow while keeping personal data out of places it should not be.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Support tickets, scanned forms and screenshots all contain personal data, and the people asking for automated triage rarely want to train a model. OCI Language and Vision offer pretrained models behind regional endpoints, which is a good fit when the goal is to route and summarize rather than to research.

The design question is where personal data goes. I wanted the masking to happen before anything gets stored or forwarded, and I wanted a trail showing which call touched which document.

Options and trade-offs

  • Language service (entities, sentiment, key phrases, PII detection): good for text pipelines, as long as PII is masked before downstream storage.
  • Vision (document and image analysis, text detection, object detection): good for PDFs and images, with batch jobs and custom models available.
  • Inline versus asynchronous jobs: inline is simpler for a small payload, and batch jobs backed by Object Storage scale better.

My recommendation

Use inline calls for small, interactive requests and Object Storage backed jobs for volume. Run PII masking first in the text path. Store only the masked output, keep request identifiers for audit, and set a retention period before the first production run.

Worked example

Masking personal data in a piece of text with the Language service. This uses the PII entity detection call with a masking option, and it needs a Python environment with the OCI SDK configured for your tenancy.

import oci
 
config = oci.config.from_file()
language = oci.ai_language.AIServiceLanguageClient(config)
 
doc = oci.ai_language.models.TextDocument(
    key="example-document", text=ticket_text, language_code="en")
 
resp = language.batch_detect_language_pii_entities(
    oci.ai_language.models.BatchDetectLanguagePiiEntitiesDetails(
        documents=[doc], masking={"ALL": {"mode": "MASK"}}))
 
masked = resp.data.documents[0].masked_text   # store this, not ticket_text

Analyzing a scanned document in Object Storage with Vision. The result is text you can pass to the masking step above.

vision = oci.ai_vision.AIServiceVisionClient(config)
 
result = vision.analyze_document(
    oci.ai_vision.models.AnalyzeDocumentDetails(
        compartment_id=compartment_ocid,
        document=oci.ai_vision.models.ObjectStorageDocumentDetails(
            source="OBJECT_STORAGE",
            namespace_name=namespace,
            bucket_name=input_bucket,
            object_name="scan-0007.pdf"),
        features=[oci.ai_vision.models.DocumentTextDetectionFeature(
            feature_type="TEXT_DETECTION")]))
 
print(result.headers.get("opc-request-id"))   # keep for the audit trail

For larger volumes, create a document job through the CLI or SDK with input and output locations in Object Storage, then poll for completion. Run the workload as an instance or resource principal and grant it only the Language, Vision and bucket access it needs.

Checklist

  1. Mask or remove PII before storing any text.
  2. Use inline calls for small payloads and batch jobs for volume.
  3. Keep outputs only as long as you need them.
  4. Record request IDs and compartment ownership for audit.
  5. Check supported file formats and languages before choosing a feature.
  6. Use instance or resource principals instead of keys in code.

Where this doesn't apply

Fully air-gapped environments cannot call these cloud endpoints. They need models that run locally instead.

One honest limitation

Bulk analysis produces a lot of metadata and intermediate output. Decide on redaction and retention rules up front, or the results bucket turns into its own data-protection problem.

Sources

  • OCI Documentation: Language, Detecting Personally Identifiable Information
  • OCI Documentation: Vision, Document AI Overview
  • OCI Python SDK Reference: AIServiceLanguageClient and AIServiceVisionClient

atom:entry.atom:title: Migrating to Microsoft Entra Verified ID
atom:entry.atom:summary: A neutral playbook for issuing and verifying user-owned credentials with open standards, and wiring the verification step into an existing app.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Many apps verify identity attributes with a bespoke token: a signed JWT that only the issuing system can produce and only your app can parse. That locks the user into one issuer's flow and forces every verifier to build a custom integration. Microsoft Entra Verified ID uses open standards (decentralized identifiers, W3C verifiable credentials, OpenID for Verifiable Credentials) so a person can hold a credential in a wallet, such as Microsoft Authenticator, and present it to any verifier that trusts the issuer.

Options and trade-offs

  • Issuer setup: bind a decentralized identifier to your domain (did:web), keep signing keys in Key Vault, grant the Request Service the permissions it needs, and define a credential contract (display and rules). The result is portable credentials, at the cost of setup steps and a dependency on a wallet.
  • Verifier setup: a separate app, ideally in a separate tenant from the issuer, that creates presentation requests, receives callbacks and validates what comes back. It gets privacy-respecting, user-approved presentations instead of passwords or shared secrets.
  • Hybrid designs: where a server must query an issuer continuously, user presentation is a poor fit. Combine it with server-side checks instead of replacing them.

My recommendation

Migrate one low-risk attribute first, such as proof of employment or membership, and keep the existing check running in parallel. Verify the credential's issuer, signature and status, and accept only the claims you need. Expand once the flow is reliable.

Minimal working example

The verifier flow has three parts: get a token for the Request Service, create a presentation request, and handle the callback.

Step 1: get an access token with the client credentials flow, using the Verifiable Credentials Service Request scope (confirm the exact scope value in the current docs):

curl -s -X POST "https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/oauth2/v2.0/token" \
  -d "client_id=<app-id>" \
  -d "client_secret=<secret-or-use-a-certificate>" \
  -d "grant_type=client_credentials" \
  -d "scope=3db474b9-6a0c-4840-96ac-1fceb342124f/.default"

Step 2: create a presentation request:

POST https://verifiedid.did.msidentity.com/v1.0/verifiableCredentials/createPresentationRequest
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <token>

{
  "authority": "did:web:verifier.example.com",
  "includeQRCode": true,
  "registration": { "clientName": "Example Verifier" },
  "callback": {
    "url": "https://verifier.example.com/api/presentation-callback",
    "state": "<unique-request-id>",
    "headers": { "api-key": "<shared-callback-secret>" }
  },
  "requestedCredentials": [
    {
      "type": "ProofOfEmployment",
      "purpose": "Confirm your employer before granting access",
      "acceptedIssuers": [ "did:web:issuer.example.com" ]
    }
  ]
}

The response includes a QR code and a deep link for the wallet. Step 3: handle the callback and authorize only on a verified presentation:

// Callback handler (framework-agnostic sketch)
void onCallback(String apiKeyHeader, JsonNode body) {
    if (!MessageDigest.isEqual(apiKeyHeader.getBytes(UTF_8), EXPECTED_KEY.getBytes(UTF_8))) {
        throw new SecurityException("bad callback key");
    }
    String status = body.path("requestStatus").asText();
    switch (status) {
        case "request_retrieved"      -> markScanned(body.path("state").asText());
        case "presentation_verified"  -> grantAccess(body.path("state").asText(),
                                                     body.path("verifiedCredentialsData"));
        case "presentation_error"     -> markFailed(body.path("state").asText());
        default                       -> { /* ignore unknown statuses */ }
    }
}

Test it: run the flow with a test credential and confirm access is granted only after presentation_verified. Then present a credential from an issuer that is not in acceptedIssuers and confirm it is rejected.

Checklist

  • Use did:web with domain binding, serve it over HTTPS, and avoid redirects on the well-known path.
  • Keep signing keys in Key Vault and plan rotation before you need it.
  • Check the issuer DID against an allowlist, and confirm the credential status, not just the signature.
  • Use a unique state value per request, and authenticate callbacks with a secret you compare in constant time.
  • Request only the claims you will use, and explain the purpose to the user.
  • Align on the supported standards (VC Data Model, OpenID4VC, Presentation Exchange) so you can work with other wallets and verifiers.

Where this doesn't apply

Scenarios that need continuous server-side queries to an issuer rather than a user presenting a credential. Use a hybrid design there.

Sources

  • Verified ID introduction and standards
  • Request Service REST API presentation specification
  • Configure your tenant for Verified ID

atom:entry.atom:title: AKS confidential containers for model isolation
atom:entry.atom:summary: What kata-cc isolates, how attestation ties to key release, and operational constraints.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Some AI workloads need runtime confidentiality: protect model artifacts and user data from the host OS/kernel and operators. AKS confidential containers (kata-cc) isolate the pod in a confidential utility VM with attestation and policy controls. Trade-offs include startup time, debugging limitations, and preview status constraints.

Options and trade-offs

  • AKS confidential VM node pool: Node-level boundary; simpler lift-and-shift; not per-pod sandbox.
  • AKS confidential containers (kata-cc): Pod-level confidential sandbox, policy generator and attestation; more operational constraints; supports Azure Linux and specific VM SKUs; preview limitations apply.
  • ACI confidential containers: Container group boundary; suitable for event-driven jobs; fewer orchestration features than AKS.

Minimal working example

Prereqs

  • Azure CLI 2.44.1+; aks-preview and confcom extensions; Azure Linux; KataCcIsolation on node pool; enable workload identity and OIDC issuer if key release requires identity linkage.

    • Create cluster (example)

az aks create --resource-group rg --name aks-cc \
  --kubernetes-version 1.25.0 \
  --os-sku AzureLinux \
  --node-vm-size Standard_DC8as_cc_v5 \
  --workload-runtime KataCcIsolation \
  --enable-oidc-issuer --enable-workload-identity

Deploy consumer with attestation sidecar and policy Generate policy with confcom; apply as annotation; tie Key Vault key release to attestation measurement. Test: Remove kata-cc spec and policy; confirm ciphertext (no key release).

Checklist

  • Confirm supported SKUs and OS; Azure Linux only for kata-cc at present.
  • Enable and maintain policy (do not use :latest tags because layers are measured).
  • Expect longer pod startup and limited troubleshooting (exec/stdio require policy change).
  • Integrate attestation with Key Vault for secure key release.

Where this doesn't apply

Windows node pools; or workloads requiring frequent interactive debugging incompatible with kata-cc constraints.

Sources

  • Confidential containers (Preview)
  • Deploy AKS with confidential containers policy
  • Confidential containers overview (Azure confidential computing)

atom:entry.atom:title: UCP pool tuning for resilience and validation
atom:entry.atom:summary: The handful of Universal Connection Pool settings I change first, and the arithmetic behind the sizes.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

UCP has dozens of properties, and the defaults work. What I wanted was predictable behavior under stress: callers that fail fast instead of hanging, bad connections that are caught before they reach the application, and a pool that does not quietly use up the database's session budget.

Options and trade-offs

  • A small pool with a modest maximum: gentle on the database, and it may add latency while the pool warms up.
  • A larger minimum or initial size: faster first requests, and idle sessions you are paying for.
  • Validation on borrow: safer, with a small cost on each borrow. A short trust window reduces that cost.

My recommendation

Set the minimum and maximum sizes on purpose, turn on validation on borrow with a short trust window, and give callers a wait timeout. Then measure and adjust. Change one property at a time, so you know which change helped.

Worked example

Start from the database's limit and work backwards. If a database can comfortably serve 200 sessions for this application and you run 8 service instances, a maximum of 20 per instance already reaches 160, which leaves room for failover and administration.

PoolDataSource pds = PoolDataSourceFactory.getPoolDataSource();
pds.setConnectionFactoryClassName("oracle.jdbc.pool.OracleDataSource");
pds.setURL("<jdbc_url>");
pds.setUser(System.getenv("DB_USER"));
pds.setPassword(System.getenv("DB_PASSWORD"));
 
// Sizing
pds.setInitialPoolSize(2);
pds.setMinPoolSize(2);
pds.setMaxPoolSize(20);
 
// Resilience
pds.setValidateConnectionOnBorrow(true);
pds.setSecondsToTrustIdleConnection(5);   // skip re-validation for 5 s
pds.setConnectionWaitTimeout(3);          // seconds a caller waits for a connection
pds.setInactiveConnectionTimeout(300);    // release idle connections after 5 min

To watch the pool, log the borrowed and available counts on a timer, or expose them through JMX:

log.info("ucp borrowed={} available={}",
         pds.getBorrowedConnectionsCount(),
         pds.getAvailableConnectionsCount());

If borrowed stays close to the maximum and callers start timing out, the first suspect is a slow query or a leaked connection, not the pool size.

Checklist

  1. Derive the maximum from the database's session budget and the number of instances.
  2. Turn on validation on borrow, and use a short trust window if the overhead matters.
  3. Set a connection wait timeout so callers cannot hang.
  4. Log or export the borrowed, available and waiting counts.
  5. Test failover and a database restart.
  6. Revisit sizes after load testing, in small steps.

Where this doesn't apply

Large Oracle RAC deployments that rely on Fast Application Notification and replay need high-availability features configured, and that is a separate tuning exercise.

One honest limitation

Validation costs a little on every borrow. Only widen the trust window after the basic reliability picture is clear, or you may hide the very failures you wanted to catch.

Sources

  • Oracle Universal Connection Pool Developer's Guide: Setting Connection Pool Properties
  • Oracle UCP Java API Reference: PoolDataSource
  • Oracle UCP Developer's Guide: Monitoring the Pool with JMX

atom:entry.atom:title: From Compose to a Public URL: Ports, Health, and Scale-to-Zero
atom:entry.atom:summary: What changes when a local demo needs a real address, and how to keep it close to free when nobody is looking at it.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

A local demo is easy. A public one raises new questions: which port is exposed, how the platform knows the app is healthy, what the first request does after a quiet night, and how to be sure a traffic spike does not turn into a surprise bill. You do not need a cluster for this. A managed container platform with scale-to-zero gives you a URL that costs almost nothing when idle.

Options and trade-offs

  • Run a VM and keep it on: simple, but you pay for the idle hours.
  • Run a cluster: powerful, and far more than a demo needs.
  • Use a managed container platform with scale-to-zero: you accept a cold start in return for near-zero idle cost.

My recommendation

Make the app platform-friendly first: it listens on a configurable port, has a health endpoint, and redirects the root path somewhere useful. Then deploy a digest-pinned image with a minimum of zero replicas, managed TLS, and budget alerts set well below the ceiling.

Worked example

A tiny Java server with no dependencies. It reads the port from the environment, answers a health check, and redirects the root path to the docs.

import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpExchange;
import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.OutputStream;
import java.net.InetSocketAddress;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        int port = Integer.parseInt(System.getenv().getOrDefault("PORT", "8080"));
        HttpServer server = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress(port), 0);

        server.createContext("/health", ex -> respond(ex, 200, "application/json", "{\"status\":\"ok\"}"));
        server.createContext("/docs", ex -> respond(ex, 200, "text/html", "<h1>Docs</h1>"));
        server.createContext("/", ex -> {
            if ("/".equals(ex.getRequestURI().getPath())) {
                ex.getResponseHeaders().add("Location", "/docs");
                ex.sendResponseHeaders(302, -1);
                ex.close();
            } else {
                respond(ex, 404, "text/plain", "not found");
            }
        });
        server.start();
    }

    private static void respond(HttpExchange ex, int status, String type, String body) throws IOException {
        byte[] bytes = body.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        ex.getResponseHeaders().add("Content-Type", type);
        ex.sendResponseHeaders(status, bytes.length);
        try (OutputStream out = ex.getResponseBody()) {
            out.write(bytes);
        }
    }
}

The deployment description is illustrative, since every platform has its own field names, but the shape is the same everywhere:

{
  "name": "demo-app",
  "image": "registry.example.com/team/app@sha256:<digest>",
  "containerPort": 8080,
  "healthCheckPath": "/health",
  "ingress": { "tls": true },
  "autoscale": { "minReplicas": 0, "maxReplicas": 3 }
}
docker compose up --build
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/health

Checklist

  1. Read the port from the environment, and expose the one the platform expects.
  2. Add a cheap health endpoint, and point the platform at it.
  3. Redirect the root path to something useful.
  4. Deploy by digest, with managed TLS.
  5. Set minimum replicas to zero, and test the first request after idle.
  6. Set a budget alert well under your ceiling, and send it somewhere you will see it.

Where this doesn't apply

If you need steady low latency, scale-to-zero is the wrong choice, because the first request after a quiet period will be slow.

One honest limitation

A cold start on a JVM service can take seconds. You can soften it with a smaller image and class-data sharing, but you cannot remove it, so decide whether a slow first visit is acceptable for the demo.

Sources

  • Docker Docs: Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK
  • Oracle Java Documentation: com.sun.net.httpserver package

atom:entry.atom:title: Roadmaps Next to Your Code: GitHub Projects for Platform Teams
atom:entry.atom:summary: How to run a roadmap in GitHub Projects using table, board, and roadmap views, custom fields, and built-in automations.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

External roadmap tools fall out of date because they are not connected to issues and pull requests. GitHub Projects sits alongside issues and PRs and gives each team a view suited to its question: a prioritized backlog, the current iteration board, or a timeline roadmap.

Options and trade-offs

  • Table view: dense and good for prioritization. It needs consistent field values.
  • Board view: a status-based layout for iteration planning. It works best with work-in-progress limits.
  • Roadmap view: a timeline across dates or iterations. It suits communicating schedules to others.
  • Built-in workflows: add items, set status, and archive without code. They are limited compared with custom automation.
  • Insights: charts for status and progress. Useful for a quick read, not a full reporting tool.

My take

Use one organization-level project for the platform roadmap, keep tactical bug work out of it, and save a small set of views that answer the questions people actually ask.

Decision lens: review latency and team workload.

Example setup: a platform roadmap project with Priority, Estimate, Iteration, and Owner fields, auto-add filters for the relevant repositories, and three saved views: backlog by priority, the current iteration board, and the quarter roadmap.

Template

Project fields: a single-select Priority field, a number field for Estimate, and an iteration field.

Views: Table for the backlog, Board for the current iteration, and Roadmap for milestones.

Workflows: auto-add issues with a chosen label, set new items to Todo, and archive items that have been Done for a set period.

Project README: link the saved views and describe the naming and labeling rules.

Checklist

  1. Create an organization project and define the fields.
  2. Save table, board, and roadmap views.
  3. Configure auto-add and status workflows.
  4. Add milestone markers to the roadmap view.
  5. Document label and ownership conventions.
  6. Set work-in-progress limits on the board.

Common mistakes

  • Mixing bug triage with strategic planning in one project. Split them.
  • Not saving views, so collaborators lose context.
  • Skipping automation, which lets status drift from reality.

Where this doesn't apply

  • Teams required to use an external project management system. Mirror the data through the API if needed.

How to get involved

  • Good first issue: propose a saved view that would improve backlog triage.
  • Discussion: what fields should the roadmap track?

atom:entry.atom:title: API gateway enforcement for LLM APIs
atom:entry.atom:summary: Putting Azure API Management in front of Azure OpenAI: managed identity to the backend, token validation at the edge, and rate limits per caller.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

When every team calls the model endpoint directly, governance is a spreadsheet: who has access, how much they use, and what they send. Putting a gateway in front of the model gives you one place to authenticate callers, enforce limits and log usage. Azure API Management (APIM) can authenticate to Azure OpenAI with its own managed identity, so no API keys are stored or shared, and it can validate caller tokens before anything reaches the model.

Options and trade-offs

  • Managed identity to the backend: APIM holds the identity, callers hold nothing that works against the model directly. It is simple for service-to-service access, and every caller shares the same backend privileges.
  • OAuth 2.0 validation at the gateway: callers present Entra tokens, and APIM checks audience and roles before forwarding. You get per-caller control and audit, with more setup.
  • Per-caller limits: rate limits keyed on the caller's identity stop one team's runaway loop from using the shared quota.

My recommendation

Use both layers. Validate the caller's token at the gateway, then use the gateway's managed identity to call the backend. Add a rate limit keyed on the caller. Disable key-based access on the model resource once traffic flows through the gateway, so there is no way around it.

Minimal working example

Enable a managed identity on the APIM instance and grant it access to the model resource:

az role assignment create \
  --assignee <apim-principal-id> \
  --role "Cognitive Services OpenAI User" \
  --scope <azure-openai-resource-id>

Then add the inbound policy. It validates the caller, limits usage, and swaps the caller's token for the gateway's backend token:

<inbound>
  <base />

  <!-- 1. Validate the caller's Entra token -->
  <validate-jwt header-name="Authorization" failed-validation-httpcode="401"
                failed-validation-error-message="Unauthorized">
    <openid-config url="https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration" />
    <audiences>
      <audience><gateway-app-id></audience>
    </audiences>
    <required-claims>
      <claim name="roles" match="any">
        <value>LLM.Invoke</value>
      </claim>
    </required-claims>
  </validate-jwt>

  <!-- 2. Limit usage per caller -->
  <rate-limit-by-key calls="60" renewal-period="60"
      counter-key="@(context.Request.Headers.GetValueOrDefault("Authorization","").AsJwt()?.Subject)" />

  <!-- 3. Authenticate to the backend with the gateway's managed identity -->
  <authentication-managed-identity resource="https://cognitiveservices.azure.com"
      output-token-variable-name="managed-id-access-token" ignore-error="false" />
  <set-header name="Authorization" exists-action="override">
    <value>@("Bearer " + (string)context.Variables["managed-id-access-token"])</value>
  </set-header>
</inbound>

Test it: call the gateway with a valid token and confirm a normal response, call without a token and confirm a 401, and call in a loop to confirm the rate limit returns 429.

Checklist

  • Use the model resource's custom subdomain endpoint, and confirm the role assignment scope.
  • Validate the audience and a role claim at the gateway, not just that a token exists.
  • Key the rate limit on the caller's identity, not on an IP address that may be shared.
  • Disable local (key) authentication on the model resource after cutover.
  • Log request metadata for audit, and keep prompt and completion content out of default logs.
  • Check that your policy ordering does what you expect: validation first, then limits, then backend authentication.

Where this doesn't apply

Backends that do not support Entra authentication or gateway integration. There, the gateway still helps with limits and audit, but backend authentication needs another design.

Sources

  • Authenticate and authorize to LLM APIs with Azure API Management
  • authentication-managed-identity policy

atom:entry.atom:title: Revocation Is the Hard Part
atom:entry.atom:summary: Issuing is easy; keeping credentials current without leaking who asked is the challenge.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Issuing verifiable credentials is straightforward: define a claim, sign it, return it to the holder. Revocation is harder: you need to detect when a credential should no longer be accepted, ideally without creating a surveillance channel that reveals who asked and when.

The failure mode

A verifier calls a central revocation endpoint for every check. The endpoint sees who asked (IP or key), when, for which credential ID, and what outcome occurred. Even if the credential is privacy-preserving, the revocation lookup becomes a “phone home” channel that leaks context. Users and regulators won’t love that.

What I learned

Understand the revocation design space

Status list (offline)

The issuer publishes a privacy-preserving list of credential status values (for example, a bitstring status list) that verifiers fetch periodically. Verification checks against the local list.

Online status check

The verifier queries a status endpoint per credential. Freshness improves; privacy worsens.

Holder stapling

The holder obtains a fresh status attestation and presents it along with the credential. The verifier checks the stapled proof without contacting the issuer per verification.

Short-lived credentials:

Expire credentials quickly so revocation windows are short. This reduces reliance on revocation checks.

Privacy-preserving lists: batch and compress

A status list can represent many credentials without revealing individual identities. Verifiers download the list on a schedule (e.g., every policy-defined freshness window), cache it locally, and check bits/entries offline. Lists can be partitioned or hashed to limit list size.

Stapling shifts “phone home” to holder flow

With stapling, the holder requests a status proof from the issuer (or a delegated service) at a cadence, then presents it to verifiers. This avoids per-verification lookups by verifiers but still requires the holder to contact the issuer on some schedule. The privacy difference is who calls whom and when.

Short-lived credentials reduce time at risk

If credentials expire quickly, revocation needs are less acute. This shifts load from revocation infrastructure to issuance (more frequent renewals). Combine with holder stapling to keep verification fast and private.

Model cache freshness and failure modes

Verifiers should track the freshness of status lists. If a list is too old (e.g., beyond your policy window), treat the result as “unverifiable” rather than “accepted,” and prompt re-fetch or stapling. Distinguish “cache stale” from “revoked.”

Avoid per-ID URLs in logs

If you must hit an online status endpoint, avoid logging per-ID lookups in a way that identifies a particular holder or verifier. Aggregate metrics instead. Keep any necessary identifiers hashed or pseudonymous.

Distinguish revocation from expiry and audience

Revocation says “this specific credential is no longer valid.” Expiry says “credentials of this type are only valid until T.” Audience says “this verifier is permitted to consume the claim.” Don’t overload revocation with other policy failures.

Illustrative status-list freshness check

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class StatusSnapshot:
    fetched_at: datetime
    bits: bytes

def is_fresh(snapshot: StatusSnapshot, max_age_seconds: int) -> bool:
    age = datetime.now(timezone.utc) - snapshot.fetched_at
    return age.total_seconds() <= max_age_seconds

# Choose the freshness window from policy and operational requirements.
# Stale status should have an explicit outcome, such as "unverifiable".

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

Offline lists vs freshness: Lists preserve privacy but can be stale. Address with frequent, batched updates.

Stapling vs issuer load: Stapling shifts calls to holders; issuer still handles periodic status proofs. Load is manageable with caching and rate limits.

Short-lived credentials vs user friction: Frequent renewals add UX overhead. Balance with clear prompts and automated refresh flows.

Failure modes

“Phone home”: Per-verification lookups leak context. Solution: offline lists or stapling.

“Stale cache”: Verifiers use outdated lists. Solution: freshness checks and policy windows that treat stale as “unverifiable.”

“Revocation conflation”: Treating expiry or audience failure as revocation. Solution: separate policy checks.

Try it yourself

Implement an offline status list with a freshness window. Treat stale lists as “unverifiable.”

Add holder stapling to your demo: the holder fetches a status proof and presents it alongside the credential.

Track performance for offline list checks vs online status calls. Compare privacy and tail behavior.

Further reading

  • Revoke a verifiable credential as an issuer
  • W3C Bitstring Status List v1.0
  • Plan a Verified ID verification solution

atom:entry.atom:title: Designing for Partial Data: Unknown vs False
atom:entry.atom:summary: Sealed types and exhaustive pattern matching keep “unknown” distinct from “zero” throughout a service.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Partial data is normal. Missing signals and unverifiable sources happen. If you collapse “unknown” into “false” or “zero,” you erode trust. As an engineering manager, I’ve learned to design services that treat “we don’t know” as a first-class outcome. In Java, sealed types and exhaustive pattern matching make this straightforward and enforceable.

The failure mode

Your aggregator treats null as “0.0,” sums four dimensions, and displays a neat number. A caller misreads that as “complete and low.” In reality, two dimensions were missing, and one was unverifiable. The number masked uncertainty.

What I learned

Keep partial states in the domain layer, not just at the edges

Don’t convert unknowns to defaults at the boundary. Let domain logic operate on sealed types. If you must produce a single number, force policy conversion in a dedicated function so that the decision is auditable.

Policy example

public final class AggregationPolicy {
public static double conservativeAverage(List<ScoreOrUnknown> dims) {
int count = 0;
double sum = 0.0;
for (ScoreOrUnknown d : dims) {
switch (d) {
case Score sc         -> { sum += sc.value(); count++; }
case Missing miss     -> { /* exclude; track missing elsewhere */ }
case Unverifiable unv -> { /* exclude; track unverifiable */ }
}
}
if (count == 0) return Double.NaN; // no numeric evidence
return sum / count;
}
public static boolean okToDisplay(List<ScoreOrUnknown> dims) {
long unknowns = dims.stream().filter(x -> !(x instanceof Score)).count();
return unknowns == 0; // or choose a threshold
}
}

Propagate uncertainty deliberately

Unknowns should travel with the data: into logs, decisions, and UI. For example, if two dimensions are unknown, surface that count alongside any numeric aggregation. The goal is to prevent silent conversions that distort confidence.

Make unknown-handling policies explicit and testable

Write tests that assert what happens when all dimensions are unknown, when some are missing, and when a single unverifiable dimension appears. Pattern matching keeps these tests aligned with the domain states. Don’t assume a “best effort” numeric default; decide and encode.

Resist “default values” in DTOs

If you serialize to JSON, include a type field in each dimension and omit value when the state isn’t Score. A consumer reading {"type":"Missing","reason":"timeout"} can act accordingly. Defaulting to 0.0 or “unknown=false” invites misuse.

Teach callers to branch by type, not numeric checks Documentation should show switch examples, not “if value is 0 then unknown.” This reduces coupling and preserves room for future states (e.g., “Contested,” “Deprecated”).

Audit conversion points with a linelist List every place where ScoreOrUnknown becomes a single number or a boolean. Audit these conversions periodically. If you discover accidental flattening, refactor to preserve states or add proper policy functions.

Accept that aggregation may return “no number” Returning NaN or omitting a field is reasonable when inputs are fully unknown. Treat this as normal, not exceptional. UI can show “insufficient evidence” with counts; APIs can document this outcome clearly.

JSON serialization with a type field

// Using a simple custom serializer sketch

public record Score(double value) implements ScoreOrUnknown {}
public record Missing(String reason) implements ScoreOrUnknown {}
public record Unverifiable(String note) implements ScoreOrUnknown {}
public Map<String, Object> toJson(ScoreOrUnknown s) {
return switch (s) {
case Score sc         -> Map.of("type", "Score", "value", sc.value());
case Missing miss     -> Map.of("type", "Missing", "reason", miss.reason());
case Unverifiable unv -> Map.of("type", "Unverifiable", "note", unv.note());

};

}

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

Transparency vs brevity: Returning types and reasons increases payload size but improves clarity. Favor clarity when ambiguity matters.

Strictness vs convenience: Throwing on invalid scores and disallowing defaults catches bugs early but may frustrate callers used to flexible shapes.

NaN vs explicit omission: NaN signals “no numeric value” but can be mishandled by consumers. Omitting a field or providing a separate state field avoids confusion.

Failure modes

“Silent flattening”

A downstream transforms unknowns to zero—likely out of habit. Catch this in contract tests.

“Enum drift”

If reason codes evolve, consumers break. Document codes and provide a safe default handling path.

“Partial measures hiding in averages”: An average of one numeric with three unknowns looks “complete” unless you also surface unknown counts.

Try it yourself

Refactor one DTO to embed a sealed state rather than a nullable numeric field. Add a type field in JSON. Update consumers to switch on type.

Write aggregation policies that return NaN or omit fields when inputs are fully unknown. Test behavior explicitly.

Add metrics that count unknowns and unverifiable states separately from numeric distributions.

Further reading

  • Records (JEP 395)
  • Sealed Classes (JEP 409)
  • Pattern Matching for switch (JEP 441)

atom:entry.atom:title: KV Cache Governance: Bound LLM Memory in OpenVINO Model Server
atom:entry.atom:summary: A procedure for choosing a KV-cache size for Model Server, observing real memory use with ordinary tools, and writing the limit and its evidence into a runbook.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

A language-model server keeps attention keys and values for every token of every active sequence. That memory grows with context length and concurrency. Unlike model weights, it is not a fixed cost, so a deployment that looks fine in a short test can run short of memory under a different traffic mix.

OpenVINO Model Server lets you set the cache memory with --cache_size, and its documentation examples pass explicit values. Choosing that number deliberately is the heart of governing the cache.

The friction points are picking a limit, observing real usage against it, documenting the number and its basis, and deciding in advance what the service does when a request does not fit.

Options and trade-offs

  • Explicit limit: pass --cache_size in gigabytes. The documentation's examples use values such as 20 on a large CPU system and 2 in a GPU example, which shows that the right value depends on the model, precision, and hardware.
  • Prefix reuse: with prefix caching enabled, repeated prompt prefixes avoid recomputation. A larger cache can hold more reusable history, so cache size and the benefit of prefix caching are linked.
  • Concurrency and context length are the two drivers of cache growth. Limit the maximum prompt size and the number of simultaneous requests at your gateway so the cache you chose is a realistic fit.
  • Observation: use operating-system and container tools to watch the server process's memory over time. You do not need special server features to see a trend and compare it with the limit you set.
  • Overflow policy: decide whether the service should reject oversize requests with a clear error, shorten context, or queue. Silent failure or a crash is the outcome to avoid.
  • Model and precision changes: a different model or precision changes memory per token, so a limit chosen for one is not valid for another.
  • Recommendation: start with a conservative value in the style of the documentation's examples, run a realistic mix of context lengths and concurrency, and watch the memory trend. Increase the cache until your largest realistic request fits with headroom, and stop there. Write the limit in the runbook with the model, precision, hardware, and the observed peak that justified it.
  • Decision lens: predictable memory versus refusing some requests. Example setup: a single-host service with an explicit --cache_size, a gateway that rejects prompts over a set length with a clear message, and an alert when process memory reaches a chosen fraction of the host.

Minimal working example

Prereqs

  • A Model Server container named ovms serving a language model, started with an explicit --cache_size.
  • Docker and Python 3 with requests.

memory_watch.sh (sample the container's memory while a load test runs)

while true; do
  docker stats --no-stream --format "{{.Name}} {{.MemUsage}}" ovms
  sleep 5
done

load_profile.py

import requests

URL = "http://localhost:8000/v3/chat/completions"
MODEL = "OpenVINO/Qwen3-8B-int4-ov"  # use the model name you deployed

def send(words):
    prompt = "word " * words
    r = requests.post(URL, json={"model": MODEL, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}], "max_tokens": 16})
    return r.status_code, r.elapsed.total_seconds()

for words in [200, 1000, 4000, 8000]:
    print(words, send(words))

Increase the prompt sizes until the server starts refusing or slowing down, and record what it returns.

Adjust file names, model names, and paths to your own setup.

Test: Start memory_watch.sh in one terminal and run load_profile.py in another with increasing prompt sizes. Note the memory trend, the largest prompt that completes, and exactly what the server returns for a prompt that is too large. Change --cache_size, restart, and repeat.

Record: model, precision, Model Server version, and host memory; the --cache_size values tested; the memory trend; the largest prompt that completed for each cache size; the server's response to an oversize prompt; latency as prompt size grows; your chosen limit and the evidence for it.

Checklist

  • Set --cache_size explicitly.
  • Observe memory over a realistic load and find the largest prompt that fits.
  • Test the overflow path on purpose.
  • Limit prompt size and concurrency at the gateway.
  • Document the limit with hardware, model, and precision, and repeat after any change.
  • Avoid: sizing from a single short test.
  • Avoid: having no defined behavior for oversize requests.

Where this doesn't apply

Short prompts with low concurrency on a host with ample memory, and services behind a managed platform that sets cache limits for you.

Sources

  • Agentic AI with OpenVINO Model Server (example commands)
  • Model Server continuous batching demo
  • Model Server performance tuning guide
  • OpenVINO Model Server parameters

atom:entry.atom:title: Codespaces Without Surprise Bills
atom:entry.atom:summary: How to use devcontainers and prebuilds for fast contributor setup, and how to set machine limits, retention, and spending caps so costs stay predictable.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Codespaces is fast to start and well integrated with GitHub, but it is metered. Compute is billed by the hour, and storage is billed by the gigabyte-month. Stopped codespaces can keep accruing storage until they are deleted. Personal accounts and organizations have different included quotas, so check the billing page for your account type.

Options and trade-offs

  • Devcontainers: make environments reproducible and speed up onboarding. They need ongoing maintenance of the image and its setup scripts.
  • Prebuilds: speed up opening large repositories. They consume Actions minutes, so they suit heavy projects.
  • Machine size policy: limit the cores and memory contributors can pick. Smaller machines cost less but run slower.
  • Retention and idle timeouts: reduce storage and runaway compute. They add some admin overhead.
  • Spending limits: cap organization spend. Set them before rollout, not after the first surprise bill.

My take

Ship one default devcontainer sized for typical work, enable prebuilds only on the main branch, and set a short idle timeout. Teach contributors to delete codespaces they no longer need rather than only stopping them.

Decision lens: new-contributor friction and maintenance cost.

Example setup: a service repository with a 4-core default devcontainer, prebuilds on the main branch, a 30-minute idle timeout, automatic deletion after 7 days of inactivity, and a monthly spending cap for the organization.

Template repository

.devcontainer/devcontainer.json: Base image, post-create commands, default machine size, and recommended extensions.

.github/workflows/prebuild.yml: Prebuild configuration limited to main and release branches. Check the Codespaces prebuild docs for the current configuration syntax.

README.md ("Use Codespaces" section): Machine choices, the difference between stopping and deleting, budget notes, and a link to contributor docs.

Checklist

  1. Define a devcontainer with a sensible default machine size.
  2. Enable prebuilds for large repositories and watch Actions minutes.
  3. Set idle timeout, retention, and spending limits at the organization level.
  4. Document the differences between personal and organization billing.
  5. Tell contributors to delete unused codespaces.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming a stopped codespace costs nothing. Storage keeps accruing until deletion.
  • Leaving machine sizes unlimited, so contributors default to the largest option.
  • Enabling prebuilds without tracking the Actions minutes they consume.

Where this doesn't apply

  • Teams that need local-only development or hardware that Codespaces does not support.
  • Toolchains that need macOS, iOS, or Windows-only environments.

How to get involved

  • Good first issue: add a prebuild for a documentation repository.
  • Discussion: share your default machine size and budget caps.

Sources (verify current rates)

  • Codespaces billing: https://docs.github.com/billing/managing-billing-for-github-codespaces/about-billing-for-github-codespaces. Compute and storage billing, included quotas, and organization metering.
  • GitHub plans: https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/learning-about-github/githubs-plans. Personal and organization plan differences.
