atom:entry.atom:title: Debugging Minimal Containers: Exit Codes and Thread Dumps
atom:entry.atom:summary: How I diagnose a failing Java container without baking a shell and a toolbox into the production image.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

A container fails and all you get is an exit code and perhaps a log line. The tempting response is to add a shell, curl, a debugger and a package manager to the image so that next time you can look around. That is the wrong trade. Production images should be small and boring, and your tools should arrive only when needed and leave no trace.

Options and trade-offs

  • Bake debugging tools into the image: convenient, but it enlarges the attack surface and the image.
  • Add an admin endpoint: useful for version and uptime, but it is one more thing to secure.
  • Use the platform: logs, exit codes, signals, and a separate short-lived container that shares the target's network.

My recommendation

Start with the exit code and the last logs. Use signals the JVM already understands, such as a thread dump on SIGQUIT, before reaching for tools. Make crashes leave evidence, and attach any tooling from outside.

Worked example

The first look should cost nothing. Exit code 137 usually means the process was killed, often for memory, and 143 means it was asked to stop:

docker ps -a --filter name=api
docker inspect --format '{{.State.ExitCode}} oom={{.State.OOMKilled}}' api
docker logs --since 15m api

The JVM prints a full thread dump to standard output when it receives SIGQUIT, so you need no tools inside the container:

docker kill --signal=SIGQUIT api
docker logs --tail 200 api

Make a crash leave something behind. These flags write a heap dump on an out-of-memory error to a mounted volume:

services:
  api:
    image: demo/api:1.4.2
    environment:
      JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: >-
        -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
        -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps
        -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError
    volumes:
      - ./dumps:/dumps

And have the application log one structured line when it dies, so the exit code has context:

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler((thread, error) -> {
            System.err.printf("{\"level\":\"FATAL\",\"thread\":\"%s\",\"error\":\"%s\"}%n",
                    thread.getName(), error.getClass().getName());
            error.printStackTrace();
        });
        Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(new Thread(() ->
                System.err.println("{\"level\":\"INFO\",\"msg\":\"shutdown\"}")));
        // start the application
    }
}

When you need to poke around the network or a volume, use a throwaway container that shares the target's network namespace:

docker run --rm -it --network=container:api -v api-data:/data:ro alpine sh
# inside: wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/health

Checklist

  1. Read the exit code, OOMKilled flag and recent logs before changing anything.
  2. Use SIGQUIT for a thread dump instead of installing tools.
  3. Configure heap dumps on out-of-memory errors, with a size cap and a clean-up plan.
  4. Log one structured fatal line with no secrets.
  5. Attach tools from a separate short-lived container and remove it afterwards.

Where this doesn't apply

If the failure is inside a native library or the container never starts, thread dumps will not help. You will need the platform's events and the host's logs.

One honest limitation

An outside container can see the network and volumes but not the process's memory. Heap dumps are sensitive too, since they can contain secrets, so store them carefully and delete them quickly.

Sources

  • Docker Docs: docker container logs
  • Docker Docs: docker container kill (signals)
  • Oracle Java Documentation: Troubleshooting guide (thread dumps and heap dumps)

atom:entry.atom:title: JDBC/UCP to Oracle over TLS or mTLS with wallets
atom:entry.atom:summary: My baseline for connecting a Java application to Autonomous Database or another Oracle service securely.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

A Java application needs to talk to a database, and the connection should be encrypted, should check it is talking to the right server, and should not carry a password in the source. Those three requirements are simple to state and easy to get partly wrong.

I wanted one baseline that I can adjust upward to mutual TLS when a policy asks for it, without relying on settings that change from driver version to driver version.

Options and trade-offs

  • Plain TCP with a username and password: simplest, with no transport protection and no server identity check.
  • Server-authenticated TLS: protects traffic and verifies the server, with fewer files to handle. Many services allow it.
  • Mutual TLS with a wallet: the client proves itself too. You need the wallet and a safe way to deliver it.

My recommendation

Default to TLS, and use mTLS with a wallet when policy requires client authentication. For Autonomous Database, use the TNS alias from the wallet's tnsnames.ora. Keep the password out of code by injecting it at start-up, and keep the pool conservative.

Worked example

With a wallet, point the driver at the directory that holds it and use the alias as the connection target. The ojdbc.properties file in the wallet supplies the wallet location.

// TNS_ADMIN is set outside the code (environment or -Doracle.net.tns_admin)
PoolDataSource pds = PoolDataSourceFactory.getPoolDataSource();
pds.setConnectionFactoryClassName("oracle.jdbc.pool.OracleDataSource");
pds.setURL("jdbc:oracle:thin:@dbname_high");   // alias from tnsnames.ora
pds.setUser(System.getenv("DB_USER"));
pds.setPassword(System.getenv("DB_PASSWORD"));  // injected, not hard-coded
pds.setMinPoolSize(2);
pds.setMaxPoolSize(10);
pds.setValidateConnectionOnBorrow(true);

Then prove that the connection really is encrypted, instead of assuming it:

try (var c = pds.getConnection();
     var s = c.createStatement();
     var rs = s.executeQuery(
        "SELECT sys_context('USERENV','NETWORK_PROTOCOL') FROM dual")) {
    rs.next();
    System.out.println(rs.getString(1));   // expect: tcps
}

The aliases in a downloaded wallet normally include a server certificate name check. Leave it on. If you use an auto-login wallet file with an older driver, you may also need the Oracle PKI jars on the classpath, so check the driver documentation for the version you run.

Checklist

  1. Fetch the wallet securely, set TNS_ADMIN, and keep the files out of source control.
  2. Use UCP with modest minimum and maximum sizes, and validate on borrow.
  3. Choose TLS by default and mTLS only when required.
  4. Inject database credentials from a secret store at start-up.
  5. Keep the server certificate name check enabled.
  6. Log connection failures and test a failover before go-live.

Where this doesn't apply

Old drivers that lack the TLS features you need should be upgraded first. Databases from other vendors use different drivers and different security models.

One honest limitation

Wallets add operational work, such as delivery, rotation and cleanup. Treat the wallet like any other secret and automate its life cycle before the first rotation, not after.

Sources

  • Oracle JDBC Developer's Guide: Client-Side Security Features
  • Oracle Universal Connection Pool Developer's Guide: Setting Connection Pool Properties
  • Oracle Autonomous Database Documentation: Connect with JDBC Thin and a Wallet

atom:entry.atom:title: The Hidden Price of "One More Log": Observability Costs on the JVM
atom:entry.atom:summary: Logging, tracing, and sampling choices that protect your p99
atom:entry.atom:content:
Where the cost comes from

  • Formatting. Building a message string you never emit is wasted work.
  • Allocation. Varargs arrays, boxed values, and message objects add garbage.
  • I/O and locking. A synchronous appender can block request threads on disk or on a shared lock.
  • Volume. Ten log lines per request at high traffic is a data pipeline you have to pay for.
  • Cardinality. Metric and span attributes with unbounded values (user IDs, request IDs as labels) explode storage and backend cost.

Logging guardrails

// Bad: concatenation always runs
log.debug("Fetched profile " + id + " in " + elapsedMs + "ms");

// Good: SLF4J formats only if DEBUG is enabled
log.debug("Fetched profile {} in {}ms", id, elapsedMs);
if (log.isDebugEnabled()) {
    log.debug("State: {}", expensiveDump(state));
}
String snapshot;
synchronized (lock) {
    snapshot = state.summary();      // cheap copy
}
log.info("Rebalanced: {}", snapshot);  // logging outside the lock

Tracing guardrails

import io.opentelemetry.sdk.trace.SdkTracerProvider;
import io.opentelemetry.sdk.trace.samplers.Sampler;

SdkTracerProvider provider = SdkTracerProvider.builder()
        .setSampler(Sampler.parentBased(Sampler.traceIdRatioBased(0.05)))   // ~5% of new traces
        .build();
  • Keep span attributes low-cardinality. Put high-cardinality identifiers in logs, not metric labels.
  • Avoid creating spans in tight loops. Instrument the request and the major dependencies.
  • Cap attribute value sizes.

Measure the overhead

import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.*;
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;

@State(Scope.Thread)
@BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime)
@OutputTimeUnit(java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)
public class LoggingBenchmark {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(LoggingBenchmark.class);   // level = INFO
    private final String id = "user-12345";
    private final long elapsed = 42;

    @Benchmark
    public void concatenation() {
        log.debug("Fetched profile " + id + " in " + elapsed + "ms");
    }

    @Benchmark
    public void parameterized() {
        log.debug("Fetched profile {} in {}ms", id, elapsed);
    }
}

Failure modes

  • High-cardinality labels that overload the metrics backend.
  • Log amplification, where one failure triggers retries that each log at ERROR.
  • Synchronous appenders blocking request threads.
  • Tracing everything in staging, then discovering production cannot afford it.

A starter checklist

  1. Parameterized logging everywhere, with guards for expensive arguments.
  2. No logging inside locks or tight loops.
  3. Async appender with a bounded queue.
  4. Parent-based ratio sampling, with the ratio justified by numbers.
  5. Attribute and label cardinality reviewed.
  6. A benchmark or load test whenever you add instrumentation to a hot path.

Takeaways

  • Observability has a runtime cost that shows up in the tail.
  • Sample traces, bound log queues, and keep cardinality low.
  • Benchmark instrumentation like any other hot-path code.

atom:entry.atom:title: Packaging Inference for Production
atom:entry.atom:summary: Reproducible conversion, versioned artifacts, visible precision, and tested fallbacks—before you press “deploy.”
atom:entry.atom:content:
A model can be accurate and still be hard to operate if conversion is manual, artifacts are opaque, precision changes silently, or fallbacks have never been exercised. Production readiness is the process around the model as much as the model itself.

aceu-edge-infer is a modest inference demo, but I treat its packaging path as if another engineer will need to rebuild, inspect, and recover it. Its outputs remain illustrative, not evaluative of real people. This checklist is about making that kind of service repeatable.

Make model conversion reproducible

Keep conversion in a script or build step rather than a shell history. Record the source model hash, tool and runtime versions, input shapes, conversion options, and warnings. Use separate, reviewable configuration for FP32 and INT8 artifacts, and retain the conversion logs with the release build.

from pathlib import Path
import openvino as ov

source = Path("models/source.onnx")
output = Path("build/models/model_fp32.xml")
output.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

model = ov.convert_model(source)
ov.save_model(model, output)

This example shows the conversion step only. Production automation should also validate model inputs, run parity checks, record the tool version, and fail when expected artifacts are missing.

Version and identify the artifacts

Give model artifacts versions tied to the code and conversion configuration that produced them. Store IR XML and weights together, record hashes, and keep them immutable after release. If calibration or quantization changes, publish a new model version rather than overwriting a file called latest.

A release manifest can record the information operators need without embedding the model itself:

{
  "model_version": "<release-version>",
  "source_format": "ONNX",
  "runtime": "OpenVINO",
  "precision_artifacts": ["FP32", "INT8"],
  "device_policy": "CPU",
  "source_sha256": "<source-model-hash>",
  "conversion_config_sha256": "<config-hash>"
}

Replace the placeholders during the build. These are identifiers to calculate and record—not measured values to guess.

Disclose the execution path

Include the precision and device used in logs or response metadata. Where it makes sense for the product, provide a controlled option to route sensitive work through FP32. That small bit of transparency can make rollout analysis and incident response much faster. Keep the API contract stable and avoid exposing internal details that callers do not need.

Test fallbacks before a release

Simulate an unavailable optimized runtime and verify the intended behavior. A valid fallback should either return correct outputs on a supported slower path or fail clearly with a non-ready/unavailable state. It should not manufacture placeholder results or quietly claim the preferred precision.

If custom operators exist, test the fallback with representative inputs and confirm that the selected path is visible in logs. Document what operators or hardware are required for each execution mode.

Package the runtime deliberately

Use a multi-stage image where it keeps build tools out of the runtime. Run as a non-root user, keep the base image and dependencies maintained, copy only the application and model artifacts required at runtime, and provide a bounded health check.

# Illustrative Python service image; adapt paths and dependencies to your app.
FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /build
RUN python -m venv /venv
ENV PATH="/venv/bin:$PATH"
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.12-slim AS runtime
RUN useradd --uid 10001 --create-home appuser
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /venv /venv
COPY --chown=10001:10001 app/ ./app/
COPY --chown=10001:10001 models/ ./models/
ENV PATH="/venv/bin:$PATH" \
    PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
USER 10001
EXPOSE 8000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD python -c 'import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen("http://localhost:8000/health", timeout=2)' || exit 1
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

Confirm that the chosen base image contains everything the service actually needs. The Docker health check should stay lightweight; configure a separate platform readiness check if model loading or a sample inference must gate incoming traffic.

Build, validate, and scan in CI

Use the same conversion scripts in local development and CI. Check that expected files exist, compare model outputs against a golden set, build the service image, and scan it before release. Make missing artifacts, failed parity checks, and scan failures visible release blockers. Keep exceptions owned and time-bounded.

Keep operational notes close to the code

Give the README short, findable sections for conversion, artifact versions, precision modes, fallback behavior, and hardware assumptions. Add an incident note describing what to inspect when latency or output parity changes, and point to the known-good artifact for rollback.

Trade-offs and failure modes

  • Process rigor vs. prototype speed: scripts and manifests take effort once and save time on the next rebuild.
  • More API metadata vs. smaller contract: publish only what helps callers; keep additional operational detail in logs.
  • Strict readiness vs. faster first traffic: waiting for model load and checks reduces false-green deploys.

“Mystery IR” files, silent FP32 fallbacks, and changed base images without review all make a service harder to reproduce. Version the inputs and outputs, disclose the selected path, and exercise rollback before you need it.

Try it before your next release

  1. Script FP32 and INT8 conversion and retain logs with immutable model artifacts.
  2. Record source and configuration hashes in a release manifest.
  3. Add actual precision/device metadata and a tested force-FP32 option if the product needs it.
  4. Test missing-runtime and unsupported-operator behavior before launch.
  5. Build, validate, and scan the same container image in CI that you intend to deploy.

Closing thought

Packaging inference for production is about repeatability, transparency, and safe recovery. When another engineer can recreate the model, identify the execution path, and trigger a tested fallback, the service is ready for more than a successful demo.

Further reading

  • OpenVINO model conversion and saving IR
  • Docker build best practices
  • Docker multi-stage builds

atom:entry.atom:title: Designing for Other People’s Code
atom:entry.atom:summary: Make extension safe and approachable: narrow interfaces, documentation-by-example, and sandboxed execution for contributed code.
atom:entry.atom:content:
The best way to attract contributions is to make the path small, clear, and safe. Big, powerful extension APIs are intimidating and fragile. A plugin interface is easier to adopt when it has a small typed contract, a complete example, and clear isolation boundaries for contributed code.

The failure mode

You want contributions, so you design a rich, flexible plugin API. The first contributor struggles to understand how the parts fit together. Another contributor introduces side effects that break core behavior. You spend time triaging issues rather than merging useful additions. The fix is to narrow the contract and improve examples.

What I learned

Keep the interface tiny

Use a single method with a small, typed result. Avoid optional hooks and deep callback trees. If you need flexibility, let plugins implement it internally. Keep core expectations documented and enforced with tests.

Illustrative plugin contract

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal, Protocol

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class EvidenceResult:
    status: Literal["present", "missing", "unverifiable"]
    note: str = ""

class EvidenceSource(Protocol):
    name: str
    def evaluate(self, profile: dict[str, object]) -> EvidenceResult: ...

Documentation-by-example beats long narratives

Write a short “Adding a plugin” doc that starts with a complete code example and a test. Follow with two variations that show common patterns (e.g., reading a field, combining small signals). Keep the words sparse and the code complete.

Sandboxing contributed code — practical guardrails

Run plugins within constraints:

Timeout per plugin evaluation.

Limit memory-intensive operations or external calls in the demo environment.

Validate types and restrict dangerous imports in plugin modules if possible.

A thread timeout is not a security sandbox: a host process cannot safely terminate arbitrary plugin code. For untrusted extensions, use a separate process or container with resource limits and restricted credentials, or load only trusted plugins.

Versioning and compatibility checks (keep them light)

Require plugins to declare supported interface versions and run contract tests. Keep the declaration simple, and make the CI failure message actionable (e.g., “Plugin supports 1.1.0; core is 1.2.0 — update SUPPORTED_VERSIONS”).

Golden paths and anti-patterns

Show five “golden path” examples contributors should follow:

Pure function: read inputs, return EvidenceResult, no side effects.

Lightweight computation: avoid heavy loops or large allocations.

Deterministic outputs: no random behavior or time-dependent outputs.

Typed result: always return one of the three states with a note.

No external calls: for demo simplicity, avoid network calls.

If you allow external calls, define strict limits and document them clearly.

Error messages designed for contributors

When a plugin fails a contract test, the message should name the plugin, the failing expectation, and the fix. Prefer helpful failures over terse stack traces. Provide a “common issues” page with targeted guidance.

“Hello world” PR built into the docs

Include a numbered guide that results in a merged PR:

Create plugin file.

Add minimal test.

Run pytest -q.

Open PR with the template.

Expected CI jobs and how to interpret them.

Merge expectations.

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

Small interface vs expressiveness: Narrow contracts limit advanced features; they also reduce fragility and cognitive load. For small projects, this trade-off is worth it.

Sandboxing vs performance: Timeouts and thread isolation add overhead. Keep limits modest and configurable.

Documentation-by-example vs thorough reference: Examples speed onboarding; deep reference can come later if demand arises.

Failure modes

“Stealth side effects”: Plugins write to global state or files unexpectedly. Solution: sandbox and contract tests; make side-effect-free behavior a rule.

“Doc drift”: Examples fall behind reality. Solution: run example snippets in CI and fail when they don’t compile.

“Silent timeouts”: Sandboxing hides errors without surfacing enough context. Solution: attach structured error notes to EvidenceResult.

Try it yourself

Shrink your plugin interface to a single method that returns a small typed object.

Add a sandbox wrapper with timeouts and typed error handling. Run plugins through it in CI contract tests.

Write a “hello world plugin” guide with a copy-paste example and a minimal test, then merge a sample PR to validate the path.

Further reading

  • GitHub Actions: Building and testing
  • Semantic Versioning 2.0.0
  • Keep a Changelog

atom:entry.atom:title: Reproducible Java Builds
atom:entry.atom:summary: “It built on my machine” still happens. Here’s how I pin versions, lock dependencies, and verify reproducibility in CI.
atom:entry.atom:content:
I’ve seen Java builds succeed locally and differ in CI—transitive dependencies float, plugin versions advance, or caches hide changes. Reproducibility takes intention: pin versions, use lock files, and verify clean-room rebuilds. In a Java build, dependency locks and clean CI environments help reveal resolution drift before artifacts are released.

The failure mode

You set versions in pom.xml but leave transitive ranges unconstrained. Locally, a cached artifact hides a minor release; in CI, it resolves a new version. Behavior changes. The fix is not “rerun until green.” It’s making builds deterministic and verifying them under clean conditions.

What I learned

Pin dependencies and plugins explicitly

Use dependencyManagement to pin versions of critical dependencies and plugins. Avoid wildcard ranges. If you depend on a BOM (bill of materials), understand what it pins and add explicit versions for anything critical that the BOM leaves flexible.

Example

<dependencyManagement>
<dependencies>
<dependency>
<groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
<artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
<version>5.10.2</version>
</dependency>
<!-- pin more -->
</dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

Use a lock mechanism to freeze transitive versions

A lock file captures resolved versions so CI doesn’t “discover” new transitive artifacts. Tools exist for Maven and Gradle that generate and enforce locks. The specifics depend on your chosen plugin; the principle is the same: generate once, commit, and enforce.

Generate lock file locally (or in CI).

Commit it.

Configure the build to fail if resolutions differ from the lock.

Clean-room rebuild in CI

Build in an isolated environment with a cleared local repository. Verify that resolving dependencies succeeds strictly against your lock. Optionally run the build twice—once with the lock (expected success), once with lock enforcement disabled to detect version drift. The second build should fail if drift occurred.

CI steps (illustrative)

- name: Clean local repo
run: rm -rf ~/.m2/repository
- name: Verify dependency locks
run: mvn -q -B clean verify -P enforce-lock
- name: “Clean room” rebuild
run: docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/w" -w /w eclipse-temurin:21-jdk bash -lc "mvn -q -B clean verify -P enforce-lock"

Reproducible artifacts (timestamps and ordering) Ensure JARs are reproducible: strip timestamps, stabilize entry ordering, and avoid embedding environment-specific paths. Many build tools support “reproducible build” flags. Enable them and verify artifact hashes are stable across clean rebuilds.

Digest references for external assets If your build fetches external tools or base images (for integration tests, for example), reference them by digest. Tags are mutable; digests fix identity. The trade-off is manual refresh when security updates appear—worth it for determinism.

Automate updates safely

Use a dependency-update bot that proposes version bumps. Gate those PRs with tests and scanning. Accepting updates becomes explicit, and drift is no longer silent.

Document the “how to fix drift” playbook

When lock enforcement fails, the fix should be documented: regenerate lock with your plugin, review changes, run tests, and commit. Avoid ad-hoc local resolutions—keep the workflow consistent.

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

Pins vs agility: Strict pins and locks slow updates but eliminate surprises. Use bots to keep pace safely.

Clean rooms vs speed: Clean rebuilds take longer. For CI, prioritize correctness over a few minutes of build time.

Digests vs tags: Digests provide determinism; tags ease maintenance. For production-critical assets, default to digests.

Failure modes

“Partial pins”: You pin direct deps but miss transitive ones. Locks solve this; without locks, drift leaks in.

“Plugin drift”: Build plugins advance silently. Pin plugin versions in pluginManagement.

“Non-reproducible JARs”: Differences in timestamps or ordering break hash equality. Turn on reproducible flags and verify.

Try it yourself

Add dependency and plugin pins in dependencyManagement/pluginManagement.

Integrate a lock mechanism; commit the lock file; add an enforcement profile.

Run a clean-room rebuild in CI and compare the artifacts. Confirm artifact hashes match between runs.

Further reading

  • Maven dependency management
  • Gradle dependency locking
  • Reproducible Builds Maven plugin

atom:entry.atom:title: Keys Don’t Belong in the Image
atom:entry.atom:summary: Managed secret stores, rotation, and guarding against the “oops, we baked a key” failure mode.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Signing keys are crown jewels in identity services. If they leak, attackers can mint forged credentials that look real. The easiest way to leak a key is to bake it into a container image or configuration file. Load signing keys at runtime from a managed secret store; keep private key material out of source files, build arguments, and image layers.

The failure mode

A contributor tests locally with a .env file containing a signing key. A sloppy Dockerfile copies everything under the project directory, including .env. CI builds the image; the key ends up in a layer. The image is pushed to a registry. Even if you rotate later, the leak is permanent in history.

What I learned

Secrets never live in source or image layers

Keep signing keys out of your repository and artifact layers. Use a managed secret store pattern to provide keys at runtime via secure mounts or platform-managed environment variables that never touch the image.

.dockerignore is a security control

Treat .dockerignore as part of your security posture. Explicitly ignore .env, credential files, test fixtures containing secrets, and local caches. Keep the build context as small as possible.

Runtime retrieval, not build-time embedding

Load keys at runtime from the secret store client library or a platform-provided mount. Fail readiness until the key loads. If the secret is missing, return clear errors and refuse to sign. Do not “fall back” to dummy keys in production—reserve test keys for explicit non-prod builds.

Rotation: short lifetimes and multiple active keys

Signing keys should rotate regularly. The verifier should accept signatures from a small set of current keys, and the issuer should roll keys with overlap: publish new key, start signing with it, keep the old key valid for verification until the overlap window expires.

Audit and scanning: prevent accidental bake-ins

Add CI checks that scan images for secret patterns. Simple rules catch common mistakes (e.g., files named .env, PEM key headers). Block the build if found. Complement this with code scanning that flags dangerous COPY patterns.

Separate test and prod key handling

For demos, use explicitly marked test keys with sandboxed scopes. Never reuse test keys in environments accessible outside controlled demos. Label logs and status endpoints so it’s obvious which environment your verifier belongs to.

Minimize key surface: hardware-backed or managed services

Where possible, use hardware-backed key stores or provider-managed keys with restricted export. Keep application access tightly scoped to “sign” and “read public key.” The app should never be able to exfiltrate private key material.

Illustrative runtime secret loading

def load_signing_key(secret_store, key_id: str) -> bytes:
    key = secret_store.read(key_id)
    if not key:
        raise RuntimeError("signing key unavailable")
    return key

# Load keys from a managed store at runtime. Never copy key material
# into source, build arguments, container layers, or sample configuration.
# Keep readiness false until the signing dependency is ready.

Example .dockerignore

.env
*.pem
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.git/
node_modules/
tests/fixtures/secrets/

Example Dockerfile pattern

FROM python:3.12-slim AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
COPY pyproject.toml poetry.lock ./
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir poetry && poetry install --no-root
COPY --chown=10001:10001 app ./app
USER 10001
EXPOSE 8000

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

Runtime dependency vs build independence: Secret store clients add runtime requirements. The gain is eliminating baked-in risk.

Rotation complexity vs safety: Overlapping keys complicate issuers and verifiers. The gain is smooth migration.

Strict readiness vs availability: Refusing to start without keys prevents undefined behavior. Availability dips are better than silent mis-signing.

Failure modes

“COPY .”: Blindly copying the entire source tree into the image. Fix with .dockerignore and explicit COPY.

“Fallback key”: Using a dummy key in production when secret load fails. Fix with hard failures and improved observability.

“Exportable private keys”: Allowing the app to export private keys. Fix with hardware-backed or provider-managed keys.

Try it yourself

Add .dockerignore entries for secrets and verify your build context (run docker build --no-cache and inspect logs).

Use strict readiness that fails until keys load from a managed store. Test rotation: accept signatures from two keys during an overlap window.

Add CI scans that fail on secret-like files in images. Track and eliminate false positives carefully.

Further reading

  • Configure Verified ID with Azure Key Vault
  • Azure Container Apps secrets
  • Docker build context and .dockerignore

atom:entry.atom:title: Tags, Digests, and Promotion
atom:entry.atom:summary: Stop deploying latest. Tag by commit, deploy by digest, and promote the exact artifact that passed your tests.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Why is staging running something different from production? If the answer involves the word latest, you have found the bug. A tag is a movable pointer, so two environments can point at different content under the same name, and nobody can say which one is right. Release hygiene comes down to one idea: the artifact that passed your tests is exactly the artifact that runs later.

Options and trade-offs

  • Mutable tags such as latest or a branch name: convenient, and impossible to trace.
  • Commit-based tags: readable and traceable, but a tag can still be moved.
  • Digests: the content address of the image, which cannot change. Deploying by digest guarantees what runs.

My recommendation

Tag every build with the commit it came from, record the digest, deploy by digest, and promote by copying the existing image rather than rebuilding. Keep a small catalog of what was released, so a rollback is just promoting an older entry.

Worked example

A release script that builds a multi-platform image, captures its digest, records it, and promotes the same digest to staging:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

REGISTRY=registry.example.com/team/app
SHA=$(git rev-parse --short=12 HEAD)

docker buildx build \
  --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
  -t "$REGISTRY:$SHA" \
  --metadata-file meta.json \
  --push .

DIGEST=$(jq -r '."containerimage.digest"' meta.json)
echo "$SHA $DIGEST $(date -u +%FT%TZ)" >> release-catalog.txt

# Promote: same content, new name. No rebuild.
docker buildx imagetools create --tag "$REGISTRY:staging" "$REGISTRY@$DIGEST"

# Deploy by digest, not tag:
echo "image: $REGISTRY@$DIGEST"

To make a running service tell you what it is, stamp the commit into the jar. In Gradle:

tasks.jar {
    manifest {
        attributes(
            "Implementation-Version" to providers.environmentVariable("GIT_SHA").orElse("dev")
        )
    }
}
public class Version {
    public static String current() {
        String v = Version.class.getPackage().getImplementationVersion();
        return v != null ? v : "dev";
    }
}

Expose Version.current() on a diagnostics route, and the answer to which build is this becomes one request.

Checklist

  1. Tag every image with the short commit hash, and never reuse a tag.
  2. Record commit, digest and time in a catalog.
  3. Deploy by digest.
  4. Promote by copying the image, not by rebuilding it.
  5. Check that the promoted manifest still contains every platform you need.
  6. Protect release images from registry clean-up so you can still debug and roll back.

Where this doesn't apply

For throwaway local images, a plain tag is fine. The discipline pays off from the first shared environment onward.

One honest limitation

Digest pinning needs tooling support, a catalog, and registry permissions to copy images. It is more work than a tag, and teams that skip the catalog lose most of the benefit.

Sources

atom:entry.atom:title: Unified Auditing: practical policies and trail hygiene
atom:entry.atom:summary: A small set of audit policies that gives you useful events without drowning in noise.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Auditing everything produces a trail nobody reads. Auditing nothing leaves you guessing after an incident. Traditional auditing was also split across several places, which made it hard to search.

Unified Auditing puts events in one trail. My question was which policies to switch on first, and how to keep that trail from filling a tablespace.

Options and trade-offs

  • Predefined policies such as ORA_SECURECONFIG and ORA_LOGIN_LOGOUT: quick wins, and worth enabling selectively.
  • Custom policies with BY, EXCEPT and WHEN: precise, and they need testing so they do not create blind spots.
  • Mirroring to syslog: improves integrity checking, and adds infrastructure to run.

My recommendation

Enable a small number of predefined policies as a baseline, then add custom policies for the actions that matter, such as privileged schema changes and key management. Schedule purging, and use the audit management package instead of deleting rows by hand.

Worked example

Start by enabling the baseline policies and confirming they are active:

AUDIT POLICY ORA_SECURECONFIG;
AUDIT POLICY ORA_LOGIN_LOGOUT;
 
SELECT policy_name FROM audit_unified_enabled_policies;

Add custom policies for high-value actions. The EXCEPT clause keeps a batch account from flooding the trail.

CREATE AUDIT POLICY ddl_pol PRIVILEGES CREATE ANY TABLE, DROP ANY TABLE;
AUDIT POLICY ddl_pol EXCEPT app_batch;
 
CREATE AUDIT POLICY keymgmt_pol ACTIONS ADMINISTER KEY MANAGEMENT;
AUDIT POLICY keymgmt_pol;
 
CREATE AUDIT POLICY hr_fail_pol ACTIONS SELECT ON hr.employees;
AUDIT POLICY hr_fail_pol WHENEVER NOT SUCCESSFUL;

Keep the trail healthy by archiving and purging through DBMS_AUDIT_MGMT:

BEGIN
  DBMS_AUDIT_MGMT.SET_LAST_ARCHIVE_TIMESTAMP(
    audit_trail_type  => DBMS_AUDIT_MGMT.AUDIT_TRAIL_UNIFIED,
    last_archive_time => SYSTIMESTAMP - INTERVAL '90' DAY);
  DBMS_AUDIT_MGMT.CLEAN_AUDIT_TRAIL(
    audit_trail_type        => DBMS_AUDIT_MGMT.AUDIT_TRAIL_UNIFIED,
    use_last_arch_timestamp => TRUE);
END;
/

Only run the purge after you have exported what you need to keep. For stronger integrity, mirror selected events to syslog so a privileged database user cannot quietly erase the only copy.

Checklist

  1. Turn on the secure configuration and login policies first.
  2. Write named policies for privileged and high-value actions.
  3. Use EXCEPT and WHEN to cut noise from known service accounts.
  4. Mirror critical events to syslog or an external system.
  5. Purge only with DBMS_AUDIT_MGMT, after archiving.
  6. Document who owns each policy and how long events are kept.

Where this doesn't apply

If a central audit platform already collects database events, coordinate scopes with it so you do not store everything twice.

One honest limitation

Broad policies create a lot of data very quickly. Start narrow, look at what you actually collect for a week, and widen only where the gaps are real.

Sources

  • Oracle Database Security Guide: Configuring Audit Policies
  • Oracle Database SQL Language Reference: CREATE AUDIT POLICY (Unified Auditing)
  • Oracle Database PL/SQL Packages Reference: DBMS_AUDIT_MGMT

atom:entry.atom:title: TDE quickstart and keystore hygiene
atom:entry.atom:summary: Turning on Transparent Data Encryption for an Oracle database, and keeping the keystore from becoming an outage.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

I wanted data at rest encrypted without rewriting applications. Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) does that, and the application stays unaware. The real work is operational: where the keystore lives, who knows its password, and what happens when it is closed or lost.

A lost keystore means unreadable data, so the hygiene matters more than the encryption command.

Options and trade-offs

  • Tablespace encryption: broad protection and a simple rollout with little application impact.
  • Column encryption: targeted protection with more DDL planning, and special care around indexes and salt.
  • Software keystore versus external key management such as OKV or OCI Vault: the software keystore is simpler, and external management centralizes keys and operations.

My recommendation

Encrypt tablespaces by default and reserve column encryption for specific fields. Configure the keystore location once, take a backup before every key change, and write the operator runbook before the first production cutover.

Worked example

Configure the keystore location. WALLET_ROOT is a static parameter, so it needs a restart. TDE_CONFIGURATION can then be set dynamically.

ALTER SYSTEM SET WALLET_ROOT = '/u01/app/oracle/admin/ORCL/wallet' SCOPE = SPFILE;
-- restart the instance, then:
ALTER SYSTEM SET TDE_CONFIGURATION = 'KEYSTORE_CONFIGURATION=FILE' SCOPE = BOTH;

Create and open the keystore, back it up, then create the master key and an auto-login keystore so the database can reopen after a restart:

ADMINISTER KEY MANAGEMENT CREATE KEYSTORE IDENTIFIED BY "<password>";
ADMINISTER KEY MANAGEMENT SET KEYSTORE OPEN IDENTIFIED BY "<password>";
ADMINISTER KEY MANAGEMENT BACKUP KEYSTORE USING 'before_first_key' IDENTIFIED BY "<password>";
ADMINISTER KEY MANAGEMENT SET KEY IDENTIFIED BY "<password>" WITH BACKUP;
ADMINISTER KEY MANAGEMENT CREATE AUTO_LOGIN KEYSTORE FROM KEYSTORE IDENTIFIED BY "<password>";

Create an encrypted tablespace, or convert an existing one online on Oracle Database 12.2 and later, then verify:

CREATE TABLESPACE secure_ts DATAFILE '<path>' SIZE 100M
  ENCRYPTION USING 'AES256' DEFAULT STORAGE (ENCRYPT);
 
ALTER TABLESPACE users ENCRYPTION ONLINE USING 'AES256' ENCRYPT;
 
SELECT wrl_type, status, wallet_type FROM v$encryption_wallet;
SELECT ts#, encryptedts FROM v$encrypted_tablespaces;

Defaults differ between releases, and multitenant databases add container-level options, so check the TDE documentation for your version before running any of this.

Checklist

  1. Set the keystore location once, and write the path down.
  2. Use AES256 for tablespace encryption unless policy says otherwise.
  3. Back up the keystore before and after every key operation.
  4. Store the keystore password and the backups separately from the database host.
  5. Check keystore status after every restart.
  6. Test export and import, and Data Guard behavior, before production.

Where this doesn't apply

Autonomous Database and many managed services already encrypt data at rest for you, so there is nothing to configure. Other database engines have their own native encryption features.

One honest limitation

The keystore is an operational dependency. If it is closed at the wrong moment, or a key rotation goes badly, the database can stop serving data. Rehearse the runbook on a non-production system first.

Sources

  • Oracle Database Advanced Security Guide: Introduction to Transparent Data Encryption
  • Oracle Database Advanced Security Guide: Configuring Transparent Data Encryption
  • Oracle Database SQL Language Reference: ADMINISTER KEY MANAGEMENT

atom:entry.atom:title: Deploying Identity Services Without a Server to Babysit
atom:entry.atom:summary: Lessons from scale-to-zero containers: cold starts, idle billing, and when latency-sensitive verifiers should stay “warm.”
atom:entry.atom:content:
Running identity-adjacent services on a scale-to-zero container platform can be delightful: no server to babysit, external HTTPS ingress, and idle billing that doesn’t punish quiet periods. With scale-to-zero containers, quiet periods can reduce idle usage. The trade-off is that the first request after an idle period may be slower, so measure that cold path against the latency needs of the service.

Identity workloads, however, bring constraints: some callers expect predictable latency, and some flows require warm caches or keys ready in memory. The trick is deciding where scale-to-zero helps and where “always on” wins.

The failure mode

You deploy a credential verifier that scales to zero. The first request after an idle period may be much slower than warm requests. A downstream system times out, retries, and amplifies load just as the platform is warming. Worse, your verifier loads keys and trust lists at startup, so the warming step is non-trivial. You saved on idle billing but created unpredictable tails.

What I learned

Cold start budget: measure and design around it

Measure cold starts: container pull, runtime initialization, key load, trust list load, and framework boot. If your end-to-end verification flow includes out-of-process checks (e.g., privacy-preserving revocation lookups), include those too. Decide whether your SLA tolerates the tails; if not, keep a minimum warm replica.

Warm critical paths with lazy loading and caches

Avoid monolithic startup. Load credential-signing keys via a managed secret store, but defer non-critical data until requested. Cache trust lists in memory and refresh asynchronously. Keep proof verification code hot by executing a tiny “self-check” during startup.

Set min replicas for latency-sensitive endpoints

If your platform supports minimum replicas, keep one verifier instance warm. Scale additional instances on demand. This hybrid approach preserves predictable latency while retaining cost controls.

Health, readiness, and the “thin ready” trap

Identity verifiers shouldn’t mark “ready” until critical dependencies (keys, trust lists) are present and a test proof passes. A “thin ready” (bare process up) can route traffic to a half-initialized instance, increasing failure rates.

Scale rules: event triggers vs queue length

If you use event-driven scale, ensure triggers reflect verifier load. Queue length or request rate are better signals than raw CPU in a verifier, since cryptographic checks are sporadic and short. Use conservative ramp-up to avoid stampedes during traffic bursts.

Idle billing: cost vs safety

Scale-to-zero saves money during periods of inactivity. In identity systems, weigh this against the cost of false timeouts and retries. For certain flows (e.g., login or checkout proofs), unpredictable tails are more expensive than idle replicas.

Pipeline hygiene: small image, quick pull

Use multi-stage builds, slim bases, and .dockerignore to keep images small. The smaller the image, the faster cold start. Avoid compiling dependencies at startup; freeze them in the image. Keep secrets out of layers entirely (next article).

Illustrative configuration

# Generic container-app.yaml structure
name: identity-service
ingress:
  external: true
  targetPort: 8000
template:
  containers:
    - image: your-registry/identity-service:tag
      resources:
        cpu: 0.5
        memory: 0.5Gi
  probes:
    liveness:
      httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8000 }
    readiness:
      httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8000 }
  scale:
    minReplicas: 1 # Keep one warm replica
    maxReplicas: 10
    rules:
      - name: http-requests
        http: { metadata: { concurrentRequests: "50" } }

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

Cost vs predictability: Scale-to-zero cuts idle spend but risks unpredictable tails. Hybrid min replicas often balance both.

Strict readiness vs fast green: Stricter readiness delays routing but avoids half-initialized failures. Bias toward strict in identity contexts.

Lazy load vs startup completeness: Deferring non-critical data speeds boot but adds first-request work. Choose wisely.

Failure modes

“Thin ready”: Traffic routed to instances without loaded keys or trust lists. Fix readiness to validate critical paths.

“Stampede”: Traffic surge triggers too many replicas and cache thrash. Fix scale rules and backpressure.

“Oversized image”: Cold starts dominated by image pulls. Fix Docker hygiene.

Try it yourself

Measure the cold start path and identify high-cost steps. Record cold-start and warm-request latency as separate measurements.

Add a minimum warm replica and track tails. Compare p95 across scale-to-zero vs hybrid.

Implement readiness that runs a tiny proof self-check and confirms secret load before returning ready.

Further reading

  • Scale applications in Azure Container Apps
  • Health probes in Azure Container Apps

atom:entry.atom:title: Device Settings Through Wrappers: ONNX Runtime and OpenVINO
atom:entry.atom:summary: How the OpenVINO execution provider for ONNX Runtime selects devices, how provider options pass per-device properties and a cache directory, and a probe that…
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Many teams use OpenVINO through another library, and ONNX Runtime's OpenVINO execution provider is one example. Each wrapper has its own configuration surface, and it is not identical to OpenVINO's own property names and behavior.

That difference causes a quiet class of problems. A setting that works when you call OpenVINO directly may be ignored or reshaped by a wrapper, and the default device may not be the one you expect.

The friction points are knowing the default device, knowing which OpenVINO version the wrapper bundles, and knowing which options your installed version really accepts.

Options and trade-offs

  • Default device: the PyPI page for the OpenVINO execution provider package states that, by default, the Intel CPU is used for inference, and that you can change this to an integrated GPU, a discrete GPU, or an integrated NPU through the provider configuration's device type argument.
  • Bundled runtime: the same page says the Linux wheels at that time came with pre-built libraries of OpenVINO 2025.4.1, so the OpenVINO inside the wrapper may differ from one you installed separately. Check the version your package carries.
  • Provider options: ONNX Runtime GenAI's documentation for the OpenVINO provider shows device_type, cache_dir, and a load_config block with per-device properties, for example INFERENCE_PRECISION_HINT and PERFORMANCE_HINT under a CPU key. The page also advises choosing the device by goal: CPU for latency, GPU for throughput, and NPU for efficiency.
  • Per-device properties: placing properties under the device they apply to, as in the load_config example, avoids applying a setting meant for one device to all of them.
  • Cache directory: the same documentation shows cache_dir as a provider option to reduce model loading time on later runs. As with direct OpenVINO use, confirm with a restart test that it works.
  • Direct OpenVINO use gives you every property OpenVINO exposes and clearer errors, at the cost of more integration code. If a wrapper does not expose something you need, consider using OpenVINO directly for that component.
  • Recommendation: treat provider options as deployment configuration. Write them in one place, record the library versions beside them, and re-run a probe whenever you upgrade. Copy option names from the page for the version you installed, not from memory, and prefer explicit device names and per-device properties in production.
  • Decision lens: convenience versus control. Example setup: a service that loads models through ONNX Runtime with one configuration file listing the device type, cache directory, and per-device properties, plus a note of the versions on which that file was tested.

Minimal working example

Prereqs

  • Python 3 in a clean virtual environment with the onnxruntime-openvino package installed. Do not install it next to the plain onnxruntime package in the same environment.
  • An ONNX model you already use.
  • A writable cache folder.

provider_probe.py

import onnxruntime as ort

print("ONNX Runtime version:", ort.__version__)
print("Available providers:", ort.get_available_providers())

providers = [("OpenVINOExecutionProvider", {"device_type": "CPU", "cache_dir": "./ov_cache"})]
session = ort.InferenceSession("model.onnx", providers=providers)
print("Session providers:", session.get_providers())

If OpenVINOExecutionProvider is missing from the available providers, your installed package does not include it, and ONNX Runtime will fall back to another provider.

Adjust file names, model names, and paths to your own setup.

Test: Run provider_probe.py and check that OpenVINOExecutionProvider appears in the available providers and in the session's providers. Run it a second time to see whether load time drops with cache_dir. If the machine has a GPU or NPU, change device_type and record what changes.

Record: ONNX Runtime and provider package versions; the OpenVINO version bundled in the package; the providers available and the providers the session reports for each device type; load time with and without cache_dir, first versus second run; behavior when a requested device is absent; the configuration you chose for production.

Checklist

  • Record every library version.
  • Confirm the provider is actually available.
  • Set the device type explicitly and place properties under the device they apply to.
  • Test cache_dir with a restart.
  • Keep the verified configuration in your repository and re-run the probe after every upgrade.
  • Avoid: assuming the wrapper's OpenVINO version matches your standalone install.
  • Avoid: copying option names from another version's documentation.

Where this doesn't apply

Applications that call OpenVINO directly, and systems using a different OpenVINO integration than ONNX Runtime.

Sources

  • onnxruntime-openvino on PyPI
  • ONNX Runtime GenAI: OpenVINO execution provider
  • OpenVINO Model Caching Overview
