atom:entry.atom:title: OCIR basics: push/pull, private repos, auth tokens
atom:entry.atom:summary: The registry commands I actually run, and the small details that cause most login failures.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Registry (OCIR) is simple once you know the rules, and confusing until then. Most failures come from the same few places: a wrong region endpoint, a wrong username format, or an expired token.

I wanted a short reference that gets a private repository working and keeps it private.

Options and trade-offs

  • Public repositories: easy to share, and only suitable for images that are safe for anyone to pull.
  • Private repositories with auth tokens: the standard approach, and it needs good token hygiene.
  • Short-lived or bearer-style credentials: possible for pipelines, with more setup to maintain.

My recommendation

Use private repositories and user auth tokens. Create the repository explicitly in the compartment that owns it, instead of letting a first push create it. Keep the regional endpoint and the username format written down where the team can find them.

Worked example

Log in with the registry endpoint for your region. The username begins with your tenancy namespace. If your user belongs to a non-default identity domain or is federated, the username format changes, so check the documentation for your case.

docker login <region-key>.ocir.io
# Username: <tenancy-namespace>/<username>
# Password: <auth-token>
 
oci artifacts container repository create \
  --compartment-id <compartment_ocid> \
  --display-name myteam/myapp \
  --is-public false
 
docker tag myapp:1.4.2 <region-key>.ocir.io/<tenancy-namespace>/myteam/myapp:1.4.2
docker push <region-key>.ocir.io/<tenancy-namespace>/myteam/myapp:1.4.2

And the policies, kept separate for people who browse and people who manage:

Allow group image-viewers to inspect repos in tenancy
Allow group image-publishers to manage repos in compartment registry

I tag with a version, not latest, so a rollback is a one-line change. A user can hold only a small number of auth tokens, so plan token replacement for your pipelines before it is urgent.

Checklist

  1. Know the endpoint for your region and use it consistently.
  2. Use the tenancy namespace in the username, and the auth token as the password.
  3. Create repositories explicitly and confirm they are private.
  4. Set separate policies for viewing and managing repositories.
  5. Tag images with versions, and avoid latest in production.
  6. Set a retention rule, and watch pulls for surprises.

Where this doesn't apply

Air-gapped clusters cannot reach OCIR directly. They need a mirrored or internal registry instead.

One honest limitation

Auth tokens expire or get replaced, and a stale token in a pipeline fails at the worst time. Treat it like any other credential and give it an owner and a rotation date.

Sources

  • OCI Documentation: Pushing Images Using the Docker CLI
  • OCI Documentation: Logging in to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Registry
  • OCI Documentation: Required Policies for Container Registry

atom:entry.atom:title: Programmatic rollout of Workload Identity
atom:entry.atom:summary: Scope, phasing and incident readiness when moving AKS workloads from AAD Pod Identity or static secrets to Workload Identity.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

AKS Workload Identity replaces the deprecated AAD Pod Identity and removes static secrets from pods. A rollout touches the control plane, depends on SDK versions in every workload, and can fail in ways that only show up under load or after a token refresh. Without a plan, the first sign of a problem is an application that cannot reach its database.

Options and trade-offs

  • Enable the OIDC issuer and Workload Identity on the cluster: a one-time change with a short control-plane impact. Announce a window for it.
  • Parallel migration: run Workload Identity next to Pod Identity, move one workload at a time, verify each, then remove Pod Identity. It is slower, and it is the only approach with a clean rollback.
  • Sidecar proxy for older SDKs: a temporary bridge that intercepts calls to the instance metadata endpoint for workloads that cannot upgrade yet. Treat it as a deadline, not a destination.

My recommendation

Migrate per namespace, starting with a low-risk internal workload. Define rollback criteria before the first change: error rate on token acquisition, authentication failures to the target service, and pod restarts. Do not remove Pod Identity until every workload has run on Workload Identity through at least one full token-renewal cycle.

Minimal working example

Enable the cluster features and look up the issuer:

az aks update --resource-group <rg> --name <aks> \
  --enable-oidc-issuer --enable-workload-identity

OIDC_ISSUER=$(az aks show -g <rg> -n <aks> --query "oidcIssuerProfile.issuerUrl" -o tsv)

Create a managed identity and federate it with one service account:

az identity create --name app-identity --resource-group <rg>
CLIENT_ID=$(az identity show -n app-identity -g <rg> --query clientId -o tsv)

az identity federated-credential create \
  --name app-fic \
  --identity-name app-identity \
  --resource-group <rg> \
  --issuer "$OIDC_ISSUER" \
  --subject system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:app-sa \
  --audience api://AzureADTokenExchange

Annotate the service account and label the pod:

apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: app-sa
  namespace: <namespace>
  annotations:
    azure.workload.identity/client-id: "<client-id>"
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: <namespace>
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: app }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: app
        azure.workload.identity/use: "true"
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: app-sa
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: <registry>/app:<tag>

Test it: deploy one workload, confirm it acquires a token and reaches its Azure dependency, then restart it and confirm it still does after the token refreshes.

Checklist

  • Inventory workloads that still call the instance metadata endpoint or use older SDKs, and decide per workload whether to upgrade or bridge.
  • Use one service account and one federated credential per workload identity, and keep least-privilege Azure RBAC on the identity.
  • Write down rollback criteria and who decides, before the change window.
  • Migrate one namespace at a time, and watch token errors and pod restarts after each.
  • Remove Pod Identity only after every workload has been stable on Workload Identity, and confirm the add-on's end-of-support dates.
  • Keep a record of every federated credential so stale ones can be cleaned up.

Where this doesn't apply

Kubernetes clusters outside Azure. They need the equivalent OIDC issuer configuration and federation, if the platform offers it.

Sources

  • Workload Identity overview
  • Migrate from Pod Identity
  • Use AAD Pod Identity (deprecation notice)

atom:entry.atom:title: Records Aren’t Just Less Typing: Modeling Ambiguity Without Nulls
atom:entry.atom:summary: How I use records, sealed interfaces, and pattern matching to model “present,” “missing,” and “unverifiable” — and force callers to handle every case.
atom:entry.atom:content:
I’m an engineering manager with a background in Java backend systems. One lesson that keeps paying dividends is this: ambiguity deserves types, not comments. Nulls and booleans blur meaning. “false,” “zero,” and “we don’t know” are not interchangeable. With modern Java (records, sealed interfaces, pattern matching), I model uncertainty explicitly and make ambiguity impossible to ignore.

Modern Java can express these outcomes as records and sealed types: Present, Missing, and Unverifiable. The same pattern works in ordinary service domains; it does not depend on a scoring model.

The failure mode

You return a number for a score and a boolean “hasEvidence.” A caller subtracts two scores and treats “0” as “no evidence,” then logs an anomaly when “0” appears alongside “hasEvidence=true.” The model caused this. Nulls and booleans encourage shortcuts and misinterpretation.

What I learned

Use records for immutable, transparent domain data

Records let me define concise, immutable carriers without boilerplate. They encourage a bias toward immutability and make the intent clear.

Example response

public record AceuResponse(
ScoreOrUnknown authenticity,
ScoreOrUnknown credibility,
ScoreOrUnknown empathy,
ScoreOrUnknown uniqueness
) {}
public sealed interface ScoreOrUnknown permits Score, Missing, Unverifiable {}
public record Score(double value) implements ScoreOrUnknown {
public Score {
if (Double.isNaN(value) || value < 0.0 || value > 1.0) {
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Score must be [0,1]");
}
}
}
public record Missing(String reason) implements ScoreOrUnknown {}
public record Unverifiable(String note) implements ScoreOrUnknown {}

Records keep the data small and immutable. The sealed hierarchy enforces the set of states at compile time.

Replace nulls and boolean flags with sealed states

The temptation to use Double/Boolean and encode special states with null or false is strong. Resist it. Sealed interfaces make the valid state space explicit and force exhaustive handling. A boolean can’t distinguish “not applicable,” “not yet computed,” and “calculation failed.”

Use pattern matching for exhaustive case handling

Pattern matching in switch makes code read like the domain. It also turns omissions into compile errors when you use exhaustive switches.

Example handler:

public String render(ScoreOrUnknown s) {
return switch (s) {
case Score sc          -> "score=" + sc.value();
case Missing miss      -> "missing=" + miss.reason();
case Unverifiable unv  -> "unverifiable=" + unv.note();

};

}

By handling each case explicitly, I make it impossible to “forget” one or conflate states.

Prefer intent-rich types over ad-hoc maps and strings

When a state needs more context (e.g., why data is missing), capture it in the type. Missing(String reason) and Unverifiable(String note) beat opaque strings and comments. If callers need to act differently based on the reason, add a reason code enum to the record.

Keep aggregates typed—don’t flatten too early

A response with four dimensions should preserve each dimension’s state. Avoid flattening to a single “overall score.” The minute you collapse, you discard information the caller needs for good decisions. In the demo, each dimension returns a ScoreOrUnknown. Only the caller decides how to combine them, and the compiler forces handling of unknowns.

Embed validation where it belongs

Put invariants in the type’s constructor. Scores are [0,1]; reasons should be concise, not multi-paragraph blobs. Records make these guardrails trivial to implement consistently.

Use test fixtures that exercise every branch

Define parameterized tests for your sealed states. For each dimension, test Score, Missing, and Unverifiable. Assert that pattern matching hits each branch, and that any new state added later causes compilation failures in exhaustive switches until it’s handled.

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

More types vs fewer booleans: Sealed types add structure and a few extra classes. The upside is clarity and compile-time enforcement; the downside is minor boilerplate, which records minimize.

Exhaustiveness vs flexibility: Exhaustive switches break on new states until handled. That’s a feature (safety) but can feel strict when you prototype quickly.

Text reasons vs structured codes: Free-form strings are easier; structured enums enable programmatic handling. Choose based on how callers use the data.

Failure modes

“Shadow nulls”

A downstream library returns null and you forget to wrap it in a sealed state. Guard external boundaries with adapters.

“State leakage”: Someone serializes ScoreOrUnknown to a shape that drops the state label (e.g., value=0.0 only). Add JSON configuration that includes a type field and test the wire format.

“Catch-all case”: Using a default branch in pattern matching reintroduces ambiguity. Avoid default; keep exhaustive cases explicit.

Try it yourself

Replace nullable fields for ambiguous states with a sealed interface and record implementations. Add exhaustive pattern matching where you consume them.

Write tests that construct each state per dimension and assert wire-format correctness (e.g., JSON includes the state “type”).

Audit one path where a null sneaks through and add an adapter to convert it into Missing or Unverifiable with a reason code.

Further reading

  • Records (JEP 395)
  • Sealed Classes (JEP 409)
  • Pattern Matching for switch (JEP 441)

atom:entry.atom:title: AUTO vs Explicit Devices vs HETERO in OpenVINO
atom:entry.atom:summary: A practical comparison of three ways to choose where OpenVINO runs a model, what AUTO actually does at startup, and a test that shows which strategy holds up…
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

OpenVINO lets you name a device directly, ask for AUTO selection, or split a model across devices with HETERO. They look like three spellings of one decision, but they behave differently when a device is missing, when you restart, and when you cache compiled models.

The wrong choice rarely fails loudly. It shows up as a first request served by a different device than you expected, a cache that never hits, or a fallback that quietly runs on the CPU and misses a latency target.

The friction points are knowing what AUTO does at startup, knowing where work actually ran, and testing restarts instead of only first starts.

Options and trade-offs

  • Explicit device: compile for CPU, GPU, or NPU by name. The behavior is easiest to reason about, and the compiled-model cache belongs to that concrete device. Routing and failover are your application's job.
  • AUTO: the documentation says AUTO detects available devices and selects the best one automatically. By default it starts inference on the CPU unless there is a cached model for the best-suited device, because the CPU can start with no additional delay. While the CPU runs inference, AUTO keeps loading the model onto the better device and hands the work over when ready.
  • AUTO startup behavior is configurable: the enable_startup_fallback property controls whether the CPU is used as the initial helper device (default true), and enable_runtime_fallback controls whether a failed inference request is retried on another device (default true). Excluding the CPU from the priority list disables the initial CPU acceleration.
  • AUTO reports where work actually ran: the execution_devices property lists the devices currently executing inference. Logging it is the cheapest way to avoid surprises.
  • A published OpenVINO blog describes AUTO trying the next best device if the model does not compile on the first choice, with the CPU as the final fallback because it supports all operations and precisions.
  • HETERO splits one model across several devices. It is meant for cases where a model does not fit on one device or part of it needs different hardware. It adds configuration and testing work, so treat it as a special-purpose tool and test the exact model and device pair you intend to ship.
  • Caching interaction: compiling explicitly for each device you use makes cache behavior easy to reason about. With AUTO, early requests may be served by the CPU while the better device loads, so first-request latency depends on whether a cached model exists for that better device.
  • Recommendation: use an explicit device when you need predictable startup and cache behavior, and put routing and failover in your application where you can log and test them. Use AUTO when portability across machines matters more than deterministic timing, and always log execution_devices. Treat HETERO as an advanced option adopted only when a specific model needs it.
  • Decision lens: predictability versus portability. Example setup: an application that runs on laptops with varied hardware uses AUTO and logs its execution device; a service on a fixed server fleet compiles explicitly for the device it has.

Minimal working example

Prereqs

  • Python 3 with the openvino package installed.
  • A machine with at least two device types if possible, such as CPU and an integrated GPU or NPU.
  • A model you already run.

compare_devices.py

import sys, time
import openvino as ov

model_path = sys.argv[1]
core = ov.Core()
core.set_property({"CACHE_DIR": "./model_cache"})
print("Available devices:", core.available_devices)

for target in ["CPU", "AUTO"]:
    start = time.perf_counter()
    compiled = core.compile_model(model_path, target)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    print(target, f"compile {elapsed:.3f}s", "executing on:", compiled.get_property("EXECUTION_DEVICES"))

Add "GPU" or "NPU" to the list if your machine has them.

Adjust file names, model names, and paths to your own setup.

Test: Run compare_devices.py twice in separate processes, once with an empty cache folder and once with a populated one. Note the device reported by EXECUTION_DEVICES right after compilation and again after a few inferences, because AUTO can switch devices. If you can do it safely, disable a device and rerun to see how each strategy reacts.

Record: devices present and OpenVINO version; device reported by AUTO right after compile and after warm-up; time to first inference for each strategy with an empty and a populated cache, as median and 95th percentile; behavior when the preferred device is unavailable; your decision and the reason.

Checklist

  • Log the executing device in every run.
  • Compile explicitly per device when cache behavior must be predictable.
  • Review the startup and runtime fallback settings if you use AUTO.
  • Test restarts, not only first starts, and pin the versions you tested.
  • Document the failover behavior you observed.
  • Avoid: assuming AUTO serves the first request on the best device.
  • Avoid: adopting HETERO without testing the exact model.

Where this doesn't apply

Single-device deployments where the choice is trivial, systems whose hardware is fixed and known (explicit selection is simpler), and models too large for any single device, where HETERO may be unavoidable.

Sources

  • Automatic Device Selection documentation
  • Automatic Device Selection and Configuration (OpenVINO blog)
  • OpenVINO Model Caching Overview

atom:entry.atom:title: Cache Correctness: Verifying Warm Starts
atom:entry.atom:summary: What reusing a compiled-model cache assumes, how to check that a cache exists and results match, and how to make a service fail closed on a bad warm start.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Caching exists to save time, so it is tempting to treat it as invisible. But a cached artifact is a compiled program saved to disk. Reusing it assumes that the conditions that produced it still hold: the same device, a compatible software version, and the same model and input shapes.

Two things make this risky in practice. OpenVINO's documentation says devices without import and export support run normally but do not get the speed-up, so a missing cache does not announce itself. And an artifact left over from an earlier version or a different model can be picked up by accident if folders are not separated.

The friction points are confirming that a cache was created, confirming that a warm start produces the same outputs as a cold start, and refusing to serve when it does not.

Options and trade-offs

  • Check that something was cached: after the first run, the cache folder should contain new files. An empty folder after a successful compile suggests the device does not support caching or the folder is not writable.
  • Compare outputs: run one fixed input through a freshly compiled model and through a model loaded from the cache, then compare the results with a tolerance you choose in advance. For deterministic models on the same device, exact equality is a reasonable expectation; choose a tolerance only if your pipeline needs one.
  • Separate cache folders by software version, model version, device, and input shape. This costs nothing and removes a whole class of confusing failures.
  • Fail closed: if the output comparison fails or loading from the cache raises an error, delete that cache entry, recompile, and log the event. Do not serve from a cache you could not verify.
  • Keep the check cheap: a single fixed input at startup usually catches a gross failure, and it can run alongside your warm-up request.
  • Be cautious with outside reports: issue trackers contain reports about specific edge cases. Treat them as leads for your own tests, and do not build policy around a problem you cannot reproduce on your version.
  • Recommendation: add a verification step to startup. After the model loads, run one fixed input and compare it with a stored reference. If the comparison fails, discard the cache entry, recompile, and record that the warm start was rejected. Log whether each start was cold or cached, how long compilation took, and which device and versions were involved.
  • Decision lens: speed against silent error risk. Example setup: a service checks one reference input after every restart, treats a mismatch as a failed start, and writes each version's cache to its own directory so an upgrade never reads the previous version's files.

Minimal working example

Prereqs

  • Python 3 with openvino and numpy installed.
  • A model with a floating-point input; adjust the dtype in the script if yours differs.
  • A writable cache folder.

verify_cache.py (run with fresh first, then cached twice)

import sys
import numpy as np
import openvino as ov

model_path, mode = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]  # mode: fresh or cached
core = ov.Core()
if mode == "cached":
    core.set_property({"CACHE_DIR": "./model_cache"})
compiled = core.compile_model(model_path, "CPU")

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
shape = [d.get_length() for d in compiled.input(0).partial_shape]
x = rng.random(shape, dtype=np.float32)  # adjust dtype to match your model
result = compiled(x)[compiled.output(0)]

if mode == "fresh":
    np.save("reference.npy", result)
    print("saved reference")
else:
    reference = np.load("reference.npy")
    print("max abs difference:", float(np.max(np.abs(reference - result))))

Adjust file names, model names, and paths to your own setup.

Test: Run verify_cache.py with fresh to store a reference, then with cached to populate the cache, then with cached again to compare an imported model against the reference. Next, change the model file (or its version folder) and confirm that your folder naming prevents the old cache from being used. Repeat after upgrading OpenVINO. A difference larger than the tolerance you chose is a failed start.

Record: device, operating system, OpenVINO version, and model; files present in the cache folder after the first run; maximum absolute output difference between cold and cached; the tolerance you chose and why; behavior after the model changes; behavior after an upgrade; time added by the startup check.

Checklist

  • Confirm the cache folder is populated after the first run.
  • Compare a fixed output between a cold run and a cached run, and record your tolerance.
  • Separate cache folders by version, model, device, and shape.
  • Fail closed and recompile on a mismatch.
  • Log cold or cached on every start, and re-run the check after every upgrade.
  • Avoid: assuming a cache exists because no error appeared.
  • Avoid: reusing one cache folder across versions or models.

Where this doesn't apply

Services that never use compiled-model caching, and systems that already compare outputs against a reference on every start.

Sources

  • OpenVINO Model Caching Overview
  • OpenVINO Model Server parameters
  • OpenVINO NPU device documentation

atom:entry.atom:title: A Breaking Change in Someone Else’s PR
atom:entry.atom:summary: When a plugin interface change passes CI and breaks downstream work, you need versioning, deprecation windows, and contract tests.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Community projects depend on contributions from people who did not write the original code. That openness creates a compatibility challenge: a change can pass local unit tests while still breaking plugins written against the documented interface. Extensibility needs contract tests and clear versioning.

The failure mode

A contributor refactors a plugin interface, renaming a method and changing its return shape. Their tests pass. Your CI passes. You merge. One week later, a different contributor’s PR, built on the previous interface, fails unexpectedly. You didn’t catch the breaking change because you had no compatibility tests enforcing the plugin contract.

What I learned

Treat extension points as public contracts

If you support a plugin API, document it as a minimal, stable contract. Keep it small, reduce optional features, and define explicit versioning. Favor additive changes; avoid changing semantics quietly.

Minimal contract (illustrative)

# your_project/core.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class EvidenceResult:
type: str  # "present" | "missing" | "unverifiable"
note: str = ""
score_delta: float = 0.0
class EvidenceSource:
name: str
def evaluate(self, profile: dict) -> EvidenceResult:
"""
Input: dictionary of profile fields (synthetic in demo)
Output: EvidenceResult with type, note, and optional score_delta
"""
raise NotImplementedError

Version the interface explicitly

Add an interface version constant in the core module. Plugins import and declare the version they target. CI checks that plugin declarations match the core version and that any bump is accompanied by a deprecation window.

Versioning example:

# your_project/core_version.py
INTERFACE_VERSION = "1.2.0"  # semantic versioned
# plugin declares support
SUPPORTED_VERSIONS = {"1.2.0"}  # plugins can add multiple supported versions

Deprecation windows — commit to dates and behavior When you change the interface, announce deprecations with a grace window: two minor releases or a set number of weeks. During the window, keep the old behavior working and warn at runtime (without breaking tests). At the end, remove the old path and bump the interface version.

Contract tests in CI

Unit tests validate plugin internals. Contract tests validate extension points. Write tests that load every plugin and execute a baseline scenario: call evaluate() with a standard profile, assert return types and fields, and assert compatibility with the current core version. Fail the build on mismatch.

Contract test skeleton:

import importlib

from your_project.core import EvidenceResult
from your_project.core_version import INTERFACE_VERSION

PLUGIN_MODULES = ["your_project.plugins.example_plugin"]

def test_all_plugins_implement_contract():
    for module_name in PLUGIN_MODULES:
        module = importlib.import_module(module_name)
        plugin = module.ExamplePlugin()
        result = plugin.evaluate({"example": True})
        assert isinstance(result, EvidenceResult)
        assert result.status in {"present", "missing", "unverifiable"}
        assert INTERFACE_VERSION in module.SUPPORTED_VERSIONS

Your CI should run both unit and contract tests. If the core changes, test the change against every supported plugin. If external plugins live in separate repositories, publish a small test harness they can add to their own CI.

Communicate interface changes in release notes Semantic version your interface. A breaking change to the plugin API is a major bump. The release notes should list exactly what changed and a minimal migration example. They should also link deprecation windows and final removal dates.

Example release note

## Plugin API 2.0.0 (breaking)
- Keep the result status field unchanged.
- Make the score delta field required.
- Migration: provide a zero delta when a plugin has no score change.
- Publish a deprecation window and removal date.

Keep extension points narrow Every new method or field in a plugin contract increases fragility. Keep it small. If contributors want flexibility, let them model complexity inside their plugin; keep the core contract simple, documented, and testable.

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

Strict contract tests vs contributor agility: Some contributors will feel slowed by extra checks. Counterbalance with templates and examples.

Deprecation windows vs maintenance overhead: Maintaining old paths for a window adds complexity. Keep windows short and focused for small projects.

Central testing vs distributed plugins

If plugins live elsewhere, you can’t run their tests pre-merge. Provide a harness and encourage adoption.

Failure modes

“Silent break”

A contributor changes the contract; unit tests pass; no compatibility suite fails. Solution: contract tests that load plugins and validate the core expectations.

“Major bump fatigue”: Frequent major bumps erode trust. Solution: batch breaking changes and make additive changes where possible.

“Ambiguous release notes”: Vague notes cause confusion. Solution: concrete migration steps and example code in release notes.

Try it yourself

Add an INTERFACE_VERSION constant and require plugins to declare supported versions.

Implement CI contract tests that import and execute all plugins against the core contract.

Document a deprecation window policy in CONTRIBUTING.md. Commit to timelines and stick to them.

Further reading

  • Semantic Versioning 2.0.0
  • Keep a Changelog
  • GitHub Actions: Building and testing

atom:entry.atom:title: Vault + DB wallets: secure distribution patterns (illustrative)
atom:entry.atom:summary: Generating an Autonomous Database wallet, keeping it in Vault, and rebuilding it only where it is needed.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Mutual TLS to Autonomous Database needs a wallet. In practice that wallet ends up in a chat thread, in a repo, or baked into a container image, and rotating it means finding every copy.

I wanted the wallet to have one home, a controlled way out, and a short life on disk.

Options and trade-offs

  • Copying the wallet files around: fast, hard to rotate and hard to audit.
  • Wallet files as Vault secrets: access is governed by IAM and logged. The files need encoding and a rebuild step.
  • Server-authenticated TLS without a wallet: fewer artifacts. It depends on the database allowing TLS connections without mTLS.

My recommendation

Generate the wallet from the database service, store its files as Vault secrets, and let the runtime principal read them at startup. The application recreates the files in a protected directory, sets TNS_ADMIN, and connects through the TNS alias.

Worked example

Generate the wallet and push the files into Vault. The CLI needs base64 content, while the Console encodes plain text for you.

oci db autonomous-database generate-wallet \
  --autonomous-database-id <db_ocid> \
  --file wallet.zip \
  --password "<wallet_password>"
 
unzip wallet.zip -d wallet
base64 -w0 wallet/cwallet.sso > cwallet.sso.b64
 
oci vault secret create-base64 \
  --compartment-id <compartment_ocid> \
  --vault-id <vault_ocid> \
  --key-id <symmetric_key_ocid> \
  --secret-name db_wallet_cwallet_sso \
  --secret-content-content "$(cat cwallet.sso.b64)" \
  --secret-content-stage CURRENT

Repeat for the other files the connection needs, usually tnsnames.ora, sqlnet.ora and ojdbc.properties. At startup, the app reads each secret, decodes it and writes it into a directory only its own user can access. The sketch below shows the permission handling.

Path dir = Files.createTempDirectory("wallet",
    PosixFilePermissions.asFileAttribute(PosixFilePermissions.fromString("rwx------")));
for (var e : walletSecrets.entrySet()) {          // name -> base64 content
    Files.write(dir.resolve(e.getKey()), Base64.getDecoder().decode(e.getValue()));
}
// start the JVM or pool with -Doracle.net.tns_admin=<dir> or TNS_ADMIN=<dir>

The ojdbc.properties file that ships in the wallet refers to the TNS_ADMIN directory for its wallet location, so it works unchanged when you rebuild the directory.

Checklist

  1. Generate the wallet from the database service and track when it expires.
  2. Store each file as a secret, using base64 for CLI and API paths.
  3. Give the runtime principal read access to those secrets only.
  4. Rebuild the wallet directory at runtime with owner-only permissions, and never bake it into an image.
  5. Confirm the server certificate name check is on, and log wallet reads.
  6. Keep the previous secret version for a short time in case rotation goes wrong.

Where this doesn't apply

If your policy allows server-authenticated TLS, you may not need a wallet at all. That removes the distribution problem entirely.

One honest limitation

Wallets are multi-file, and the cleanup of temporary files is easy to forget. Test the rebuild path and the deletion path as carefully as the connection itself.

atom:entry.atom:title: Container limits and the JVM: why your heap is not your memory limit
atom:entry.atom:summary: A practical look at memory and CPU limits for Java services: sizing the heap, surviving back-pressure and recognising an out-of-memory kill.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Without limits, a hot container can starve its neighbours. With limits that are too tight, it gets killed and restarts in a loop. Either way, the failure spreads: one tier is slow, upstream timeouts fire, retries pile up, and a small problem becomes an outage. On the JVM there is an extra trap. The heap is only part of the memory a process uses. Metaspace, thread stacks, the code cache, direct buffers and GC structures all live outside it, so a container limit equal to the heap size is almost guaranteed to be exceeded.

Options and trade-offs

  • No limits: nothing gets killed by the runtime, but one runaway service can degrade the whole host.
  • A hard limit with a fixed -Xmx: predictable, but easy to get wrong when the limit changes and the heap flag does not.
  • A hard limit with a percentage-based heap: the JVM sizes the heap from the container limit, and you leave headroom for everything else.

My recommendation

Set a memory limit, let the JVM size its heap from it with a percentage, and leave real headroom for native memory. Bound every queue so overload becomes a fast, explicit refusal instead of a slow death. Make the out-of-memory case easy to recognise.

Worked example

The Compose file sets the limit and tells the JVM to use 70 percent of it for the heap. The rest is headroom.

services:
  api:
    image: demo/api:1.4.2
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8080:8080"
    environment:
      JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError"
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.0"
          memory: 512M

A tiny program shows what the JVM actually sees inside the container, which is the first thing to check when sizing goes wrong:

public class WhatDoIHave {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Runtime rt = Runtime.getRuntime();
        System.out.printf("processors=%d maxHeap=%dMB%n",
                rt.availableProcessors(), rt.maxMemory() / (1024 * 1024));
    }
}

For back-pressure, use a bounded queue and refuse work when it is full, instead of accepting everything and falling over later:

import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class BoundedWorkers {
    private final ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
            4, 4, 0L, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS,
            new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100),
            new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy());

    /** Returns an HTTP-style status: 202 accepted, 503 over capacity. */
    public int submit(Runnable task) {
        try {
            pool.execute(task);
            return 202;
        } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) {
            return 503;
        }
    }
}

When a container disappears with exit code 137, check whether the kernel killed it:

docker inspect --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.State.ExitCode}}' api
docker stats --no-stream api

Checklist

  1. Set memory and CPU limits, and write down why each number was chosen.
  2. Use a heap percentage, and leave headroom for native memory.
  3. Bound every queue, and return a clear over-capacity response when it is full.
  4. Log queue depth, rejected work and memory use so the problem is visible before the kill.
  5. Load test with the real limits applied, and watch what the upstream tier does.

Where this doesn't apply

These numbers are starting points for a small service. Large heaps, many threads or heavy direct-buffer use all change the headroom you need, and only measurement on your own workload settles it.

One honest limitation

Limits shrink the blast radius but do not prevent incidents. A service that is out of memory still fails; the point is that it fails predictably and recovers quickly.

Sources

  • Docker Docs: Resource constraints
  • Oracle Java Documentation: Java in containers (JVM ergonomics)
  • Docker Docs: docker container inspect

atom:entry.atom:title: Java Records and Jackson: Null Safety and Schema Evolution
atom:entry.atom:summary: Designing JSON contracts that survive years of change, with property-based tests
atom:entry.atom:content:
A record as a contract

import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonIgnoreProperties;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonInclude;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.Optional;

@JsonInclude(JsonInclude.Include.NON_ABSENT)
@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)
public record Profile(String id, Optional<String> headline, List<String> skills) {

    public Profile {
        Objects.requireNonNull(id, "id");
        headline = headline == null ? Optional.empty() : headline;
        skills = skills == null ? List.of() : List.copyOf(skills);
    }
}
  • The compact constructor makes id required and normalizes missing optional data, so no code downstream handles null for headline or skills.
  • Optional<String> marks headline as optional in the type itself. (Records with Optional need Jackson's jackson-datatype-jdk8 module registered.)
  • NON_ABSENT leaves an absent optional out of the JSON instead of writing an explicit null.
  • ignoreUnknown = true lets this reader tolerate fields that newer producers add.
ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper()
        .registerModule(new Jdk8Module());

Why not plain POJOs?

The silent coercion trap

Profile p = mapper.readValue("{\"id\": 42}", Profile.class);
// p.id() is "42", with no error
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.cfg.CoercionAction;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.cfg.CoercionInputShape;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.type.LogicalType;

ObjectMapper strict = new ObjectMapper().registerModule(new Jdk8Module());
strict.coercionConfigFor(LogicalType.Textual)
      .setCoercion(CoercionInputShape.Integer, CoercionAction.Fail)
      .setCoercion(CoercionInputShape.Float, CoercionAction.Fail);

Null, absent, and present

Evolving schemas safely

  • Add new fields as optional, with a defined default.
  • Never change a field's type in place. Add a new field and deprecate the old one.
  • Never reuse a removed field's name for different data.
  • Treat enum changes with care. Configure an unknown-value fallback (for example READ_UNKNOWN_ENUM_VALUES_USING_DEFAULT_VALUE with a default) so old clients survive new symbols.

Property-based round-trip tests

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.datatype.jdk8.Jdk8Module;
import net.jqwik.api.ForAll;
import net.jqwik.api.Property;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;

class ProfileRoundTripTest {

    private final ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper().registerModule(new Jdk8Module());

    @Property
    void roundTripPreservesData(@ForAll String id,
                                @ForAll Optional<String> headline,
                                @ForAll List<String> skills) throws Exception {
        Profile original = new Profile(id, headline, skills);

        String json = mapper.writeValueAsString(original);
        Profile parsed = mapper.readValue(json, Profile.class);

        assertEquals(original, parsed);
    }
}

Failure modes

  • Silent type coercion hiding a producer's breaking change.
  • Explicit null written by one serializer and omitted by another.
  • Enums that fail on unknown values in old clients.
  • A required field added without a default, breaking old documents.

Demo to build

Takeaways

  • Put invariants and null normalization in the record's compact constructor.
  • Turn off silent coercion where the contract is strict.
  • Evolve schemas additively, and keep golden files from every release.
  • Property-based round-trip tests guard the serialization invariants.

atom:entry.atom:title: Foundry RBAC that prevents over-privilege
atom:entry.atom:summary: Mapping Microsoft Foundry roles to tasks for projects, models and agent endpoints, so developers get what they need and nothing more.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Teams over-assign roles because it is faster. One person ends up able to create projects, deploy models and publish agents because it was easier to grant a broad role once than to think about it. Foundry has built-in roles that separate these tasks, and using them well is the cheapest security improvement available. One thing to know up front: the roles were renamed. What used to be called Azure AI User is now Foundry User, and Azure AI Project Manager is now Foundry Project Manager. If your infrastructure code still uses the old names, update it.

Options and trade-offs

  • Foundry User: the least-privilege developer role. It gives reader access to the project and resource plus the data actions needed to build and test agents. It does not allow deploying or managing models.
  • Foundry Project Manager: everything Foundry User can do, plus creating and managing projects, publishing agents, and assigning the Foundry User role to others. It does not include model deployment.
  • Foundry Account Owner and Foundry Owner: manage the account and projects, including deploying models. These are broad. Use them sparingly and for platform owners only.
  • Agent consumers: callers who only need to invoke a published agent should get access to the agent endpoint, not a build or admin role.

My recommendation

Give developers Foundry User and nothing else on the resource. Give team leads Foundry Project Manager so they can create projects and invite developers without waiting on a platform team. Reserve Foundry Account Owner for the few people who actually deploy models. Review assignments on a schedule, because over-privilege creeps back.

Minimal working example

Assign roles by name at the narrowest scope that works:

SUB=<subscription-id>
RG=<resource-group>
ACCOUNT=<foundry-resource-name>
SCOPE="/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/$ACCOUNT"

# Developers: least privilege
az role assignment create \
  --assignee <developer-object-id> \
  --role "Foundry User" \
  --scope "$SCOPE"

# Team lead: can create projects, publish agents, invite developers
az role assignment create \
  --assignee <lead-object-id> \
  --role "Foundry Project Manager" \
  --scope "$SCOPE"

# Platform owner who deploys models
az role assignment create \
  --assignee <platform-owner-object-id> \
  --role "Foundry Account Owner" \
  --scope "$SCOPE"

Audit who has what:

az role assignment list --scope "$SCOPE" \
  --query "[].{principal:principalName, role:roleDefinitionName}" -o table

Test it: sign in as a Foundry User and confirm you can build and run an agent but cannot deploy a model. Sign in as a Project Manager and confirm you can publish an agent but still cannot deploy a model.

Checklist

  • Start every developer at Foundry User on the resource, and elevate only for a named task.
  • Check the permission tables for "manage models" and deployment before granting Account Owner or Owner.
  • Remember that Project Manager can assign only the Foundry User role, which makes delegated onboarding safe.
  • Give service principals and end users that only invoke agents the narrowest role that allows it.
  • Update scripts and templates that still reference the old Azure AI role names.
  • Review role assignments at a regular interval, and remove access when people change teams.

Where this doesn't apply

Older hub-based (classic) projects have a different role surface. If you run both, map roles carefully and do not assume names carry across.

  • Elevated-role tasks in Microsoft Foundry
  • Azure built-in roles for AI + machine learning

atom:entry.atom:title: Content filters for prompts and outputs
atom:entry.atom:summary: Prompt Shields, groundedness, protected material, and blocklists for enterprise moderation.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

GenAI agents must resist prompt injection, avoid harmful outputs, and maintain provenance. Azure AI Content Safety offers moderation for text/images and safety features (Prompt Shields, groundedness detection, protected material) with configurable thresholds and blocklists.

Options and trade-offs

  • Prompt Shields (direct and indirect injection): Detect jailbreak attempts and document-borne attacks; low false-positive rates; add latency; configurable block vs annotate modes.
  • Groundedness detection (Preview): Detect ungrounded completions relative to sources; helps provenance and QA; preview scope limits.
  • Protected material detection (text GA, code preview): Identifies copyrighted segments in completions; supports compliance; English scope.
  • Blocklists and custom categories: Enforce organization-specific terms and custom detection; stored encrypted at rest with CMK options.

Minimal working example

Text moderation (Python) Requirements: requests or SDK; endpoint; subscription key or Entra auth.

import requests, json
endpoint = "https://YOUR-CONTENT-SAFETY.cognitiveservices.azure.com"
headers = {"Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key": "KEY","Content-Type":"application/json"}
payload = {"text": "Sample text", "blocklistNames": []}
r = requests.post(f"{endpoint}/contentsafety/text:analyze?api-version=2024-09-01",
                  headers=headers, data=json.dumps(payload))
print(r.json())

Test: Inspect categoriesAnalysis severities; adjust thresholds; add blocklists.

Checklist

  • Configure separate input/output filters; turn on Prompt Shields for inputs; add groundedness and protected material for outputs.
  • Confirm API rate limits and payload size limits per modality/tier.
  • Use blocklists for brand/PII terms; understand storage and deletion controls.

Where this doesn't apply

Offline moderation pipelines with proprietary classifiers; integrate but consider Content Safety for complementary coverage.
