atom:entry.atom:title: Same Dockerfile, Different Build: Reproducible Container Builds
atom:entry.atom:summary: Pin it, lock it, and verify what you actually built—across local and cloud.
atom:entry.atom:content:
I once pushed a change after a healthy local run of aceu-trust-demo. The cloud build resolved a newer FastAPI version—0.142.2 instead of 0.141.1 locally—and pulled an additional package, opentelemetry-api. The Dockerfile was the same; the dependency ranges were not locked.

That kind of drift is easy to miss. A repeatable build takes more than a Dockerfile: it needs a locked dependency graph, a deliberate base-image update policy, and a way to inspect the artifact that actually shipped.

Why “same Dockerfile” can produce a different image

Version ranges allow resolvers to choose newer compatible releases. A mutable base-image tag can also point to a newer image later. Build caches may keep an older layer locally while CI fetches fresh inputs. The source recipe is unchanged, but the resolved inputs differ.

Lock the dependency graph

Use exact direct-dependency pins and commit a lock file that records the resolved transitive versions. Where the package manager supports it, include hashes and install in locked mode. A short input file might look like this:

# requirements.in — human-maintained direct dependencies
fastapi==0.141.1
uvicorn==0.30.1

# Resolve and lock transitive dependencies, including hashes.
pip-compile --generate-hashes --output-file requirements.txt requirements.in

Commit both files. Install from the generated lock in CI rather than re-resolving ranges during every image build:

pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt

Pins make change deliberate; they do not remove the need to update packages for fixes.

Choose tags or digests deliberately

Tags are convenient and can move to newer images. Digests identify a specific image immutably. A digest gives a reproducible base, but it will not advance to security fixes on its own—you must monitor updates and refresh it deliberately.

# Illustrative digest placeholder: replace with a verified digest
FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:<verified-digest>

If you use tags, track when they change and refresh the base during scheduled builds. --pull tells Docker to attempt to pull referenced images before the build:

docker build --pull --tag aceu-trust-demo:main .

Make updates reviewable

Use a dependency update bot or scheduled update pull requests, then gate those changes with tests and image scanning. For production-critical dependencies, document which updates need an explicit reviewer. Prefer a visible, tested update over a silent change arriving through a floating version range.

Keep registry access safe and documented

CI needs a clear path to authenticate, tag, and push. Store credentials in the CI secret manager, use a short-lived token where available, and send passwords over standard input instead of exposing them in command arguments:

# REGISTRY_USER and REGISTRY_TOKEN come from the CI secret store.
printf '%s' "$REGISTRY_TOKEN" | docker login "$REGISTRY_HOST" \
  --username "$REGISTRY_USER" --password-stdin

IMAGE="$REGISTRY_HOST/aceu-trust-demo:$GIT_SHA"
docker build --pull --tag "$IMAGE" .
docker push "$IMAGE"

Document who owns the credentials, how rotation works, and what a failed login looks like. Never print secret values into build logs.

Compare artifacts when behavior changes

If local and cloud behavior diverge, inspect the image’s package inventory or generate an SBOM. Compare the resolved versions and base-image digest, then decide whether to re-lock, refresh the image, or accept the change with an appropriate test update. Looking at the built artifact beats guessing from the Dockerfile alone.

Trade-offs and failure modes

  • Exact pins vs. security updates: pins improve repeatability, while scheduled updates and scans keep them current.
  • Tags vs. digests: tags are easier to refresh; digests make the selected base explicit and immutable.
  • Locks vs. setup time: generating a lock adds a step, but saves time when builds need to be compared.
  • Registry authentication: expired tokens or changed scopes should produce an explicit CI failure, not a misleading successful pipeline.

Try it in your pipeline

  1. Replace floating version ranges with exact direct pins and commit a full lock file.
  2. Pick a base-image policy: tag plus scheduled refresh, or digest plus an explicit update cadence.
  3. Build with --pull when you want CI to check for updated base images.
  4. Record the image tag or digest produced by CI and inspect its packages when behavior changes.

Closing thought

“Same Dockerfile” rarely guarantees “same runtime.” Lock files, explicit base-image policy, and artifact inspection turn hidden drift into a change the team can review.

Further reading

  • Docker Buildx build options, including --pull and SBOM attestations
  • Pulling an image by immutable digest
  • pip-tools documentation for Python dependency locking

atom:entry.atom:title: JFR as the Default: Enabling Continuous Flight Recording Safely
atom:entry.atom:summary: Bounded, always-on recordings you can dump during an incident, and a parser that turns them into flame graph input
atom:entry.atom:content:
Why continuous recording

A safe baseline configuration

-XX:FlightRecorderOptions=repository=/var/tmp/jfr
-XX:StartFlightRecording=name=continuous,delay=2m,disk=true,maxage=30m,maxsize=250m,settings=default,dumponexit=true,filename=/var/tmp/jfr/exit.jfr
  • delay=2m waits until the application has started and warmed up before recording, so startup noise does not fill your window.
  • disk=true writes data to disk, which allows long windows without holding everything in memory.
  • maxage=30m and maxsize=250m bound the recording. The data is discarded when either limit is hit, which is what keeps disk use predictable.
  • settings=default selects the standard event template, which is designed to be low overhead. Use the heavier profile template only for short, targeted sessions.
  • dumponexit=true saves the recording when the JVM exits, which helps with crashes and deliberate restarts.

Capturing data during an incident

jcmd <pid> JFR.dump name=continuous filename=/var/tmp/jfr/incident-$(date +%s).jfr

Defaults per service class

Analyze a recording in Java

import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordedEvent;
import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordedFrame;
import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordedStackTrace;
import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingFile;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.PrintWriter;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.*;

public final class JfrAllocationFolder {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Path jfr = Path.of(args[0]);
        Path out = Path.of(args[1]);

        Map<String, Long> bytesByStack = new HashMap<>();

        for (RecordedEvent event : RecordingFile.readAllEvents(jfr)) {
            if (!"jdk.ObjectAllocationSample".equals(event.getEventType().getName())) {
                continue;
            }
            RecordedStackTrace trace = event.getStackTrace();
            if (trace == null) {
                continue;
            }
            List<RecordedFrame> frames = trace.getFrames();
            List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int i = frames.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {         // root first
                var method = frames.get(i).getMethod();
                names.add(method.getType().getName() + "." + method.getName());
            }
            String key = String.join(";", names);
            bytesByStack.merge(key, event.getLong("weight"), Long::sum);
        }

        try (PrintWriter w = new PrintWriter(out.toFile())) {
            bytesByStack.forEach((stack, bytes) -> w.println(stack + " " + bytes));
        }
    }
}

Gate your visualizations

Failure modes

  • Oversized recordings. Always set maxage and maxsize.
  • Mismatched JDK versions. A recording from one JDK may not parse with a very different tool version. Keep your analysis tools at or above the JDK you run.
  • Using the heavy template by default. Reserve profile for short investigations.
  • No access plan. Decide in advance who can dump recordings and where they are stored, because recordings can contain sensitive data such as stack traces and thread names.

Demo to build

Takeaways

  • Continuous JFR is safe when it is bounded by age and size.
  • Dump on demand with jcmd and analyze with the consumer API or a flame graph.
  • Verify that data exists before visualizing it.

atom:entry.atom:title: Identity Domains: SAML/OIDC federation setup notes
atom:entry.atom:summary: What I configure first so an external identity provider works cleanly with OCI.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Most teams already have an identity provider such as Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) or Okta, and nobody wants a second set of passwords for the cloud console. Federation solves that, but a careless setup can lock out administrators or leave group membership drifting away from what the IdP says.

I wanted a repeatable order of operations that keeps a way back in at every step.

Options and trade-offs

  • Console setup: straightforward and visible, and it needs careful mapping and testing.
  • API or automation: repeatable, but there are more moving parts to get wrong the first time.
  • Default sign-on and IdP policies versus custom rules: the defaults are a fine start, but confirm what they do to administrators before you rely on them.

My recommendation

Use the Identity Domains flow with a SAML identity provider. Exchange metadata, decide which assertion attribute identifies the user, map IdP groups to IAM groups, and test with a staged non-admin account before an administrator. Change federation and MFA separately so a problem can be traced to one change.

Worked example

The sequence I follow in the Console. It is a checklist, not a script, because the exact screens differ a little between tenancies.

1. Keep a local break-glass admin that does NOT use the new IdP.
2. Identity Domains > Security > Identity providers > Add SAML IdP.
   - Upload the IdP metadata XML (or enter the endpoints and signing cert).
   - Choose the attribute that carries the username (NameID or email).
3. Export the domain's service provider metadata and import it into the IdP.
4. Map IdP groups to IAM groups (group mapping / JIT provisioning).
5. Add the IdP to an identity provider policy rule and activate it.
6. Test: non-admin user first, then an admin. Confirm group-based access.
7. Record the metadata expiry date and who owns the mapping table.

For Entra ID the pattern is the same. You create an enterprise application, upload the service provider metadata, download the federation metadata XML and import it into the domain. OIDC-based identity providers follow the same ideas, with a client ID and secret in place of metadata files.

Checklist

  1. Keep a break-glass local administrator outside federation.
  2. Document the group mappings and name an owner for each.
  3. Test a non-admin sign-in before you test an admin sign-in.
  4. Watch for attribute mismatches, and fix the mapping instead of widening a policy.
  5. Track the IdP signing certificate expiry and the metadata refresh process.
  6. Do not change federation and MFA policy in the same maintenance window.

Where this doesn't apply

A very small tenancy with no external IdP is better off with local users and a strong sign-on policy. Federation adds value when there is already an identity source to follow.

One honest limitation

An expired or rotated IdP certificate can break sign-in without warning. I keep a calendar entry for it and a short, written refresh procedure.

Sources

  • OCI Documentation: Federating with Identity Domains (SAML identity providers)
  • OCI Documentation: Identity Provider Policies in Identity Domains
  • OCI Documentation: Manually Federating Your Tenancy

atom:entry.atom:title: Ship verifiable releases with GitHub artifact attestations
atom:entry.atom:summary: How to add signed build provenance and SBOM attestations to a release, so anyone downstream can check what was built, from which commit, by which workflow.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

A release asset is a promise: this file came from this project. Most consumers have no way to check it. If a binary is rebuilt outside CI, swapped in transit, or built from a different commit than the tag suggests, the file name looks identical and nothing flags the difference. Checksums help only if you trust the place you got the checksum from. Build-pipeline compromises such as the 2020 SolarWinds attack are the reason this problem is taken seriously.

GitHub artifact attestations address this with a signed statement that binds an artifact's digest to its build provenance: the repository, workflow, commit and runner that produced it. The statements follow the in-toto and Sigstore formats. You can verify them with the GitHub CLI, online or offline. An SBOM (software bill of materials) can be attached in the same way, so a consumer can see what is inside the artifact as well as where it came from.

Options and trade-offs

  • Do nothing: no friction, and no way for anyone to verify anything.
  • Checksums only: catches accidental corruption, but proves nothing about origin if the checksum file sits next to the artifact.
  • SBOM only: shows contents, but without a signed link to a build it is just another unverified file.
  • Build provenance attestation: a signed statement tying the artifact digest to the workflow run. This is the strongest single step for most projects.
  • Provenance plus an SBOM attestation: adds contents transparency on top of origin. Verifying the SBOM requires naming its predicate type explicitly, because verification defaults to provenance.
  • Custom predicates: record your own assertions (test results, policy checks) in the in-toto format when provenance and SBOM are not enough.

My recommendation

Attest provenance for every released binary and container image, and add an SBOM attestation when consumers care about contents. Treat verification as part of the release process, not an afterthought: run gh attestation verify in the release workflow's final step so a broken attestation fails the release. Be honest in the README about what this proves. A valid attestation says the artifact came from a particular workflow run. It does not say the workflow was uncompromised or the build reproducible.

Minimal working example

A release workflow for a Java project. It builds a jar, creates an SBOM, attests both, builds and attests a container image by digest, and publishes the release:

name: release
on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]

permissions:
  contents: write        # create the release
  id-token: write        # sign with the workflow's OIDC identity
  attestations: write    # store the attestation
  packages: write        # push the image

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: "21"

      - name: Build
        run: ./gradlew --no-daemon build

      - name: Generate SBOM
        uses: anchore/sbom-action@v0
        with:
          path: .
          format: spdx-json
          output-file: sbom.spdx.json

      - name: Attest build provenance (jar)
        uses: actions/attest-build-provenance@v2
        with:
          subject-path: build/libs/*.jar

      - name: Attest SBOM
        uses: actions/attest-sbom@v2
        with:
          subject-path: build/libs/*.jar
          sbom-path: sbom.spdx.json

      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push image
        id: push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.ref_name }}

      - name: Attest image provenance (by digest)
        uses: actions/attest-build-provenance@v2
        with:
          subject-name: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}
          subject-digest: ${{ steps.push.outputs.digest }}
          push-to-registry: true

      - name: Publish release
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        run: gh release create "${{ github.ref_name }}" build/libs/*.jar sbom.spdx.json --generate-notes

Verify as a consumer:

# Provenance (the default)
gh attestation verify build/libs/app-1.0.0.jar --repo OWNER/REPO

# SBOM: name the predicate type explicitly
gh attestation verify build/libs/app-1.0.0.jar --repo OWNER/REPO \
  --predicate-type https://spdx.dev/Document/v2.3

# Container image
gh attestation verify oci://ghcr.io/OWNER/REPO:v1.0.0 --repo OWNER/REPO

Test it: release a tag, run the three commands against the published assets, then change one byte of the jar and confirm verification fails.

Checklist

  • Grant the job id-token: write and attestations: write. Add packages: write when pushing images.
  • Attest container images by digest, not by tag, and leave the tag out of subject-name.
  • Pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA and let Dependabot update them. The attest actions move between major versions, so check the current release before copying versions from any article.
  • Verify the artifact in CI before publishing, and document the verification command in the README.
  • Publish the SBOM next to the artifact, and tell users to pass the SBOM predicate type when verifying it.
  • Practice offline verification (download the attestation bundle and the trusted root with the CLI) for environments without internet access.
  • State plainly in the README what an attestation does and does not prove.

Where this doesn't apply

If you only ship source and no built artifacts, there is little to attest. Attestations for private and internal repositories need GitHub Enterprise Cloud, and the feature is not available on GitHub Enterprise Server, so check your plan first. Fully air-gapped environments need their own trust anchors.

One honest limitation

Provenance is necessary but not sufficient. A signed statement that a workflow built a file does not make the build hermetic or reproducible, and a compromised workflow produces a perfectly valid attestation. Higher assurance depends on build isolation and organizational policy, which the SLSA levels describe.

Sources

  • actions/attest-sbom
  • Verifying attestations offline
  • SLSA specification, build levels

atom:entry.atom:title: Faster Docker Builds for Java Services
atom:entry.atom:summary: Most of the speed-up comes from three boring changes: a smaller build context, a sensible layer order and a BuildKit cache mount for Gradle.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

When a container build takes minutes, people stop iterating and start batching changes, which is when bugs hide. Teams usually respond by turning caching on and hoping. That helps a little, but the real gains come from what you send to the builder and the order you ask it to do things in. A Java service is a good case. The dependencies change rarely and the source changes constantly, yet a naive Dockerfile downloads the world on every edit.

Options and trade-offs

  • Do nothing and rely on the default layer cache: fine until the first COPY of the whole repo, after which every code change re-downloads dependencies.
  • Copy only the build files first, resolve dependencies, then copy the source: much better, but a changed build file still re-downloads everything.
  • Add a BuildKit cache mount for the Gradle home: dependency downloads survive across builds, even when the layer itself is invalidated.

My recommendation

Start with a .dockerignore, because it is the cheapest win. Order layers from least to most volatile, use a cache mount for the dependency cache, and use a multi-stage build so the JDK and build tools stay out of the runtime image. Pin dependency versions so speed does not come at the cost of repeatability.

Worked example

A two-stage Dockerfile for a Gradle project. The cache mount is only available during the RUN step, so the build that needs it happens inside the same step.

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /src

# Build files first: this layer only changes when dependencies change
COPY gradlew settings.gradle.kts build.gradle.kts ./
COPY gradle gradle
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.gradle \
    ./gradlew --no-daemon dependencies > /dev/null

# Source last: this is the layer that changes on every edit
COPY src src
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.gradle \
    ./gradlew --no-daemon installDist -x test

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
WORKDIR /opt/app
RUN useradd --uid 10001 --create-home appuser
COPY --from=build /src/build/install/app/ ./
USER 10001
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/opt/app/bin/app"]

And the context file that keeps the build fast before any layer is considered:

.git
.gradle/
build/
out/
*.iml
.idea/
.env

To see the effect, time a cold build, change one line of source, and time it again:

time DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 docker build -t demo/app:dev .
echo '// touch' >> src/main/java/App.java
time docker build -t demo/app:dev .

The second build should skip the dependency steps entirely. Bump a dependency version and confirm that step does re-run.

Checklist

  1. Add a .dockerignore before changing anything else.
  2. Copy build files, resolve dependencies, then copy source.
  3. Use a cache mount for the Gradle home, and run the build in the same RUN step.
  4. Use a multi-stage build and run as a non-root user.
  5. Pin dependency versions, and rebuild without cache now and then to catch drift.

Where this doesn't apply

If your dependencies change on every commit, or the project is tiny, none of this will be noticeable. A remote build service with its own cache may also change which of these steps matter.

One honest limitation

Cache mounts live on the builder, not in the image, so a fresh CI runner starts cold unless you export and import the cache. A fast local build says little about a CI build.

Sources

  • Docker Docs: Optimize cache usage in builds
  • Docker Docs: Multi-stage builds
  • Docker Docs: Dockerfile reference (RUN --mount)
  • Docker Docs: .dockerignore

atom:entry.atom:title: Compiled-Model Caching in OpenVINO
atom:entry.atom:summary: How compiled-model caching works, how to confirm a device supports it, how it interacts with AUTO and the NPU, and how to measure cold start against cache…
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Every OpenVINO application reads a model and compiles it for a specific device when it starts. For a small model on CPU the cost is easy to ignore. For larger models, or for GPU and NPU targets, compilation can dominate the time before the first request completes. If a rollout restarts your service, the first user request can pay that price.

OpenVINO's model caching stores the compiled result so that a later start can import it instead of recompiling. You enable it by pointing OpenVINO at a cache folder. The catch is that not every device supports importing and exporting compiled models. OpenVINO's documentation says such devices work normally but do not get the compilation speed-up, so a cache you configured can quietly do nothing.

That quiet failure is the reason to measure rather than assume. The friction points are confirming device support, understanding how caching interacts with AUTO and the NPU, and measuring a restart in a way that is not fooled by process state.

Options and trade-offs

  • Application-level caching: set the CACHE_DIR property on the OpenVINO core before compiling. The first compile has extra work because it also stores the result, so it can be slightly slower. Later compiles can import the stored model.
  • Capability check: ask the device whether it supports import and export (the EXPORT_IMPORT capability). If it does not, caching will not shorten that device's compile step, whatever you configure.
  • AUTO device selection: the AUTO documentation says AUTO starts inference on the CPU by default unless there is a cached model for the best-suited device, because the CPU can begin right away. While the CPU works, AUTO keeps loading the model onto the better device and switches over when ready. A warm cache can therefore change which device serves your first request.
  • NPU: the NPU documentation and plugin README describe a driver-level compiled-model cache enabled by default in current drivers, and OpenVINO's own caching is enabled when you set cache_dir. Read how the two interact in the documentation for your driver and version.
  • Model Server: OpenVINO Model Server provides a --cache_dir option and a documentation page on its model cache. The goal is the same as in application code: faster loading on later starts.
  • Prefix caching is a different mechanism that works per request instead of per process. Model Server's performance tuning guide lists --enable_prefix_caching true as the default and describes it as reusing work for repeated prompt prefixes, which is common when chat clients resend conversation history.
  • General rule for any compiled artifact: it is tied to the device, the software version, and the model and its input shapes. Do not share one cache folder across versions or machine types.
  • Recommendation: turn caching on wherever the device supports it, keep the cache folder on storage that survives restarts, and treat the capability check as a gate. If a device does not report EXPORT_IMPORT, plan for the full compile time there. Measure restarts with fresh processes, because a second compile call inside one process does not tell you what a restart costs.
  • Decision lens: restart speed against operational risk. A persistent cache is one more thing to manage, and a stale artifact left after an upgrade is a confusing failure. Put the OpenVINO version, model version, and device name in the folder path so you can delete a whole generation at once. Example setup: a container with a volume mounted at the cache path, a startup script that logs compile time, and a health check that confirms the folder contains files after the first run.

Minimal working example

Prereqs

  • Python 3 with the openvino package installed (pip install openvino).
  • An OpenVINO IR model (model.xml and model.bin) or an ONNX file you already use.
  • A writable folder for the cache, on the same filesystem the production service will use.

capability_check.py

import openvino as ov
import openvino.properties.device as device

core = ov.Core()
for name in core.available_devices:
    supported = "EXPORT_IMPORT" in core.get_property(name, device.capabilities)
    print(name, "supports caching" if supported else "no import/export")

cold_vs_cached.py (run it in a new process each time)

import sys, time
import openvino as ov

model_path, device_name = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
core = ov.Core()
core.set_property({"CACHE_DIR": "./model_cache"})

start = time.perf_counter()
compiled = core.compile_model(model_path, device_name)
print(f"compile_model on {device_name}: {time.perf_counter() - start:.3f}s")

Delete the model_cache folder to get a cold run. Run the script again without deleting it to get a cached run.

Adjust file names, model names, and paths to your own setup.

Test: Run capability_check.py and note which devices report support. Run cold_vs_cached.py ten times with the cache folder deleted before each run (cold), then ten times without deleting it (cached), each in a new process. If the cached median is clearly lower, caching is working on that device. If the two medians are close, the device probably does not support caching or the folder is not being used, which is also a useful answer.

Record: device, OpenVINO version, operating system, and model; capability check result; cold compile time as median and 95th percentile; cached compile time as median and 95th percentile; cache folder size; time to first token cold versus cached if you serve a language model; whether outputs match between the two.

Checklist

  • Run the capability check for every device you plan to use.
  • Set CACHE_DIR (or --cache_dir in Model Server) and confirm files appear after the first run.
  • Put version, model, and device in the cache path and store it on persistent storage.
  • Measure in separate processes and report percentiles.
  • Compare outputs between a cold run and a cached run.
  • Avoid: assuming caching works without checking the device's capabilities.
  • Avoid: timing two compiles in one process and calling it a restart test.

Where this doesn't apply

Workloads where the model is compiled once for a long-running process and restarts are rare, cases where first-token latency is dominated by something other than compilation (network time or input parsing), and devices that do not support import and export.

Sources

  • OpenVINO Model Caching Overview
  • Automatic Device Selection documentation
  • Automatic Device Selection and Configuration (OpenVINO blog)
  • OpenVINO NPU device documentation
  • Intel NPU plugin README
  • Model Server performance tuning guide
  • OpenVINO Model Server parameters

atom:entry.atom:title: Serving ONNX models on AKS GPU without surprises
atom:entry.atom:summary: A hands-on path to deploy ONNX models with Triton or ORT, readiness checks, and GPU node pools.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

ONNX Runtime provides optimized inference across multiple accelerators. In production, AKS GPU node pools must be prepared (drivers/plugins), readiness and health checks must reflect model load state, and autoscaling must consider GPU allocation and throughput constraints.

Options and trade-offs

  • NVIDIA Triton with ONNX backend: Multi-framework server with health/readiness endpoints; simplifies model repos and supports gRPC/HTTP. Operationally richer; larger image footprint; excellent for multi-model serving.
  • ORT server containers: Leaner; you must select images/runtime versions and wire health probes yourself; good for single model or simple stacks.
  • Node pool strategy: Dedicated GPU node pools with NVIDIA device plugin; enforce nvidia.com/gpu limits; separate system and user pools for stable scheduling.

Minimal working example

Prereqs

  • AKS cluster; GPU node pool with NVIDIA device plugin; kubectl; Triton image; PVC for model repository.
  • Model: ResNet-50 in ONNX.

    • Deployment (Triton + ONNX)

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: triton-server
  namespace: inference
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: triton-server
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: triton-server
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: triton
        image: nvcr.io/nvidia/tritonserver:24.08-py3
        args: ["tritonserver","--model-repository=/models/repository","--strict-model-config=false"]
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
          name: http
        - containerPort: 8001
          name: grpc
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /v2/health/ready
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 60
          periodSeconds: 10
          failureThreshold: 6
        resources:
          limits:
            nvidia.com/gpu: 1
        volumeMounts:
        - name: model-vol
          mountPath: /models
      volumes:
      - name: model-vol
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: triton-model-repository-pvc

Test: kubectl get pods -n inference; wait for readiness; send inference to port 8000; confirm GPU assignment with kubectl describe. Version and runtime assumptions

  • Triton 24.08; AKS GPU plugin installed; ONNX Runtime on server side via Triton; CUDA matching driver for your GPU.

Checklist

  • Validate CUDA/cuDNN compatibility with the ORT/Triton image; mismatches silently fallback to CPU in some cases.
  • Pin readinessProbe to /v2/health/ready; initialDelaySeconds accounts for model load.
  • Use separate GPU node pools; confirm nvidia.com/gpu schedulable capacity.
  • Cap replicas by GPU capacity; ensure PVC throughput supports model load.

Where this doesn't apply

CPU-only inference; use ORT CPU builds and different autoscaling signals.

Sources

  • AI Inference on AKS with Triton + ONNX (GA blog)
  • ONNX Runtime install and CUDA requirements (GA)
  • Use GPUs on AKS Hybrid/Edge node pools (GA)
