atom:entry.atom:title: Dynamic groups with tag-based scoping (illustrative patterns)
atom:entry.atom:summary: Using compartment and tag rules so only the instances you intend can assume a group's permissions.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

A dynamic group rule that says "every instance in compartment X" is easy to write and easy to regret. The day someone launches a test box or a bastion in that compartment, it silently picks up the same permissions as your production services.

I wanted membership that is predictable and explainable: this instance is in the group because it is in this compartment and carries this tag.

Options and trade-offs

  • Compartment-only rules: simple, with broad membership that grows by accident.
  • Instance OCID rules: exact, but you edit the rule every time an instance is replaced.
  • Compartment plus tag rules: precise enough for most teams, as long as tagging is governed.

My recommendation

I combine a compartment OCID with a defined tag namespace, key and value, joined with ALL so both conditions must be true. Then I treat the tag like an access-control input and restrict who can apply it. Without that last step, anyone who can tag an instance can effectively add it to the group.

Worked example

A rule that requires both the compartment and the tag. The tag here uses a namespace called department and a key called runtime.

ALL {instance.compartment.id = '<apps_compartment_ocid>',
     tag.department.runtime.value = 'payments'}

When a group should cover two compartments, use ANY around the compartment checks and keep the tag condition outside it:

ALL {
  ANY {instance.compartment.id = '<apps_compartment_ocid>',
       instance.compartment.id = '<shared_compartment_ocid>'},
  tag.department.runtime.value = 'payments'
}

The Console rule builder covers the simple cases, but you will type tag rules by hand. Changes to a rule or to a tag are not instant, so I verify the effective membership rather than assuming it, and I keep the rule text in version control next to the policy it supports.

Checklist

  1. Define the tag namespace, key and allowed values before writing the rule.
  2. Use ALL so the compartment and the tag must both match.
  3. Limit who may apply or change the tag through IAM.
  4. Keep the rule text and the reason for it in version control.
  5. Plan for a delay after rule or tag changes, and verify membership before cutting over.
  6. Re-check the effective membership after each deployment.

Where this doesn't apply

Short-lived experiments are better served by an instance-specific rule, or by a throwaway compartment that will be deleted. A tagging scheme is overhead you do not need there.

One honest limitation

The delay before membership changes take effect can surprise a rollout. I stage the change, test that the policy works for the new instances, and only then retire the old rule.

Sources

  • OCI Documentation: Managing Dynamic Groups (matching rules)
  • OCI Documentation: Tagging Overview
  • OCI Documentation: Calling Services from an Instance

atom:entry.atom:title: G1 vs ZGC at JDK 17+: Choosing a Collector and Sizing the Heap
atom:entry.atom:summary: When G1 still wins, what ZGC costs in memory and CPU, and how to measure it yourself
atom:entry.atom:content:
What each collector optimizes

  • G1 is the default collector since JDK 9. It balances throughput and pause time, and works well across a wide range of heap sizes.
  • ZGC is built for low pause times that stay short regardless of heap size, using concurrent work. On JDK 17 it is non-generational, so it examines the whole heap each cycle. JDK 21 added a generational mode (JEP 439), which lowers memory and CPU overhead compared with the single-generation version JEP 439.
# JDK 17
-XX:+UseG1GC
-XX:+UseZGC

# JDK 21+ (generational ZGC)
-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational

Where the cost shows up

  • Plan for more memory when upgrading. Moving a service from G1 on an older JDK to ZGC can require a noticeably bigger heap and more native memory. Budget for it in your container limits, or the kernel's OOM killer will make the decision for you.
  • Watch RSS, not just heap. Total process memory includes metaspace, thread stacks, code cache, GC data structures, and direct buffers. A container limit equal to -Xmx is almost always too small.

When G1 still wins

  • Small to medium heaps where G1 pauses are already well inside your latency budget.
  • Throughput-oriented batch jobs, where a few longer pauses cost less than constant concurrent overhead.
  • CPU-constrained containers with very few cores, since concurrent GC threads need cores to run on.

When ZGC is worth it

  • Large heaps or strict tail-latency targets where G1's pauses show up in your p99.
  • Services with enough spare CPU and memory to give the collector room.
  • Workloads where a measured test shows fewer long pauses and no allocation stalls.

Heap sizing rules of thumb

  1. Measure the live set (memory still reachable after a full collection) from GC logs.
  2. Start with a heap at roughly 2x to 3x the live set for concurrent collectors, then adjust from measurement.
  3. Set -Xms equal to -Xmx for steady services, to avoid resize pauses.
  4. Keep the container limit well above -Xmx to leave room for native memory.
  5. Always turn on GC logging in production:
-Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/app/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m

A load generator you can run

import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom;

public final class AllocationLoad {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int cacheEntries = Integer.parseInt(args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "2000000");
        int operations   = Integer.parseInt(args.length > 1 ? args[1] : "5000000");

        Map<Integer, byte[]> cache = new HashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < cacheEntries; i++) {
            cache.put(i, new byte[64]);                       // long-lived data
        }

        long[] latencyNanos = new long[operations];
        ThreadLocalRandom rnd = ThreadLocalRandom.current();

        for (int i = 0; i < operations; i++) {
            long start = System.nanoTime();

            byte[] shortLived = new byte[512 + rnd.nextInt(2048)];     // garbage
            shortLived[0] = 1;
            if ((i & 0x3FF) == 0) {                                    // occasional churn in the cache
                cache.put(rnd.nextInt(cacheEntries), new byte[64]);
            }
            blackhole += shortLived.length;

            latencyNanos[i] = System.nanoTime() - start;
        }

        Arrays.sort(latencyNanos);
        System.out.printf("p50=%dus p99=%dus p99.9=%dus max=%dus%n",
                latencyNanos[operations / 2] / 1_000,
                latencyNanos[(int) (operations * 0.99)] / 1_000,
                latencyNanos[(int) (operations * 0.999)] / 1_000,
                latencyNanos[operations - 1] / 1_000);
    }

    static volatile long blackhole;
}
for heap in 2g 4g 8g; do
  java -Xms$heap -Xmx$heap -XX:+UseG1GC  -Xlog:gc*:file=g1-$heap.log  AllocationLoad
  java -Xms$heap -Xmx$heap -XX:+UseZGC   -Xlog:gc*:file=zgc-$heap.log AllocationLoad
done

What to chart

Failure modes

  • A heap sized to the old collector's needs, causing allocation stalls under ZGC.
  • A container limit too close to the heap size, causing out-of-memory kills from native memory.
  • Judging by averages. GC problems live in the tail.

Takeaways

  • ZGC reduces pauses by spending CPU and memory. G1 remains a strong default.
  • Size the heap from the measured live set, and size the container from RSS.
  • Decide with your own tail-latency numbers, not slogans.

atom:entry.atom:title: Least-privilege IAM policies for workloads (compartment-first)
atom:entry.atom:summary: The policy patterns I reach for to keep OCI access narrow, readable and easy to audit.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

IAM policies tend to grow the same way: someone is blocked, someone writes a broad statement to unblock them, and that statement lives forever. Tenancy-wide grants and "manage all-resources" lines are the usual result, and they are hard to walk back once other things depend on them.

I wanted a default that is easy to follow under time pressure. Scope every statement to a compartment, name the resource family, and pick the verb that matches the job.

Options and trade-offs

  • Tenancy-level policies: quick to write and a large blast radius. I keep them for a few shared administrative duties with tightly limited verbs.
  • Compartment-first policies: they line up with ownership and cost boundaries. The price is that you need a compartment structure and consistent names.
  • Conditional policies: precise, using where clauses on bucket, secret or operation. They also need documentation and testing, or they turn into puzzles.

My recommendation

Start in the compartment that owns the workload. OCI's verbs run from inspect to read to use to manage, so give runtime principals read or use and keep manage for operators. Prefer resource families such as instance-family or object-family over all-resources, and review the policy set on a schedule so it does not drift.

Worked example

Here is the shape I aim for with an application compartment called apps. Runtime access is narrow, and the platform team gets a separate, more powerful statement.

# Runtime: what the app itself needs
Allow dynamic-group app-runtimes to read objects in compartment apps
  where target.bucket.name = 'app-config'
Allow dynamic-group app-runtimes to use log-content in compartment apps
 
# Operators: separate group, separate statements
Allow group platform-admins to manage instance-family in compartment apps
Allow group platform-admins to read policies in compartment apps

Compare that with what usually shows up in a review:

Allow group developers to manage all-resources in tenancy

The second line is shorter and works on day one, which is why it keeps appearing. It is also impossible to explain to an auditor. When delegating to a sub-team, use a compartment path such as A:B so the grant follows the hierarchy.

Be careful with the ability to manage policies. Whoever can manage policies in a compartment can usually grant themselves more, so I keep that permission with a very small group.

Checklist

  1. Use read or use for runtime principals, and keep manage for people who operate the service.
  2. Scope by compartment, and by compartment path when delegating.
  3. Write one purpose per statement, and add a short comment on who, what and why.
  4. Use resource families instead of all-resources.
  5. Put a condition on the statements that touch sensitive buckets or secrets.
  6. Review grants on a schedule and remove the stale ones.

Where this doesn't apply

Incident response across many compartments is a case where a temporary tenancy-level grant is sensible. Time-box it, write down who approved it, and delete it when the incident closes.

One honest limitation

Narrow policies mean more statements, and more statements need maintenance. A naming convention and a template for new compartments, set up early, keep that from becoming the bottleneck.

Sources

  • OCI Documentation: Policy Syntax
  • OCI Documentation: Policy Reference (verbs and resource families)
  • OCI Documentation: Managing Compartments

atom:entry.atom:title: Running Is Not Ready: Operating Containerized Services
atom:entry.atom:summary: Why startup, readiness, and liveness are different—and how to keep rollouts reversible when real systems fail.
atom:entry.atom:content:
One of the most reliable lessons from operating containerized services is simple: running is not ready. A process can be alive, a port can be open, and yet the service may not be able to handle real traffic. Treat startup, readiness, and liveness as separate concerns, verify each one deliberately, and design rollouts with recovery in mind.

This article uses a small public demo, aceu-trust-demo, as a running example. It uses a multi-stage image, a non-root user, a health endpoint, and a container deployment behind external HTTPS ingress. Its ACE-U output is illustrative and based on synthetic evidence; it is not a validated assessment of real people. The operational lessons apply more broadly.

The “green” deployment that still fails

A deployment reports “running” and the dashboard looks healthy, but requests time out. A dependency is still warming up. The process is alive, so the liveness signal stays green; the service is simply not ready to serve traffic yet. The failure began when one signal was expected to answer two different questions.

Give each signal one job

Startup: has initialization finished?

Startup covers work such as loading configuration, opening required connections, or priming a cache. Slow startup should not be mistaken for a dead process.

Readiness: can this instance take traffic now?

Readiness is a promise to callers. Keep it false until the dependencies required for the service’s critical path are available. A TCP connection alone may not be enough if the application depends on a loaded index or credentials.

Liveness: is the process stuck in a state that needs a restart?

Liveness should detect an unrecoverable condition, such as a deadlock. It should not fail merely because a downstream system is briefly unavailable: repeatedly restarting healthy processes can amplify an outage.

Docker’s HEALTHCHECK records a container health state. It does not, by itself, define how a particular load balancer or orchestrator routes traffic. In Kubernetes, configure startup, readiness, and liveness probes for their distinct purposes.

A bounded Docker health check

If Python is already part of the runtime image, a tiny local endpoint check avoids adding a separate curl package just for health status:

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD python -c 'import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen("http://localhost:8000/health", timeout=2)' || exit 1

Keep this endpoint cheap and local. Put stricter dependency checks in a separate readiness endpoint, then configure your platform to use that endpoint to gate traffic.

Roll out in stages and predefine rollback

Do not move all traffic at once. Start with a small cohort, hold it under real load for a defined soak period, then expand. Write the rollback condition before the release—for example, a measured latency threshold sustained for a defined duration, or an error rate that crosses a set limit. The thresholds should come from the service’s baseline and risk profile, not be guessed after the rollout starts.

Shut down gracefully

When a platform scales down an idle container, the process may receive SIGTERM. Stop accepting new work, let in-flight requests finish within a deadline, close outbound clients, flush metrics, and exit. Treat SIGKILL as the forced fallback. Without a drain period, a routine scale-down can become partial writes, dangling sessions, or noisy retries.

Make the dependency chain visible

Under pressure, teams often blame the topmost service. Keep a runbook that follows dependencies below the application: runtime, network, storage, cache or index, and external services. Document how each layer fails and how to check it without adding load. Infrastructure problems such as CPU starvation, memory pressure, or network saturation can surface as application timeouts and backpressure.

A green health endpoint can also miss a heavy or rarely used path. Pair alerts with lightweight, non-sensitive transition logs such as ready=false reason=index_warming and ready=true checks=passed. A weekly on-call handoff—what broke, the likely cause, and which mitigation helped—turns recurring cold starts and slow dependency warm-ups into work the team can fix.

Trade-offs to make explicit

  • Strict readiness vs. first-green speed: better gating can delay traffic, while reducing user-facing failures.
  • Longer soak vs. delivery pace: more observation lowers rollout risk but delays full exposure.
  • Graceful drain vs. implementation effort: draining takes work; skipping it risks incomplete operations.
  • Frequent liveness checks vs. flapping: overly sensitive checks can restart a service during resource spikes and worsen an incident.

Try it in your service

  1. Add a separate /ready endpoint that checks the critical dependency before returning success.
  2. Write down a staged rollout, soak period, and rollback trigger before your next release.
  3. Handle SIGTERM by draining requests and closing resources cleanly.
  4. Extend your runbook with infrastructure checks and first suspects for latency spikes.

Closing thought

Separating startup, readiness, and liveness reduces confusion during incidents and helps limit their blast radius. The demo illustrates the distinction with a local health endpoint and a reversible deployment path. Its ACE-U dimensions—Authenticity, Credibility, Empathy, and Uniqueness—remain conceptual in this context, not a judgment of real people.

Further reading

  • Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK reference
  • Kubernetes startup, readiness, and liveness probes

atom:entry.atom:title: Azure OpenAI authentication patterns without API keys
atom:entry.atom:summary: How to authenticate services and agents to Azure OpenAI using Entra ID, managed identity, and AKS Workload ID.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

API keys are static credentials that must be distributed, rotated, and audited; they are unsuitable for high-assurance environments and agent frameworks at scale. Azure OpenAI supports Microsoft Entra ID authentication, enabling keyless access via managed identities and workload identities. The friction points are: enabling identity where the app is hosted, scoping roles correctly, and handling client capability differences (service vs AKS vs user-interactive).

Options and trade-offs

  • System-assigned managed identity (App Service/Functions/Container Apps): Azure hosts present a managed identity; applications obtain Entra access tokens (DefaultAzureCredential) and call Azure OpenAI via the resource's custom subdomain endpoint. Minimal credential handling; role assignment required ("Cognitive Services OpenAI User").
  • User-assigned managed identity (App Service/ACA/VMs): Provides explicit identity reuse across multiple hosts; requires client_id configuration and role assignment at resource, RG, or subscription scope. Slightly more setup, clearer scoping.
  • AKS Workload Identity: Pods use a Kubernetes service account projected token; a federated identity credential links the service account to a managed identity. This enables short-lived, passwordless authentication to Azure OpenAI from AKS without storing secrets in pods. Requires enabling OIDC issuer, Workload Identity, service account annotations, and pod labeling.
  • User-delegated (interactive apps): Use user-based authentication in frontends/worker apps; appropriate when the user context is required (for example, per-user metering or consent). More complexity around token flows, less suitable for daemon agents.

Minimal working example

Prereqs

  • .NET 8 or Python 3.9+, Azure.Identity 1.10+ and Azure.AI.OpenAI/Microsoft.Extensions.AI for .NET, or openai 1.x with azure-identity for Python.
  • Azure OpenAI resource with a custom subdomain endpoint (required for Entra tokens).
  • Role: Cognitive Services OpenAI User assigned to the identity at the resource scope.

    • A) .NET (App Service with system-assigned MI) Packages: Azure.Identity, Azure.AI.OpenAI, Microsoft.Extensions.AI

using Azure.Identity;
using Azure.AI.OpenAI;

var credential = new DefaultAzureCredential();
var client = new OpenAIClient(new Uri("https://YOUR-RESOURCE.openai.azure.com/"), credential);

var resp = await client.GetChatCompletionsAsync("gpt-4o", new ChatCompletionsOptions
{
    Messages = { new ChatMessage(ChatRole.User, "Hello from Entra auth!") }
});
Console.WriteLine(resp.Value.Choices[0].Message.Content);

Test: Deploy to App Service with identity enabled; assign Cognitive Services OpenAI User on the OpenAI resource; call endpoint and inspect server logs for successful token acquisition. B) AKS Workload Identity (secure access sample) Steps: Enable OIDC issuer and Workload Identity; create user-assigned MI; create federated credential; annotate service account; label pods. Pod manifest snippet:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: ai-service
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: ai-service
        azure.workload.identity/use: "true"
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: workload-identity-sa
      containers:
      - name: ai-service
        image: ghcr.io/azure-samples/aks-store-demo/ai-service:latest
        env:
        - name: USE_AZURE_OPENAI
          value: "True"
        - name: USE_AZURE_AD
          value: "True"
        - name: AZURE_OPENAI_DEPLOYMENT_NAME
          value: "DEPLOYMENT"
        - name: AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT
          value: "https://YOUR-RESOURCE.openai.azure.com/"

Test: kubectl apply; confirm tokens acquired via Workload ID; verify successful calls to Azure OpenAI.

Checklist

  • Use the OpenAI resource's custom subdomain endpoint for Entra tokens.
  • Assign the Cognitive Services OpenAI User role to the managed identity at the correct scope.
  • On AKS, enable Workload Identity and OIDC issuer; configure service account annotations and azure.workload.identity/use label.
  • Prefer DefaultAzureCredential for host portability; provide client_id for user-assigned MI.
  • Map workloads to least-privilege scopes (resource vs RG vs subscription).

Where this doesn't apply

Purely external, non-Azure hosting lacking managed identity support; use service principals with key vault-backed secrets only as a transitional measure (with rotation and audit).

Sources

  • Authenticate an Azure hosted .NET app to Azure OpenAI using Entra ID (GA)
  • Foundry (classic) Entra auth for Azure OpenAI (GA)
  • Secure access to Azure OpenAI from AKS (GA)

---

atom:entry.atom:title: A Playbook for GenAI Latency on Intel Hardware
atom:entry.atom:summary: A decision framework for latency and memory budgets and for defaults on caching, device selection, and KV-cache limits, with the evidence recorded for each…
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Teams adopting OpenVINO for generative workloads meet the same set of switches: compiled-model caching, prefix caching, device selection, KV-cache sizing, and device-specific properties. Each can help. Switched on in different combinations by different people, they produce behavior that nobody can explain.

A playbook turns those switches into decisions with owners and evidence. It starts from budgets, derives defaults from measurements, and records for each default what was measured and on which hardware.

The friction points are deciding the budgets, keeping defaults tied to evidence, and reviewing them when software or hardware changes.

Options and trade-offs

  • Budgets: define time to first token at a stated percentile, throughput, and a memory limit for each service. Without a target, tuning has no end.
  • Cold-start policy: use compiled-model caching where devices support it, and verify it with the capability check and the output comparison from earlier in the series.
  • Device policy: choose explicit devices for predictable behavior, use AUTO where portability matters, and log the executing device. AUTO may serve early requests on the CPU unless a cached model exists for the better device.
  • Memory policy: set the KV-cache size explicitly, keep prefix caching on for conversational traffic, limit prompt size and concurrency at the gateway, and define what happens to an oversize request.
  • NPU gate: require a compile smoke test, a recorded driver version, a list of the device's supported properties, and a CPU fallback before enabling the NPU for users.
  • Evidence rule: every default points to a measurement with the hardware and versions it came from. A default without evidence is a guess and should be labeled as one.
  • Recommendation: write the playbook as configuration plus a short decision table in your repository, not as a document nobody reads. Each setting gets a reason, an owner, and a link to the measurement that justified it. Review it whenever OpenVINO or Model Server versions, models, hardware, or traffic change.
  • Decision flow in four questions: Is cold start a risk? Enable caching and verify it. Are contexts long or repeated? Keep prefix caching on and set an explicit KV limit. Is an NPU planned? Pass the readiness checklist first. Do you need portability across machines? Use AUTO for routing and log where work ran.
  • Decision lens: consistency and defensibility. Example setup: a platform team with one configuration repository, a benchmark job that reruns the key tests on each version upgrade, and a one-page decision flow that new services follow.

Minimal working example

Prereqs

  • Results from the earlier articles for the services you run.
  • A repository or folder where configuration and results files can live together.

defaults.yaml (outline of a policy file; fill every value from your own measurements)

service: chat-assistant
budget:
  ttft_p95_seconds: <your target>
  memory_limit_gb: <your limit>
caching:
  compiled_model_cache: true
  cache_path: /var/cache/ov/<ov-version>/<model-version>/<device>
  evidence: results/cold-vs-cached.md
device:
  strategy: explicit   # or auto
  log_execution_device: true
  evidence: results/device-strategy.md
kv_cache:
  cache_size_gb: <from observation>
  prefix_caching: true
  overflow_behavior: reject-with-message
  evidence: results/kv-cache.md

Every evidence entry should point to a results file you produced from the earlier articles.

Adjust file names, model names, and paths to your own setup.

Test: Pick one default in defaults.yaml and find the results file that justifies it. Upgrade OpenVINO or Model Server in a test environment and rerun the relevant measurement. If the numbers changed, update the default and its evidence. A default you cannot link to a measurement should be marked as a guess.

Record: the budget for each service; cold start before and after the caching policy; first-token percentile before and after the memory policy; the device strategy outcome on your hardware; the result of the rerun after the last upgrade; the evidence file for every default.

Checklist

  • Define budgets for each service.
  • Enable and verify compiled-model caching, with an output comparison for warm starts.
  • Choose a device policy and log the executing device.
  • Set an explicit KV-cache limit from observation.
  • Require a readiness checklist for the NPU, attach evidence to every default, and review after upgrades.
  • Avoid: copying another team's defaults without measuring.
  • Avoid: tuning without budgets.

Where this doesn't apply

Small experiments on one machine where defaults are adequate, and teams that cannot run repeatable measurements.

Sources

  • OpenVINO Model Caching Overview
  • Automatic Device Selection documentation
  • Model Server performance tuning guide
  • OpenVINO Model Server parameters
  • OpenVINO NPU device documentation
  • onnxruntime-openvino on PyPI

atom:entry.atom:title: Starting a Local Data Pipeline in the Right Order
atom:entry.atom:summary: How I use Compose profiles, health-gated startup and hard resource caps so a multi-service stack boots predictably and does not eat my machine.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Everyone has had the local stack that mostly works. The database is still initialising when the API connects, a worker grabs a port something else expected, and a few minutes later the fans are screaming because three containers decided they own every core. None of this is exotic. It comes from three habits: relying on start order instead of readiness, letting ports be whatever they turn out to be, and leaving resource limits at their defaults. All three are cheap to fix in a Compose file.

Options and trade-offs

  • Fixed sleeps in an entrypoint: easy to write, wrong on a slow day and wasteful on a fast one.
  • Wait-for scripts: they work, but you maintain a script per dependency and each one hides a different definition of ready.
  • Healthchecks plus depends_on with condition service_healthy: Compose does the waiting, and readiness is defined once, next to the service it describes.

My recommendation

I keep a small default stack (database and API) and put the heavy pipeline workers behind a profile, so day-to-day work does not pay for ETL. Every service gets a real healthcheck, downstream services wait on health rather than on container start, ports are bound to 127.0.0.1 and written down, and each service has a CPU and memory ceiling.

Worked example

The example below starts a Postgres database and an API by default. The worker only starts when you ask for the etl profile, and it will not start until the database reports healthy.

services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: local-only-password
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:5433:5432"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.0"
          memory: 512M

  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8080:8080"
    environment:
      DB_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/postgres
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.0"
          memory: 512M

  etl-worker:
    build: ./worker
    profiles: ["etl"]
    environment:
      DB_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/postgres
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "0.5"
          memory: 256M

Start the base stack and wait until everything is healthy, then add the pipeline when you need it:

docker compose up -d --wait
docker compose --profile etl up -d
docker compose ps
docker stats --no-stream

The last command is the quick check that the limits are actually applied. If a container sits at its memory ceiling, that is information, not a bug in the cap.

Checklist

  1. Put a real readiness check on every service that others depend on.
  2. Use condition: service_healthy instead of sleeps or start-order assumptions.
  3. Bind ports explicitly, to 127.0.0.1, and keep them in a small documented range.
  4. Set CPU and memory limits on every service, and make workers back off or fail with a clear message when they hit them.
  5. Mark throwaway volumes clearly and prune them on a schedule.

Where this doesn't apply

This is a local-development pattern. Profiles are a convenience that can drift from how the real system is orchestrated, so do not treat a passing local stack as proof that production wiring is right.

One honest limitation

Healthchecks add startup time, and a heavy check makes it worse. Keep them to a cheap probe, and remember that a limit set too low turns a slow job into an out-of-memory kill.

Sources

  • Docker Docs: Control startup and shutdown order in Compose
  • Docker Docs: Using profiles with Compose
  • Docker Docs: Compose deploy specification (resources)

atom:entry.atom:title: Java 8 to 17 in a Multi-Module Build
atom:entry.atom:summary: Using `--release`, Gradle toolchains, and a bytecode gate to upgrade one module at a time
atom:entry.atom:content:
The problem: producers and consumers upgrade at different speeds

  • A producer compiles with JDK 17 and publishes Java 17 class files (major version 61). A consumer on JDK 11 (which reads up to major version 55) gets UnsupportedClassVersionError.
  • Gradle notices first. Each published variant declares the Java version it supports, and a consumer asking for Java 11 refuses a Java 17 variant with an "incompatible" resolution error.
  • Hidden transitive dependencies or build plugins still assume Java 8 and fail on a newer toolchain.

The pattern: build with the new JDK, target the old bytecode

// build.gradle.kts (producer library)
plugins { `java-library` }

java {
    toolchain { languageVersion.set(JavaLanguageVersion.of(17)) }   // compile with JDK 17
}

tasks.withType<JavaCompile>().configureEach {
    options.release.set(11)    // emit Java 11 bytecode and restrict APIs to Java 11
}
  • It sets the class-file version, so consumers on Java 11 can load the jar.
  • It limits you to the Java 11 API surface, so you cannot accidentally call a Java 17-only method. With plain -source/-target you could compile against JDK 17's class library and fail at runtime on an older JVM.

The consumer side

// build.gradle.kts (consumer app)
java { toolchain { languageVersion.set(JavaLanguageVersion.of(11)) } }
dependencies { implementation(project(":producer")) }   // or a published artifact

A rollout sequence that works

  1. Inventory consumers, including transitive ones. This step catches most surprises. Search your dependency graph, not just your team's repos.
  2. Unlock producers with the toolchain and release pattern above. Nothing changes for consumers.
  3. Gate CI so no module accidentally publishes newer bytecode than planned (see below).
  4. Upgrade consumers one at a time, starting with leaf services.
  5. Raise release in producers once nobody depends on the older level.
  6. Upgrade build plugins early. Old Gradle plugins and annotation processors are the most common blockers.

Enforce it with a bytecode gate

import java.io.DataInputStream;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.util.zip.ZipEntry;
import java.util.zip.ZipFile;

public final class BytecodeLevelCheck {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        String jarPath = args[0];
        int maxMajor = Integer.parseInt(args[1]);
        int worst = 0;

        try (ZipFile zip = new ZipFile(jarPath)) {
            var entries = zip.entries();
            while (entries.hasMoreElements()) {
                ZipEntry entry = entries.nextElement();
                if (!entry.getName().endsWith(".class") || entry.getName().startsWith("META-INF/versions/")) {
                    continue;
                }
                try (var in = new DataInputStream(zip.getInputStream(entry))) {
                    in.readInt();                       // magic 0xCAFEBABE
                    in.readUnsignedShort();             // minor
                    worst = Math.max(worst, in.readUnsignedShort());   // major
                }
            }
        }
        if (worst > maxMajor) {
            System.err.println("Bytecode major " + worst + " exceeds allowed " + maxMajor);
            System.exit(1);
        }
        System.out.println("OK: highest major version " + worst);
    }
}

Reproducing the problem in a toy project

Failure modes to expect

  • A dependency compiled for Java 8 that uses internal APIs removed in later JDKs.
  • Build plugins that read JDK internals reflectively and break on newer versions (look for InaccessibleObjectException).
  • Containers and JVM flags: some legacy GC flags are removed or ignored after Java 8, so audit your startup options.

What you gain

Takeaways

  • Separate the compile JDK from the bytecode target with a toolchain plus options.release.
  • Inventory transitive consumers first, because the graph decides your pace.
  • Add a bytecode gate to CI so a policy becomes a failing build.

atom:entry.atom:title: Using OCI Instance Principals without leaking credentials
atom:entry.atom:summary: How I let workloads call OCI APIs with no API keys on disk, and keep the blast radius small.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Every OCI SDK sample starts the same way: drop an API key and a config file on the host. That is fine on a laptop. On a fleet of compute instances it becomes a quiet liability, because those keys never expire on their own, they get copied into images, and nobody remembers which ones are still in use.

Instance principals remove that whole class of problem. The instance proves who it is with a certificate that OCI issues and rotates for it, and IAM decides what it may do through a dynamic group and a policy. There is nothing to ship, nothing to rotate by hand, and nothing to leak from a config file.

Options and trade-offs

  • API keys in a config file: the simplest option, but it leaves a long-lived secret on disk and puts rotation on you.
  • Session or delegation tokens: shorter lived, but you still have to mint, distribute and refresh them from somewhere.
  • Instance principals with a dynamic group: no client-side secret at all. The cost is that you have to think carefully about which instances land in the group.

My recommendation

For code running on OCI compute, I make instance principals the default and write the dynamic group rule before anything else. The rule should name a compartment and a tag, and the policy should name a compartment, a resource family and, where it is practical, a single bucket. Tenancy-wide verbs are the exception and need a reason.

Worked example

The Java below runs only on an instance that belongs to the dynamic group. It reads from one bucket and has no credentials in code, environment variables or files. The namespace and bucket name come from configuration.

import com.oracle.bmc.auth.InstancePrincipalsAuthenticationDetailsProvider;
import com.oracle.bmc.objectstorage.ObjectStorageClient;
import com.oracle.bmc.objectstorage.requests.ListObjectsRequest;
 
public class ListConfigObjects {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        var provider = InstancePrincipalsAuthenticationDetailsProvider.builder().build();
        try (var os = ObjectStorageClient.builder().build(provider)) {
            var req = ListObjectsRequest.builder()
                    .namespaceName(System.getenv("OCI_NAMESPACE"))
                    .bucketName(System.getenv("CONFIG_BUCKET"))
                    .build();
            os.listObjects(req).getListObjects().getObjects()
              .forEach(o -> System.out.println(o.getName()));
        }
    }
}

The matching rule and policy for the dynamic group. The tag makes membership an explicit decision rather than a side effect of where an instance was created.

ALL {instance.compartment.id = '<apps_compartment_ocid>',
     tag.department.runtime.value = 'payments'}
 
Allow dynamic-group app-runtimes to read objects in compartment apps
  where target.bucket.name = 'app-config'
Allow dynamic-group app-runtimes to use log-content in compartment apps

If your dynamic group lives in a non-default identity domain, prefix the group name with the domain, for example dynamic-group MyDomain/app-runtimes.

Checklist

  1. Write the dynamic group rule with both a compartment and a tag.
  2. Grant the narrowest verb and resource family, and add a bucket or resource condition where you can.
  3. Remove every API key and config file from the host once the SDK uses the instance principal provider.
  4. Review the audit log and confirm the principal on each call is the instance you expected.
  5. Control who can apply the tag, because tagging an instance is what adds it to the group.
  6. Write down the rollback: edit the rule, then adjust the policy.

Where this doesn't apply

Serverless functions and other managed resources have their own identity, so use resource principals there. Anything running outside OCI has no instance principal at all and needs a different authentication path.

One honest limitation

Anyone who can get a shell on the instance inherits its permissions. Instance principals take away the secret, not the access, so SSH access and the policy have to be designed together.

Sources

  • OCI Documentation: Calling Services from an Instance
  • OCI Documentation: Managing Dynamic Groups
  • OCI Documentation: OCI SDK for Java, Instance Principals authentication

atom:entry.atom:title: Build a Scoped Bot: GitHub Apps and Octokit, the Right Way
atom:entry.atom:summary: How to authenticate a GitHub App as an installation, limit it to specific repositories and permissions, and use short-lived tokens.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Personal access tokens are broad. They grant access across every repository the account can reach. GitHub Apps define explicit permissions, install on chosen repositories, and issue installation tokens that expire. Octokit libraries handle token generation and refresh, and actions/create-github-app-token creates scoped tokens inside CI.

Options and trade-offs

  • GitHub App versus OAuth app: Apps offer per-permission and per-repository control. OAuth relies on user-granted scopes.
  • Octokit versus manual token handling: Octokit handles installation tokens and refresh. Manual handling gives more control and more code to maintain.
  • CI token action: mints a scoped token for each job, so you avoid a broad long-lived credential.

My take

Give the app the smallest permission that does the job, install it only on the repositories it needs, and avoid write access to contents unless the bot must change code.

Decision lens: security risk and maintenance cost.

Example setup: a triage bot installed on two repositories with issue write access only. Each CI run mints a token limited to those repositories, adds a comment or label, and never gets contents write access.

Template

src/appClient.js:

import { Octokit } from "@octokit/core";
import { createAppAuth } from "@octokit/auth-app";

export function installationOctokit(appId, privateKey, installationId) {
  return new Octokit({
    authStrategy: createAppAuth,
    auth: { appId, privateKey, installationId }
  });
}

CI: use actions/create-github-app-token with the narrowest permissions and repository list the job needs. Check its README for the current input names.

Checklist

  1. Register a GitHub App and generate a private key.
  2. Set the minimum permissions the bot needs.
  3. Install the app on the target repositories only.
  4. Use Octokit's app authentication for installation tokens.
  5. Mint scoped tokens in CI for each job.
  6. Avoid long-lived personal tokens.

Common mistakes

  • Granting contents write when only issue write is needed.
  • Using a personal access token, which gives the bot a wider blast radius.
  • Assuming tokens never expire. Installation tokens are short-lived, so refresh them.

Where this doesn't apply

  • Organizations that do not allow GitHub Apps or require a different authentication flow.

How to get involved

  • Good first issue: reduce the permissions of an existing bot and add repository scoping.
  • Discussion: what else should a triage bot be allowed to do?

Sources

  • Generating an installation access token for a GitHub App: https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/generating-an-installation-access-token-for-a-github-app. Installation tokens, permissions, and expiry.
  • Authenticating as a GitHub App installation: https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/authenticating-as-a-github-app-installation.
  • Octokit.js: https://github.com/octokit/octokit.js/. App authentication and installation behavior.
  • create-github-app-token action: https://github.com/actions/create-github-app-token.

atom:entry.atom:title: NPU Readiness: A Pre-Ship Checklist for Intel Core Ultra
atom:entry.atom:summary: A checklist built from the OpenVINO NPU documentation and plugin README: platform and driver, static shapes, compiled-model caching, and how to list the…
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

The neural processing unit introduced with Intel Core Ultra processors is a low-power device for AI inference. OpenVINO exposes it as the NPU device, but it has requirements and limits that the CPU and GPU do not.

Teams meet the same surprises: a model with dynamic shapes that will not compile, compile times that dwarf the first inference, driver differences between machines, and caching that behaves differently from other devices.

The friction points are driver and platform requirements, the static-shape constraint, and knowing which properties your driver actually exposes.

Options and trade-offs

  • Platform and driver: the NPU needs a supported platform and an NPU driver. Record the driver version with every result, because available properties and behavior depend on it.
  • Static shapes: Intel community guidance and published research on NPU inference state that the NPU in OpenVINO supports models with static shapes. If your model has dynamic dimensions, plan to fix them before compiling, and check the release notes of your OpenVINO version for any newer capability.
  • Driver-level cache: the plugin README and documentation say a user-mode-driver model cache is enabled by default in current NPU drivers to improve time to first inference. OpenVINO's own caching is enabled when you set cache_dir. Read how the two interact in the documentation for your driver and version.
  • Property discovery: instead of relying on remembered property names, ask the device. Querying the NPU device for its supported properties lists what your driver and OpenVINO version expose. Record that list with your results.
  • Compile time: the first compile can take much longer than the first inference. Use compiled-model caching so a restart does not repeat it, and measure it as described in the caching article.
  • Fallback: provide a CPU path for machines where the NPU is absent, the driver is outdated, or compilation fails, and log when the fallback is used.
  • Recommendation: treat NPU support as something your build proves. Add a smoke test that compiles a small static-shape model on the NPU and fails loudly if it cannot, and record the platform, driver, and OpenVINO versions. Fix input shapes before compiling, enable caching, and run twice in separate processes to confirm the second start is faster.
  • Decision lens: whether the NPU is the right target at all. If your model needs dynamic shapes or more memory than the device offers, the CPU or GPU may be simpler. Example setup: a laptop application that runs a small encoder on the NPU for power efficiency and falls back to the CPU if the smoke test fails.

Minimal working example

Prereqs

  • An Intel Core Ultra system with an NPU and a current NPU driver.
  • Python 3 with the openvino package installed.
  • A static-shape model.

npu_probe.py

import sys, time
import openvino as ov

core = ov.Core()
print("Devices:", core.available_devices)
if "NPU" not in core.available_devices:
    sys.exit("No NPU found; use the CPU fallback")

print("NPU supported properties:")
for prop in core.get_property("NPU", "SUPPORTED_PROPERTIES"):
    print(" ", prop)

core.set_property({"CACHE_DIR": "./npu_cache"})
start = time.perf_counter()
compiled = core.compile_model(sys.argv[1], "NPU")  # a static-shape model
print(f"compile on NPU: {time.perf_counter() - start:.3f}s")

Adjust file names, model names, and paths to your own setup.

Test: Run npu_probe.py twice in separate processes and keep the printed property list. Compare compile time between the first and second run. Then try a model with a dynamic dimension and record what the NPU does. If there is no NPU on the machine, the script exits with a message, which is the fallback case your application also needs to handle.

Record: platform, NPU driver version, and OpenVINO version; the property list the NPU reports; compile time with an empty and a populated cache as median and 95th percentile over at least ten fresh processes; first-inference time cold versus cached; behavior with a dynamic-shape model; fallback behavior when the NPU is unavailable.

Checklist

  • Record platform, driver, and OpenVINO versions.
  • Add an NPU compile smoke test to your build.
  • Fix input shapes before compiling.
  • Enable caching and confirm the second start is faster.
  • List the properties the device exposes, provide a logged CPU fallback, and re-run everything after a driver or OpenVINO upgrade.
  • Avoid: compiling a dynamic-shape model and expecting it to work.
  • Avoid: assuming compile time on a developer laptop matches the target machine.

Where this doesn't apply

Machines without an NPU, models that cannot be expressed with static shapes, and workloads where the GPU or CPU already meets latency and power targets.

Sources

  • OpenVINO NPU device documentation
  • Intel NPU plugin README
  • Intel community: NPU supports static shapes
  • NITRO: LLM Inference on Intel Laptop NPUs (arXiv)
  • OpenVINO Model Caching Overview

atom:entry.atom:title: Triage and Ship from the Terminal: gh CLI for Platform Teams
atom:entry.atom:summary: How to use gh CLI to create issues, review and merge pull requests, and rerun workflows, with small scripts that keep the commands consistent.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Platform teams spend much of their day in a shell. The gh CLI covers many everyday GitHub operations: issues, pull requests, projects, releases, and workflow runs. In CI, the GH_TOKEN environment variable provides authentication. With a few scripts, triage and review stop depending on tab-switching.

Options and trade-offs

  • Pull requests: list, check out, review, and merge from the terminal. Fast, but comments need discipline.
  • Issues: create, list, assign, and comment. Templates can be applied through body files.
  • Workflows: run, watch, and rerun. Rerunning only failed jobs saves time.
  • gh api: reach any REST or GraphQL endpoint and filter the output with jq. Powerful, and easy to misuse without authentication.

My take

Write a short list of scripts for the actions you repeat most, keep them in the repository, and teach the team a small core set of commands before introducing anything more complex.

Decision lens: review latency and maintenance cost.

Example setup: three scripts for approving and squash-merging a pull request, rerunning failed jobs, and opening a bug issue from a template, each logging its output to a file for an audit trail.

Template

scripts/approve_and_squash.sh:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
gh pr review "$1" --approve
gh pr merge "$1" --squash --delete-branch

scripts/rerun_failed.sh:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
gh run rerun "$1" --failed
gh run watch "$1"

scripts/new_bug.sh:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
gh issue create --title "$1" --body-file .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug.md --label bug --assignee @me

In CI, set GH_TOKEN so gh commands authenticate.

Checklist

  1. Install gh and run gh auth login.
  2. Set GH_TOKEN in any workflow that calls gh.
  3. Add scripts for pull request review and workflow reruns.
  4. Create issues from templates to keep them consistent.
  5. Log script output for audit trails.
  6. Teach a short list of core commands first.

Common mistakes

  • Missing GH_TOKEN in workflows, so gh calls fail.
  • Merging without deleting the branch, so stale branches pile up.
  • Rerunning an entire workflow when only the failed jobs need it.

Where this doesn't apply

  • Locked-down environments where the CLI is not available.

How to get involved

  • Good first issue: add a script that opens the logs for a failing run.
  • Discussion: which ten gh commands should new team members learn first?

Sources

  • Using GitHub CLI in workflows: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/using-github-cli-in-workflows. GH_TOKEN and examples.
  • gh pr checks manual: https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_pr_checks. Behavior and exit codes.

atom:entry.atom:title: Vision-Language Models: Memory and Latency Testing
atom:entry.atom:summary: Why image and video inputs change serving cost, what to vary and record, and how to find the limits of your own deployment before users do.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

A vision-language model turns images or video frames into tokens and processes them together with text. A handful of frames can contribute far more tokens than an ordinary chat message. That raises both the time to read the prompt and the memory held for it.

As a result, a service that handles video behaves differently from a text chat service even when the same server software runs both. A cache limit chosen from chat traffic may not hold, and neither may a latency target set for text.

The friction points are setting a frame budget, re-sizing memory with video in the mix, and not assuming that features which help text, such as prefix caching, help video.

Options and trade-offs

  • Input types: check the documentation for your OpenVINO GenAI and Model Server versions for which image and video inputs the vision-language pipeline accepts and how frames are sampled. This area changes quickly, so use the documentation for the version you install.
  • Frame budget: limit the number of frames and their resolution per request. Because each frame contributes tokens, this is usually the most direct control over both latency and memory.
  • Cache limit: the Model Server --cache_size option sets KV-cache memory. A limit that works for text-only traffic should be re-examined with video requests in the mix.
  • Prompt reuse: prefix caching reuses work for repeated prompt prefixes. Whether it helps when the changing part of a conversation is video is something to test directly and report either way.
  • Device choice: use --target_device to select a device explicitly, and record the device and driver with every result.
  • Recommendation: treat video as its own workload with its own limits. Choose a frame budget first, then size memory from measurements that include video requests. Measure the same text prompt with no image, one image, several images, and a short clip; the differences are the cost of each input type.
  • Decision lens: input cost versus feature value. Example setup: an internal tool that accepts clips of a few seconds, with a fixed sampling rate, a fixed memory limit, and a clear error message for longer clips.

Minimal working example

Prereqs

  • Model Server serving a vision-language model, set up as its documentation for your version describes.
  • Docker and Python 3 with requests.
  • A sample image and a short video clip.

modality_ladder.py

import time, requests

URL = "http://localhost:8000/v3/chat/completions"
MODEL = "your-vlm-model-name"  # the name you deployed

def ask(content):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    r = requests.post(URL, json={"model": MODEL, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": content}], "max_tokens": 16})
    return r.status_code, round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3)

text = {"type": "text", "text": "Describe what you see."}
print("text only:", ask([text]))
# Add image and frame entries in the format your server version documents,
# then compare request time as you add more of them.

Follow your Model Server version's documentation for the exact request format for images and video frames.

Adjust file names, model names, and paths to your own setup.

Test: Send the same text prompt with no image, one image, several images, and a short clip, at least twenty times each. Watch the server process's memory. Then raise the number of frames until the server refuses or slows sharply, and note where that happens.

Record: model, precision, device, driver, and software versions; frame sampling and resolution; request time per input type as median and 95th percentile; peak memory per input type; the frame count at which the server refuses or slows; whether prefix caching helps with a stable text history and changing video; your chosen frame budget.

Checklist

  • Use the documentation for your exact versions for input formats.
  • Set a frame budget.
  • Re-size memory using video requests.
  • Measure each input type separately and record device and driver with every result.
  • Test prefix reuse with changing video, and return a clear error for inputs over budget.
  • Avoid: sizing memory from text-only traffic.
  • Avoid: assuming prefix caching helps when the changing part is video.

Where this doesn't apply

Text-only services, models or versions without video support, and single-image tools where the cost difference is small.

Sources

  • OpenVINO Model Server parameters
  • Agentic AI with OpenVINO Model Server (example commands)
  • Model Server continuous batching demo
  • Model Server performance tuning guide

atom:entry.atom:title: Zero-Friction Docs: Deploy Static Sites to GitHub Pages with Actions
atom:entry.atom:summary: How to build and deploy a static documentation site with GitHub's Pages actions, using a short workflow and no manual steps.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Static docs should update when the code does. GitHub Pages can deploy from a branch or from a workflow. The Actions-based path uses configure-pages, upload-pages-artifact, and deploy-pages, with explicit permissions and a concurrency group that cancels outdated deploys.

Options and trade-offs

  • Deploy from a branch: the simplest setup, with limited build control. Jekyll runs by default unless you add a .nojekyll file.
  • Deploy with Actions: supports any static site generator and explicit permissions and concurrency controls.
  • Environment protection: require checks before the github-pages environment deploys.

My take

Use the Actions path for any project that needs a build step. Protect the deployment environment so a failing build cannot publish.

Decision lens: maintenance cost and review latency.

Example setup: a documentation site built with a JavaScript toolchain, split into a build job that uploads an artifact and a deploy job that publishes it.

Template

.github/workflows/deploy-pages.yml:

name: Deploy static site to Pages
on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

concurrency:
  group: pages
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/configure-pages@v5
      - name: Build site
        run: |
          npm ci
          npm run build
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: ./dist
  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4

Adjust the build commands and the artifact path for your generator.

README: describe the directory layout and note that Pages should be set to deploy from GitHub Actions.

Checklist

  1. Set Pages to deploy from GitHub Actions.
  2. Add the workflow above and adjust it for your build.
  3. Protect the github-pages environment.
  4. Add .nojekyll if you deploy from a branch with a non-Jekyll generator.
  5. Test the build on a pull request before merging.

Common mistakes

  • Missing the pages and id-token permissions, so the deploy fails.
  • No concurrency group, so an older deploy can overwrite a newer one.
  • Expecting Pages to host dynamic backends. It serves static files only.

Where this doesn't apply

  • Projects that need server-side rendering or a dynamic backend.

How to get involved

  • Good first issue: convert a manual deploy to a Pages workflow.
  • Discussion: which build steps does your docs site need in CI?

Sources

  • Creating a GitHub Pages site: https://docs.github.com/articles/creating-project-pages-manually. Branch versus Actions deployment and .nojekyll.
  • Pages deploy actions: the actions/deploy-pages and actions/upload-pages-artifact repositories on GitHub. Current action versions and inputs.

atom:entry.atom:title: Variable-Length Prompts on an NPU: Designing the Test
atom:entry.atom:summary: How to design a fair experiment for first-token latency on an NPU across prompt lengths: length buckets, padding and chunking strategies, and what to record.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

A language model has to read the whole prompt before it can produce a first token. That prefill step grows with prompt length, so time to first token depends on the prompt lengths your users actually send.

Intel community guidance and published research on NPU inference say that the NPU in OpenVINO works with static shapes. A prompt of varying length does not fit that directly, so a deployment has to choose a strategy: pad to a fixed length, process in fixed-size pieces, or keep several compiled shapes. Newer OpenVINO and GenAI releases may add dedicated support, so read the release notes for your version before designing around the limitation.

The friction points are choosing a strategy, defining prompt-length buckets that match real use, and measuring the tail instead of the average.

Options and trade-offs

  • Pad to one fixed length: simple and compatible with static shapes. Short prompts pay for the padding, so it favors uniform prompt lengths.
  • Fixed-size chunks: process the prompt piece by piece with a chunk size you choose. It avoids padding everything to the longest length, at the cost of more steps for long prompts. Check whether your OpenVINO and GenAI versions provide this directly.
  • Several compiled shapes: keep one compiled model per length bucket and route each request by its prompt length. It is predictable but uses more memory and more cache entries.
  • Streaming: returning tokens as they are generated improves perceived latency but does not shorten prefill, so track perceived first-token time and true first-token time separately.
  • Measurement unit: use prompt-length buckets such as short, medium, long, and very long, defined in tokens. An average across all prompts hides the long-prompt tail that users notice.
  • Recommendation: begin with your real prompt-length distribution; if you have none, make a reasoned guess, label it as a guess, and plan to replace it. Test each strategy your stack supports against every bucket, changing one thing at a time. Adopt a strategy only if it improves the 95th percentile for the buckets that matter, and keep the simpler setup if it does not.
  • Decision lens: user-visible first-token latency versus implementation complexity. Example setup: an assistant whose prompts are mostly short uses a small fixed length, with a separate path for the rare long prompt.

Minimal working example

Prereqs

  • An NPU machine with a language-model stack that runs on the NPU for your OpenVINO version, set up as that version's documentation describes.
  • Python 3 with transformers for the tokenizer.
  • Your model's tokenizer.

make_prompts.py (build prompts of controlled token length)

from transformers import AutoTokenizer

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("your-model-name")  # use your model's tokenizer
filler = "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog. " * 2000
ids = tokenizer(filler)["input_ids"]

buckets = {"short": 64, "medium": 512, "long": 2048}
for name, n in buckets.items():
    prompt = tokenizer.decode(ids[:n])
    print(name, len(tokenizer(prompt)["input_ids"]))

Use the prompts with whichever generation API your stack provides, and record the time from sending the request to the first generated token.

Adjust file names, model names, and paths to your own setup.

Test: Build prompts for each bucket with make_prompts.py. For each strategy your stack supports, warm up, then send at least thirty requests per bucket and record time to first token. Report the median and 95th percentile per bucket, with streaming on and off. Keep every other setting the same between runs.

Record: NPU, driver, OpenVINO, and GenAI versions; model and precision; bucket definitions in tokens; time to first token per bucket and strategy as median and 95th percentile; streaming on versus off; your chosen strategy and the reason.

Checklist

  • Read the release notes for your version about NPU and variable prompts.
  • Define buckets from real or clearly labeled estimated lengths.
  • Warm up before measuring and change one setting per run.
  • Report median and 95th percentile per bucket.
  • Track perceived and true first-token time separately, and keep the simpler strategy when a change does not help.
  • Avoid: averaging across prompt lengths.
  • Avoid: assuming a feature from release notes exists in your installed version.

Where this doesn't apply

Pipelines where all prompts have almost the same length, deployments on CPU or GPU, and versions that provide native handling of variable prompts (follow that documentation instead).

Sources

  • OpenVINO NPU device documentation
  • Intel community: NPU supports static shapes
  • NITRO: LLM Inference on Intel Laptop NPUs (arXiv)
  • Intel NPU plugin README
